title: The Boy Who Glided the Skies
tagline: Beyond that eye, what can you actually see? The injustice in this world, or the sanity we think we all have?

beats.text: The window sticks in damp weather.
You brace one hand on the sill and lean your shoulder into the frame.
Your chair won't get close enough on its own, so you use the brass latch as a handhold.
Below, the alley is a narrow strip of brick, soot, and yesterday's rain.
A pair of chimney swifts cuts over it, black against the pale morning.
The boy is already there.
Oliver Wright crouches by a crate, a screwdriver clenched between his teeth.
You rap the window.
He looks up. "Morning, window ghost."
How do you greet him back?
He grins and turns back to the crate.
It's gone before you can decide who it was for — you, or the bird.
Breakfast comes in a chipped bowl, left on the table by the window.
You drag the tray close with a cord tied to its handle.
Oliver's wearing a coat too big for him. Cracked lenses sit over his eyes, held on with a leather strap.
"Those yours?" you call.
"Borrowed."
Push on it, or let it go?

options.label: "I don't want to know, do I."

beats.text: He lifts the lenses toward a chimney swift. The bird turns, rises, slips between two rooflines.
"What are you looking for?" you ask.
He takes the goggles off. "Evidence."
"Of what?"
He points up, though there's nothing there now but cloud. "That they're doing it properly."
You've watched him for six mornings now.
He never asks what you're doing at the window. No one does.
Oliver nods at your chair. "Is that wheel meant to wobble?"
"It's meant to turn."
"It turns with conviction."
"More than can be said for your coat."
He comes up to the wall below you.
"You could oil the wheel," he says.
"You could mind your own business," or something softer?

options.label: "Maybe I like the sound it makes."

beats.text: "I am," he says. "You're in it."
That one catches you before you can throw anything back.
A cart rattles at the mouth of the alley. Oliver slips behind the rain barrel.
Two constables pass without looking down.
When they're gone, he steps back out, copper wire looped round his wrist.
"Did you see the one with the packet?" he asks.
How much do you admit to noticing?
"Crumbs on his glove," Oliver says. "That's how you know a man's never had to steal his own breakfast."
You lower the spoon. "You steal yours?"
"Sometimes breakfast steals itself."
"That's not an answer."
"It's the one I've got."
By noon the light's crossed the room. Oliver hasn't come back to the alley.
You tap the glass, because there's no reason not to.
He appears below with a sack over one shoulder. "You missed the exciting portion."
"More birds?"
"A pigeon fell off a roof."
"Did it survive?"
"Dignity damaged. Otherwise, yes."
He pulls out a curved sliver of wood, sanded smooth, a row of drilled holes down one side.
"What is that?" you ask.
"A rib."
Tease him, or ask it straight?

options.label: "You've a broken bird in that sack?"

beats.text: He holds the piece to the light. The curve looks almost too thin to trust.
He looks at the chimney, then back at you. "Something that hasn't been named yet."
Next morning he brings a tin cup of tea and sets it on the ledge — too far for you to reach.
He climbs the drainpipe and pushes it closer with one finger.
"If you fall," you say, "I'll tell everyone you were killed by tea."
"Mention the heroic rescue attempt."
He settles below your sill. There's a torn seam in his glove. Underneath, his knuckles are scraped raw.
Say something about his hands, or let it go?

options.label: You decide not to mention it.

beats.text: A sparrow lands on the gutter. He watches it. You watch him watching it.
"You're allowed to blink," you say.
"I'm saving them."
That evening the sky clears enough for the first stars.
Oliver's below, threading wire through the carved rib by the light of a stolen lantern.
"Oliver."
He glances up.
"What happens if it breaks?"
"The rib?"
"The thing you haven't named."
He studies the wire in his fingers. "Then I find out why."
"And if you can't?"
"Then I find someone who can."
He looks up at your window. "It's clear tonight. Come down — I'll show you the roofline properly, from the ground."

options.label: "Alright. Give me a minute with the latch."

lines: Oliver looks up at the dark window, then shrugs. "Ah — well. Night anyway."
He bundles the lantern under his coat and heads off down the alley.
You watch the light bob away between the buildings, then fade.
detour.resumeLine: Later, once the lamps are lit again — you both went out after all, the ordinary way, the next evening. No fuss made of it.

beats.text: A gust moves through the alley. It catches the loose edge of his coat, and for a second he looks smaller than he is.
He climbs until he can pass the lantern up through the window.
His shoulder brushes the side of your chair. He doesn't ask whether you can move back — he just finds the space that exists and works inside it.
The wire straightens under his pliers.
"There," he says.
"That's still crooked," or let him have the win?
"It's a different kind of crooked," he says.
You look past him. The swifts have gone. Above the chimneys, the stars sit clean and unreachable.
Oliver follows your gaze. "Tomorrow," he says, "I'll show you something."
One last line before the window closes.
"A proper invention," he says.
He smiles. This time it stays.
You close the window only after he's climbed down. In the quiet room, the brass wheel of your chair gives a small, answering click as you turn toward the table.
Morning again. The promised invention is waiting on the pavement below your window, wrapped in a blanket that used to be red.
It's tied with string. One corner is patched with a man's necktie.
"You could've brought it through the door," you call.
"The door has opinions."
The door is a door. Do you say so?
"It knows I'm poor," he says.
"Doors don't know things."
"This one's been trained."
He stops with his hand on the string.
"We," he repeats, like he's testing whether the word holds weight.
"It's my window," you say. "I'm entitled to a share of the crime."
He unties the string one knot at a time, the way people do when they've had things taken off them in a hurry before.
The blanket comes away.
It's a frame. Slats and spars, longer than he is tall, curved at both ends like something's been holding its breath inside it.
Every joint is wrapped in cloth. Copper wire binds two of the slats. The rest are held by nails of every size he could find.
"How many times have you built it?" you ask.
"This version?"
"The question."
He squints at the frame. "Fourteen, perhaps."
Fourteen. Perhaps.

options.label: "Perhaps? You've lost count of your own disasters?"

beats.text: "I stopped counting after the first one broke my nose."
"Which one was that?"
"The third. The first two didn't get far enough off the ground to be rude about it."

options.label: "Fourteen. And you're still out here at dawn."

beats.text: He shrugs, which is a thing he does instead of saying yes.
"The fourteenth one taught me something the thirteenth didn't," he says.
"And the fifteenth?"
"Hasn't spoken to me yet."
"You should keep a notebook," you say.
"I have one."
He says it too quickly, then puts his hand flat against his coat, over the inside pocket, as if the notebook might make a run for it.
He's waiting to see whether you'll ask.
He looks at the window. Then at the notebook. Then at the window again.
He climbs three rungs of the drainpipe and holds it up, open, so you can see without touching.
Oil-stained cover. Pages of figures. Curved spars. Lines of force drawn with a straight edge that was probably a butter knife.
One page is a bird, drawn from below. Every feather marked.
"You drew that?"
"The bird didn't volunteer."
He shuts it before you get to the next page. But he let you have that one.
The silence goes on long enough to become a decision.
He takes the notebook out himself.
"You didn't ask," he says, holding it up toward your sill.
"You'd have said no."
"Yes," he agrees, and opens it anyway.
Curved spars. Lines of force. A bird drawn from below with every feather marked, in a hand steadier than any other part of him.
"Nobody owns the sky," he says, tapping the page. "That's the whole argument."
The kitchen door bangs at the far end of the alley.
The landlord's son comes out with a broom. Seventeen, broad, and fond of finding reasons to use his size.
He sees the frame. He kicks one of the slats.
"Move your rubbish."
Oliver catches the frame before it goes over. "It isn't rubbish."
"Everything you own is rubbish."
The broom comes up. Oliver goes very still, and you understand all at once that he has been hit before and has learned not to move first.
Your hand is already on the window latch.
The boy looks up. Finds a girl in a chair at a first-floor window.
He laughs. "You paying for the pavement?"
"No. I'm paying to watch you make a fool of yourself. Do it without damaging the frame."
He works out slowly that there's no version of the next minute where he looks clever.
He mutters something about tongues and windows, and goes.

options.label: "Careful. That's the landlord's drainpipe you're standing on."

beats.text: The boy stops. Looks down at his own boots on the iron bracket.
"So?"
"So when it bends, he'll ask who bent it, and I'll be at this window, as I always am."
You've never threatened anyone before. It turns out to be mostly arithmetic.
He steps off the bracket, calls Oliver a word you won't repeat, and goes.
Oliver waits until the kitchen door shuts. Then he checks every joint, thumb pressing each knot as if listening for a fault beneath the cloth.
"You didn't have to say anything," he tells you.
"I know."
"He might complain about me."
"He complains when the weather changes."
He laughs. His eyes stay on the frame.
You've started noticing when he laughs. After constables pass. When a room goes too quiet. When his stomach makes a sound loud enough to hear through glass.
"Some people," he says, "would call that courage."
"Would they?"
"Courage is when you could run and don't." You tap the arm of the chair. "I'm just sitting here being rude at height."
He doesn't argue. He also doesn't agree, which is worse.

options.label: "It's the only kind I've got left."

beats.text: You didn't plan to say it. It comes out level, which is somehow worse than if it had wobbled.
Oliver doesn't look up at you with that face people make. He keeps his eyes on the knot under his thumb.
"Then it's a good one," he says.
That's all. He goes back to the wire. You breathe again.
"What's it meant to do?" you ask.
His fingers stop.
"It's meant to leave the ground."
The alley seems to shrink around the words. A bucket tips somewhere above you and water threads down the brick.
Leave the ground.
"No."
"A kite, then. A very large, very stupid kite."
"No."
"You're enjoying this."
"I've waited a long time to be asked properly."
He puts the pliers down. That's how you know it's coming.
"A person," he says.
"A person."
"Me. Off the ground. On purpose."
You close the window halfway. Not for the cold. The room has gone suddenly exposed.
"People don't fly."
"I'm aware."
"Birds have wings."
"So will I."
He says it the way a boy tells you he plans to mend a boot. No performance. He hasn't saved the dramatic part for you.
There's only one question left worth asking.
"Above the roofs first."
"And then?"
"Above the clouds."
That one comes out quieter than the others, and you realise he has never said it out loud before. Not to anyone. Not even to the alley.

options.label: "Why does it have to be you?"

beats.text: He thinks about it longer than you expect.
"Because nobody's coming," he says.
"That isn't a reason."
"It's the only one anyone's ever given me for anything."
Then, quieter: "Above the clouds. That's how high. I'd like to see whether it's blue all the way up or whether it stops."
He lifts the frame and carries it toward the abandoned washhouse at the end of the alley. The door has been off its hinges for years.
You take the chair as far as the broken stones allow. The front wheel drops into a gap and the jolt goes straight up your leg, white and immediate.
Oliver turns at once. You raise a hand before he can reach you.
"Don't fuss."
"I wasn't."
"You were thinking about it."
"There's a smoother path round the back," he says. He doesn't offer to push.
The path behind the washhouse runs beside a wall furred with moss.
He goes ahead of you clearing loose bricks out of the ruts with the side of his boot, and never once looks back to check whether you're managing.
Twice the wheel drops into mud. Both times he waits, hands at his sides, until you ask.
You ask once. He lifts. You don't speak about it.
The broken stones take you four minutes and cost you more than you'd admit out loud.
Oliver walks beside you at exactly your pace, talking the entire way about hinges, so that neither of you has to acknowledge what's happening.
When you reach the doorway he says, "The back path is smoother."
"I know."
"Right," he says, and lets it go, which is the kindest thing he's done all week.
Inside, the washhouse smells of wet plaster and rust. Weeds grow through the cracked floor. A patch of sky shows through the high broken window.
He sets the frame beneath a shelf.
The shelf is where he keeps the rest of it. Thin ribs. A bent pulley. A strip of silk. A brass hinge with teeth like a tiny comb.
You reach toward the hinge.
"Careful," he says, faster than he's said anything all morning.
His hand has come halfway out to stop you, and stopped itself.
"Nothing yet."
"It's brass. You don't own brass."
"I own that."
He takes the hinge off the shelf and puts it in his coat pocket, and changes the subject so obviously that it counts as an answer.
You let him have it. You'll remember the hinge for a long time.
"Only dangerous to fingers," he says, too late to be about the hinge.
"Then it's a strange thing to keep on a high shelf."
"Everything I keep is on a high shelf."
He turns the hinge over once, so the little teeth catch the light, and puts it back where it was, facing away from you.
He crouches beside the chair, at eye level, which nobody does.
"I'll make it work," he says.
"You haven't asked whether I think you should."
"I know what you think."
"Do you?"
He looks up at the patch of sky in the broken window. "You think nobody owns it."
Then he puts both hands flat on the frame.

"You're the first person I've told."

You look at the patchwork blanket, the stolen wire, the raw marks on his knuckles. Above him, through the broken window, a gull turns a full circle without moving its wings.

options.label: "Then I believe you. Don't make me regret it."

beats.text: He nods once, hard, like a man taking delivery of something heavy.
"I won't."
"You can't promise that."
"No," he says. "But you can hold me to it, which is nearly the same and much worse for me."
"Probably."
"Don't say it like that."
"How would you like it said?"
"Like something you'd mind."
He goes quiet. Actually quiet, not the performing kind.
"I'll show you the numbers," he says finally. "Every joint. You can tell me where it's wrong."
It isn't a promise to stop. It's the first time he's offered to let anyone check his work.

options.label: "I want to see what's above the clouds."

beats.text: For a second he doesn't answer, and you think you've said the wrong thing to the only person who'd have understood the right one.
"Then I'll go and look," he says, "and come back and tell you."
"That isn't the same."
"No," he says. "It's what I've got."
Neither of you says anything for a while. The gull comes round again.
The light through the broken window moves off the shelf and onto the floor. Somewhere up on the main road a horse is being shouted at.
"I should get you back before they notice the window's open," he says.
"They won't."
"They might."
"Oliver. Nobody notices the window."
He stops in the doorway with the frame's shadow lying across the floor behind him.
"I do," he says.
The last word of the morning is yours.
"I'm at it every day."
"Be at it where I can see."
He grins, and this time you get the whole thing.
He shrugs. "It was already there."
"You cleared it."
"It was in the way," he says, which is not the same as denying it, and walks ahead so he doesn't have to be thanked twice.
That night you lie awake doing arithmetic you have no business doing. Fourteen frames. One boy. No parents, no trade, no coin.
Above the roofs first. Then above the clouds.
You have been at that window for eleven months, and it is the first thing anyone has ever told you first.

guess.text: "You said a proper invention," you remind him. "I guessed a stolen object."
"It's both," he says, from somewhere behind the blanket. "That's what makes it proper."

hope.text: "You said something that flies," you remind him.
There's a pause from behind the blanket.
"I said I'd show you something," he says. "You're the one who guessed the rest."

default.text: "You promised me something," you remind him.
"I did," he says, from somewhere behind the blanket. "I'm about to be held to it."

beats.text: The first sign of trouble is a missing spoon.
You find it under the table, bent nearly in half.
Down the corridor the cook is shouting. "Three days running. Three days, Mrs. Vale. He thinks because the boy's small, nobody sees him."
Oliver is sitting on your floor, trying to fit a brass washer into a hinge. He brought the piece up through the window in his sleeve.
He hasn't looked up once since the shouting started.
"Nothing."
"The spoon's confessing."
"The spoon was already bent."
"It wasn't."
"Is it?" He doesn't look up.
"Someone's bending the cutlery."
"Terrible," he says. "The state of the world."
The washer clicks into the hinge. He turns it once and it holds.
"The washer was free," he says.
"There's no free brass."
"There's free brass if nobody's looking after it."
The shouting stops. Which is worse. Footsteps start along the corridor toward your door.
You have about eight seconds.
He shakes his head. "Too obvious."
"You're covered in coal dust."
"That's camouflage."
"You're standing in a white room."
He looks down at himself. "Excellent camouflage for a ghost."
Then he goes behind the curtain anyway, because he was always going to.

options.label: Point at the curtain. Don't speak.

beats.text: He's behind it before your hand's back on the wheel.
You've never had to explain a plan to him twice. You're not sure that's a comfort.
"The drainpipe's wet."
"Then be careful."
"Then I'd be slow," he says, "and visible, and halfway down a wall when she opens the window to shout at you."
He's right, which is intolerable. He goes behind the curtain instead.
You pull the cord tied to the tray and drag the chair back. The frame goes under your blanket. The hinge goes into your sleeve.
Mrs. Vale comes in with a basket against her hip. Square woman. A red mark across one cheek where the kitchen steam has been at her for thirty years.
"Has the boy been here?"
Behind the curtain, Oliver makes the smallest possible sound. It might be a cough.
"Don't play clever."
"I'm not playing. I'm asking for rules."
"The rule is he took from the kitchen."
"Then search the kitchen."
"I'm asking whether he's been in this room."
It comes out too smooth. You hear it land.
Mrs. Vale doesn't move. "You answered quickly."
"You asked a short question."
"Mm," she says, and comes in another step, and now she's looking at the room instead of at you.
Her eyes go to the gap in the cutlery on your tray, where the spoon should be.

Mrs. Vale comes farther in. The room isn't big enough for her, and your chair, and the frame under the blanket.

Her gaze settles on your knees.

"What's under there?"

You put both hands flat on the blanket.

"My leg."

Her face changes. Not pity. Arithmetic.

"Don't be disgusting."

"You asked."

"The boy steals because people let him."

"Then people should lock their spoons."

She takes a step. Behind the curtain there is no sound at all now, which is how you know he's stopped breathing.

You make yourself look bored. "If you found him, what would you do?"

"Send for the constable."

"For a spoon?"

"For a pattern."

There's a crust of bread under the cloth in her basket. The morning loaf. Still warm enough to smell from here.

"Mrs. Vale," you say. "I took it."
Her eyebrows go up.
"The spoon. I used it to reach something under the coal scuttle. The washer was already mine. I dropped the spoon because the chair caught on the rug."
It's a good lie. Every part of it works.
Every part of it also makes you smaller, and you knew that before you opened your mouth, and you did it anyway.
"You expect me to believe that," she says.
"No."
"Then why say it?"
There are two true answers. Only one of them is safe.

options.label: "Because a constable will ask why a kitchen spoon was in my room."

beats.text: "And?"
"And that takes an hour. You've bread in your basket and you're already late."
She looks down at the basket. That's the whole argument won, and it had nothing to do with justice.

options.label: "Because you'll believe it of me faster than you'd disbelieve it of him."

beats.text: The room gets very quiet.
Mrs. Vale looks at you for a long moment, and something behind her face gives way a little, and you hate that you used it.
"That's an unkind thing to say about yourself," she says.
"It's an unkind house."
Oliver's boot nudges the curtain. You can't see it. You feel it in the floorboards.
Mrs. Vale sighs. "The boy's not worth a beating."
"I didn't say he was."
"You said nothing."
"That's often the difficulty."
She takes the spoon from under the table. "Return it."
"It's bent."
"Then return it bent."
The door shuts with a soft click. Oliver comes out from behind the curtain with his eyes too wide.
"You took the blame."
He's looking at you like you've done something enormous. You'd rather he didn't.
"You said it was yours."
"It was under my blanket."
"That isn't how ownership works."
"It's how rooms work."
He lets it go. He also doesn't stop looking at you.
"Do what?"
"Put me somewhere I have to lie about my own leg to get you out of."
He sits down on the floor. Not the sulking kind. The kind where the legs stop agreeing.
"I didn't know she'd come up here," he says.
"You never know. That's the pattern she meant."
He kneels and pulls the frame out from under the blanket. One of the ribs has split along the grain.
"What happened?"
"Nothing."
"The rib's split."
"It was a weak rib."
"You made it."
"That explains the weakness."
There's a black smear on his wrist. The machine yard again — the one with iron spikes along the wall and a watchman who likes throwing stones.
You could pretend you didn't see the smear.

options.label: "You can't keep stealing from the foundry."

beats.text: "I don't keep stealing."
"You do it repeatedly."
"Is that what keeping means?"
"Oliver."
He sets the cracked rib next to the whole one. The two pieces are nearly identical. "If I stop," he says, "the work stops."
"Then let it stop for a day."
You look at the smear until he notices you looking, which is more effective than the sentence would have been.
He pulls his cuff down over it.
"If I stop going," he says, to the rib and not to you, "the work stops."
"Then let it stop for a day."
"You wouldn't say that about your chair."
The room goes quiet.
Oliver looks up, startled by his own sentence. He reaches for the hinge, then takes his hand back.
"I didn't mean—"
"You meant it," is the true thing. There are others.
"Yes," he says, after a while. He doesn't insult you by taking it back.
"Good."
"Good?"
"Everyone else in this house lies about it. You're at least accurate."
It isn't forgiveness. It's the only currency you've got that doesn't cost him anything.

options.label: "It isn't the same. Mine doesn't get finished."

beats.text: You hadn't planned to say it. It's out before you can stop it, and it's the truest thing in the room.
Oliver goes very still.
"No," he says. "It doesn't."
He doesn't tell you it will. He doesn't tell you doctors are clever now. He doesn't say anything at all for a while, and it is the kindest anyone has been to you in eleven months.
He takes the exit you've given him, gratefully and badly.
"Right. Yes."
He works. You watch. The thing he said sits in the corner of the room all afternoon like a third person nobody's introduced.
You move the chair toward the window. The rear wheel catches on the rug.
You pull harder. Pain goes from your ankle to your hip, white, immediate, familiar.
Oliver stands up.
He hasn't touched the chair. He's waiting to be told.
He stops where he is.
You get the wheel free yourself. The rug bunches under the tyre. For a second the chair tilts and the sill looks a long way off.
"There," you say.
His hands stay at his sides. "You could've asked."
"I could've."
He pulls the rug straight and steps back out of reach, all in about two seconds, so that it never becomes a moment.
The wheel rolls clean.
"Thank you," you say, and it costs you something, and he has the sense not to notice.
Outside, the alley's empty. A scrap of newspaper goes along the gutter and stops against the drain.
"I'm sorry," Oliver says.
"That isn't useful."
"I know."
"Then make a new rib."
He nods and goes, and the apology stays in the room after he's left it.
Near dusk he comes back with the spoon. He's flattened it against a stone.
"Mrs. Vale asked for this."
"It's worse."
"It has character."
You set it beside your bowl. He crouches and looks at the chair's rear wheel.
"The axle's loose."
"I know."
"I can fix it."
You should send him home. His face has a new mark on it that you haven't mentioned.
"With a bolt from the road."
"Roads have bolts?"
"The city's full of generous objects."
You hold the chair steady while he tightens the nut with a little wrench. His fingers move carefully and never once brush the bandage.
"There," he says.
You roll forward. The wheel turns without its old wobble.
"That's better," you admit.
"You're welcome."
"Don't become proud."
"Too late."
"It'll take four minutes."
"You've been up since before the loaf. Go home."
He looks at the wheel the way other people look at a wound they've been told not to touch.
"Tomorrow, then," he says. "It's getting worse. You can hear it from the alley."
You hadn't known it was audible from the alley. You hadn't known he was listening for it.
He goes after dark. From the window you watch him cross the alley with the cracked rib under his coat.
At the wall he stops and looks up.
"What?" you call.
"Nothing."
"You're standing there."
"I'm considering the best route."
"The route's straight."
"That's why it's suspicious."
He's about to go round the corner.
He raises a hand without turning round, which means he heard and won't.
The corner takes him.
You watch until the dark takes the shape of his coat off him and leaves only the rib.
Then that goes too.
You take the flattened spoon off the table. There's a tiny line across the handle where the stone struck it.
The lie hasn't made you noble. It's made the room different. Mrs. Vale will remember it. You'll remember that she knew.
Out on the foundry road a whistle goes. Another one answers, farther off.
You wait at the window with the lamp low, the way you do.
For the first time since the morning he showed you the frame, Oliver doesn't come back before morning.
He comes back at sunrise with a sack of willow strips and a bruise under one eye.
You've been at the window since four. You're not going to tell him that.
The bruise is the colour of a plum and it goes down into his cheek.
"Thank you."
"It wasn't praise."
"I accepted it in the spirit given."
"What happened to your face?"
"A disagreement with a wall."
"Who won?"
"The wall has a better solicitor."
The joke he'd loaded doesn't get used. You watch him put it away.
"Does it matter?"
"It does to me."
"Then a man in a yard coat," he says, "and he was slow, and I'm quick, and it's finished."
"Is it."
"It's finished today," he says, which is a different sentence, and he knows you noticed.
He's been in the washhouse all night. You can tell from the damp black along his cuffs and the way he holds one shoulder stiff.
He tips the sack out onto a folded sheet. Willow strips lie in pale flexible rows.
Beside them he sets the carved rib from the first frame. Then another. Then another. Each one shaped to the same curve.
You count twelve.
"You made all those?"
"Not all this morning."
"I was about to say."
He carries the pieces down while you take the smooth path round the back. The repaired wheel behaves until a stone turns under it.
"May I?" he says, with his hand near the chair's handle and not on it.

options.label: "If you ask again I'll assume you're ill."

beats.text: He takes you over the stone. His grip is light.
He doesn't steer you round the broken floor. He finds a route through it, which is a different thing, and he learned it without being told.
"Right."
He walks beside you instead, at your pace, carrying twelve ribs and saying nothing about the four attempts it takes you to clear the stone.
When you finally get it he says, "You didn't ask me to move it."
"No."
"Good," he says. "I'd have had to put the ribs down."
Inside, the frame has grown.
Two long spars run from a central joint. Ribs curve outward from them like fingers spread under a sheet.
"It needs a second side," Oliver says.
"Most birds have two."
"Some insects have four."
"You're not building an insect."
"Not with that attitude."
The ribs are tied to the spars with linen thread soaked in glue. He's drawn his measurements straight onto the floor in chalk.
"Where did you learn this?"
He shrugs. "Watching."
"Watching what?"
"Anything that stays together."
The first attempt hangs from the rafters on two ropes. He goes up the ladder with a strip of canvas between his teeth.
You hold the ladder's foot, because there's nobody else in the building to do it.
He's four rungs up and the ladder is older than both of you.

options.label: "If you fall, I won't catch you."

beats.text: "You'd catch me with your voice."
"My voice has poor reach."
"You've never used it properly."

options.label: "Come down. Do it from a chair."

beats.text: "There's one chair in this building and you're in it."
"Then borrow one. You're good at that."
He laughs so hard he has to hold the rafter, which is exactly the outcome you were trying to avoid.
"Two more minutes," he says. "I promise the ladder nothing."
He spreads the canvas over the ribs. It's patched out of flour sacks, an old sail, and something that used to be a green curtain.
The wind comes through the broken window. The cloth trembles. The ribs flex.
The wing makes a dry, beautiful creak.
He looks down at you from the ladder with his whole face open, waiting.
"It's remembered how," he says.
You don't have an answer to that, and he comes down the ladder grinning like a man who's won something.
He leans out and pushes the trailing edge with two fingers.
The whole shape breathes. Wood and cloth and one sound.
"Again," you say.
He does it four more times, and neither of you says anything about the fact that you asked.
On the floor the shadow of the frame lies across both of you. It reaches farther than the room.
You touch one of the knots. It's rough under your fingertip.
"What do you sit in?"
He shows you the cradle like it's an ordinary chair. A seat cut from a packing case. Two foot braces. A belt made from a butcher's apron.
"It'll hold one person."
There's a brass hinge at either side of it. You recognise one from the shelf.
"No."
"Safely?"
"That's the next question," he says, in the voice of a man reading out an agenda.

options.label: "That belt won't hold a falling boy."

beats.text: He stops.
"No," he says. "It'll hold a boy who's already stopped falling."
"That's the same belt."
"It's a different boy," he says, and then, before you can be frightened properly: "I'll double it. Two thicknesses. You're right."
He writes it on the floor in chalk while you're watching. BELT — 2. Under it, smaller: M. said.
"You stole those hinges from the machine yard."
"Borrowed."
"The yard sent a man after you."
"He wasn't from the yard."
"He wore its coat."
"People wear many coats," he says, and touches the bruise without meaning to.
"A man who writes things down."
"That's not an answer."
"He asked whose the washhouse was. He asked how long I'd been in it. He didn't ask about the hinges at all."
You put that away somewhere careful. You'll want it later. You don't know yet how much later, or what it'll cost.
You let it go, and he's so grateful he tells you the next part without being asked.
"The first fourteen failed," he says.
"You said fourteen versions."
"Fifteen, if we count the one that never left the drawing."
"What failed?"
"The first collapsed. The second spun. The third went in a pond. The fourth caught fire because I hadn't understood oil. The fifth was eaten by a dog."
"Eaten."
"The canvas."
He's got as far as the sixth. He could do this all morning, and the funny voice he's using isn't funny.
He stops.
"You've been doing this alone for three years," you say.
"Four."
"Four. And you can list them like a shopping account."
"They're my four years," he says. "I'm allowed to be brisk about them."
He gets to fifteen.
Somewhere around the ninth, the funny voice runs out and he just says them, one after another, the way people count things they've buried.
When he's done, neither of you speaks for a while.
"Sixteen, then," you say.
"Sixteen," he agrees.
You wheel to the far wall. Pieces of broken frames lean under a shelf. A bent spar. Three charred ribs. A little wheel missing one spoke.
The failures take up more room than the machine does.
"You kept them."
"Parts can be reused."
"Even the burnt ones?"
"Especially those. They know what not to do."
He crouches and lifts a feather out from between two slats. Grey at the tip, white near the stem.
He holds it the way you'd hold something borrowed.
"A rook."
"Did you hurt it?"
"No. It left."
He puts the feather down on the floor with more care than he's shown any of the brass.

options.label: Hold out your hand for it.

beats.text: He gives it over without a word.
It weighs nothing. You'd expected it to weigh something.
"Keep it," he says. "There'll be others. They leave them everywhere. Nobody picks them up."
You put it in the pocket of your dress, and you will still have it in four years, when a great deal else is gone.
"You can't make a bird out of scraps," you say.
"I'm not trying to."
He says it so plainly that you believe him.
The day turns bright and cold. He binds each rib and you pass him the thread, the knife, the glue, from the tray fixed beside your chair.
At midday you notice a small brass plate on the workbench. Filed into a shallow curve. Two tiny hinges along one edge.
"What's that?"
He covers it with his palm. "A part."
"Of the wing?"
"Not exactly."
"Of the cradle?"
"Not exactly."
His hand hasn't moved off it.
"No."
"You're hiding it badly."
"I'm hiding it perfectly. You've merely noticed."
He slides the plate into a wooden box and locks the box with a bent nail, which is not locking anything, and you both know it, and you don't open it.
He looks at you. "That would be a remarkable spoon."
"It's had a remarkable week."
He almost tells you. You watch him get right up to the edge of it — the breath, the half-turn of the plate toward the light.
Then he puts it in a wooden box and locks the box with a bent nail.
"If it's a secret," you say, "it's a poor one."
"Most good ones start that way."
When the last rib is tied he stands back. The wing fills the washhouse. The central spar goes up over his head.
The canvas hangs loose at the trailing edge. One corner has a patch stitched into the shape of a fish.
He takes a running step. The wing shivers in the draught.
"Don't run indoors," you say.
He runs again.
The frame lifts half an inch off its ropes.
It isn't a flap. It's a deep breath made out of cloth and timber.
Oliver stops dead with his eyes on the ceiling.
You laugh before you decide to.
He turns round. "What?"
You haven't made that sound since before the accident. He's heard it. You can see him hearing it.
"You laughed."
"The wing didn't."
"It will."
He puts his hand on the leading spar. The bruise pulls when he smiles and he does it anyway.

options.label: "Do that again and I'll do it again."

beats.text: He runs the length of the washhouse four times.
By the fourth he's laughing too hard to keep straight, and the wing is booming above you both like weather, and neither of you has eaten since yesterday.
It's the best hour of the year. You'll think about it later at some length.
For the first time the machine doesn't look like a heap of stolen objects. It looks like something with an argument to make.
The rain starts after sunset. Water taps through the broken roof. He gets oilcloth over the frame and checks every tie twice.
"You should sleep," you say.
"You should go upstairs."
"I am upstairs."
"Then sleep here."
He's made a narrow place beside the workbench where your chair can turn. He did that at some point and never mentioned it.
You park there. He sits on the floor with his back against the cradle. The rain fills in the silence.
"When it works," you say, "will you tell people your name?"
"Everyone knows my name."
"They know what to call you when they want you gone."
He watches the dark window. "Then I'll give them something else to call me."
"I haven't decided."
"Make sure it isn't foolish."
"That removes several excellent options."

options.label: "They'll call you a thief until the day it flies."

beats.text: "I know."
"And the day after, they'll say they always knew."
"I know that as well," he says. "I've thought about it more than the wing."
The rain goes on. "It doesn't stop me wanting them to," he says, quieter. "That's the humiliating part."
You look at the wing under its oilcloth. A pale rib presses up against the cover like a bone under skin.
Oliver rests his head back against the cradle and is asleep in under a minute, the way people sleep when they've been holding something up for four years.
The bruise is swelling. You haven't told him. He'd only make a joke and then it would be a joke.

options.label: Wet a cloth. Reach as far as you can.

beats.text: It takes you six minutes and most of what you've got, and the cloth ends up folded on the floor by his hand instead of on his face, because you cannot reach that far and there is nobody to ask.
In the morning he'll find it there and put it against his cheek without asking who.
He'll know. He always knows. He never says.
You keep the lamp low and you watch the rain move on the oilcloth until the light changes.
Nothing comes through the door. Nothing was going to.
But somebody in this building ought to be awake while he isn't, and there's only the two of you, and one of you can run.
Twelve ribs. One boy. A belt made out of a butcher's apron, doubled, because you said so.
Above the roofs first. Then above the clouds.
It's the fourth morning in a row you've watched the light come up, and the first one you haven't minded.
The sky stays clear for three days and Oliver spends all three under the washhouse roof.
He's built a bench out of a packing case. One leg is shorter than the others. He's put a folded page of his notebook under it, which means he'd rather sacrifice the page.
He measures things. The spar. The cradle. The distance from the wall to the workbench. The window. The door. The length of your armrest.
On the fourth morning he takes a length of string and puts it round your head.
The string is cold. His knuckles are not.
"I'm testing it."
"Test it further away."
He marks the string with charcoal. "Hold still."
"I am holding still."
"You're glaring."
"That isn't a movement."
"It shifts the measurement."
You hold still.
He's careful about it in a way that takes longer than it needs to, and neither of you mentions that either.
The charcoal mark goes on the string. He measures twice and writes a number down.
He lets go. The string drops round his wrist.
"What's it for?"
"A later problem."
"You're building something for my head."
"I'm building something for a problem near your head."
There's an obvious move available.
You give it seven minutes. He lasts four.
"Are you angry?"
"No."
"That answer sounded angry."
"You've a poor ear."
"I've two."

options.label: "Tell me now or don't measure me again."

beats.text: He puts the string in his pocket.
"Then I won't measure you again," he says, and means it, and you have won absolutely nothing.
Ten minutes later he asks whether he might have the number he already has. You say yes. He writes it down twice.
He goes back to sanding a narrow brass plate. The filing makes a small steady rasp. Outside, a coal cart goes past and the horse slips on the wet stones.
"You could tell me," you say.
"I could."
"You've decided not to."
"For now."
He hasn't looked up from the plate.
"Because if I tell you, you'll ask whether it works."
"Does it?"
"There," he says.
You turn the chair away from the bench. The left wheel knocks the wall.
"It might," he says, softer.
"That isn't an answer."
"It's the only honest one."
The rasp stops.
"All right?" he says. "You've never once said all right."
"I'm expanding."
He looks so unsettled by it that he tells you a piece anyway: "It won't be finished this month. It might not work at all. That's why."
"It might, though."
"It might," he says, and goes back to the plate.
He sets the plate down beside the locked box. The two tiny hinges catch the light.
At noon you ask him something he's been avoiding by being busy.
"Where did you sleep before the washhouse?"
He fits a pin into the frame. "Here and there."
"That isn't a place."
"It's several."
He's holding the pin very steady.
"Some."
"Beds?"
"Occasionally."
"People?"
He taps the pin. "Often."
You don't ask which sort of people. You'll wonder about that answer for years.
You wait. He knows you're waiting. He's better at silence than anyone you've met and he still loses.
A fly lands on the canvas and walks across the fish-shaped patch.
"There were four winters of it," he says, to the pin. "I don't keep them in order."
"My mother worked at the thread mill," he says. "My father repaired boilers, when anybody paid him."
"Then the mill closed its upper floor."
"What happened?"
"The roof came down."
He doesn't say whether they were under it.
There's a question in the room and it only has one shape.
"That's how families become stories," he says.
He turns the frame over. A knot has loosened under the spar and he attends to it.
You don't ask the question that would make him tell you where they went afterward.
His hands stop.
It's the first time you've ever seen him caught out, and you'd give a great deal to take it back.
"The mill had a certificate," he says. "Signed by a man who never went up the stairs."
"Oliver—"
"I measure everything," he says, "because somebody didn't."
Then he ties the knot again and the subject is closed like a door in a wind.
"Did you have a different name then?" he asks, after a while.
"No."
"Everyone has a different name somewhere."
"Not everyone."
"Your aunt calls you Mon."
He's got no business knowing that. Your window is open a great deal.

options.label: "She calls me that when she remembers I exist."

beats.text: "Is that why you sit at the window?"
"I sit at the window because the table's too low."
"That's a practical answer."
"You asked a practical question."
"I wasn't going to."
"Why not?"
He thinks about it properly, which is the thing about him.
"Because it's short," he says. "People shorten things they've stopped looking at."
He leans back against the bench. "Do you know why people call me Wright?"
"Because it's your name."
"Because my father was a wright. Woodwork, mostly. He could make a wheel out of a tree and have it turning by supper."
He looks at the glider frame.
"He said anything with a joint could be taught to move."
"Did he teach you?"
"He tried."
It lands without explanation. You pull the chair nearer.

He asks about your leg while the light's still good.

Not with pity. He asks because the bandage has slipped and because he's seen your hand close on the armrest.

"How did it happen?"

options.label: "A carriage overturned. I was inside it."

beats.text: "Whose carriage?"
"Not ours."
"Did anyone pay for it?"
"They sent a letter," you say. "It was very well written."
Something moves behind his face and gets put away for later.

options.label: "The doctor says it's none of your business."

beats.text: "Does he say that about everything?"
"He says it about the leg. He's more forthcoming about the weather."
Oliver nods and asks nothing else about it, then or for two years.
He asks about it in the fourth year, once, and by then you want him to.

options.label: "I don't know how to tell it without making the room smaller."

beats.text: He puts the pin down.
"Then make the room smaller," he says. "I'll sit in it."
So you tell him. Not much of it. The corner, the sound, the weight, the eleven months since.
He doesn't say a single one of the things people say. When you finish he says, "Thank you," which is not on the list at all.
Then he only asks, "Does it hurt now?"
"Yes."
"Does it always?"
"No."
"That's something."
"You're very generous with small things."
"Small things are what I can afford."
He takes the end of the bandage and shows you the frayed edge. "May I?"
Nobody has asked you that. They announce it, or they do it.
He reties it without tightening the cloth. His fingers are warm from the brass plate.
He doesn't look at the scar. He watches the knot.
It takes eight seconds and you'll remember it longer than several years.
"Right," he says, and turns fully round to the bench so that you're not being watched.
He does it without being asked to, and without making a performance of it, and he keeps the rasp going the whole time so the room has a sound in it.
When you're done he doesn't turn back until you speak.
"Can you walk?" he asks.
"Not freely."
He considers this. "Can you stand?"
"For a little while."
"Can you climb?"
He's asking like a man taking stock, not like a man being kind. It's oddly restful.

options.label: "If the building catches fire I'll become very persuasive."

beats.text: His mouth tilts.
"You don't have to answer every question," he says.
"You've spent weeks answering none."
"That's different."
"It's the same sport."

options.label: "No. Not stairs, not ladders, not ever."

beats.text: He takes it the way he takes a measurement.
"Then the door has to widen," he says, "and the bench has to come down four inches, and I'll move the shelf."
"Oliver."
"What?"
"Nothing," you say, because if you say the thing you're thinking you'll cry in a washhouse, and you've decided against that.
Later you find the name scratched into the underside of his bench.
OLIVER WRIGHT. Deep letters, made with a nail rather than a pen.
Underneath, half hidden by the short leg, another line.
DO NOT ASK FOR THE REST.
You could pretend you never got down that far.
"Did you write this?"
He looks under the bench. "No."
"Do you know who did?"
"Perhaps."
"You're becoming irritating."
"That's hereditary."
He sits on the floor to look at the letters. The ribs of the glider throw shadows over his shoulders.
You put your hand flat over the second line, as if the bench might be embarrassed.
He comes past a minute later with a coil of thread, sees where your hand is, and stops.
"You found it."
"I found a bench."
He sits down on the floor next to it, which is the closest he can get to thanking you without using words he doesn't own.
"When I was small, people used to ask where my mother was," he says. "They didn't want the answer."
"What did they want?"
"To decide what sort of boy I was."
You're still holding the string he used to measure your head.
"What sort of boy are you?"
"The sort who measures before cutting."
"That isn't a character."
"It is when you're poor."
At dusk he shuts the washhouse door and checks the alley through the crack.
The constables have started walking in pairs near the foundry road. Their boots leave clean prints in the mud, and the prints go past the washhouse both ways.
He comes back to the bench and opens the locked box.
Inside, the brass plate has been joined to a strip of leather. The tiny hinges flex when he presses them.
You say nothing. He closes the box.
"You may ask," he says.
He's given you permission, which from him is a considerable sum.
"A promise."
"That's worse than a practical answer."
He holds the box against his chest. "It'll be finished when it's ready."
"And if it's dreadful?"
"Then you may tell me."
"I will."
"I know."
That stops him properly.
"You don't want to know?"
"I want you to have one thing in this city that nobody's taken off you yet."
He stands there with the box against his chest for long enough that you look away first.
"It's a promise," he says. "That's all you're getting."
"Then it had better be a good one."
"It's the only one I've made."
He says your name on his way out. "Good night, Monica."
You've heard it hundreds of times from people who needed you to move, wait, eat, listen, or forgive.
In his mouth it sounds like a place he intends to come back to.
The man in the brown coat waits at the end of the alley every morning for a week.
He isn't a constable. Constables wear blue.
This one carries a leather ledger and a brass-tipped cane, and he lets the tip hover above the stones instead of setting it down.
Oliver calls him the Toll Man.
The name arrives already worn in. He's had it for a while.
"Whatever he thinks I owe."
"For walking?"
"For being noticed."

options.label: "How long has he been doing this to you?"

beats.text: Oliver counts it on the spar with his thumb, which means he's counting in months.
"Since the ninth frame."
"That's a year."
"He's patient," Oliver says. "That's what makes him expensive."
The man watches Oliver carry willow into the washhouse, come out with empty pockets, and come back with wire. At noon he writes in the ledger.
You roll nearer the window. The left wheel gives a faint click. Oliver hears it from the alley.
"Don't come outside," he says.
He hasn't looked up.
He smiles without looking up.
"You know what I mean."
"I do," you say, and stay exactly where you are, which is at the window, in full view of the end of the alley.
"Because he writes down what he sees."
"Then let him write me down."
"Monica."
"If I'm in the ledger, I'm in the story," you say. "People are careful with stories that have a girl in them."
He doesn't like it. He also doesn't tell you you're wrong.
On the eighth morning the Toll Man comes into the washhouse.
He ducks under the lintel, though the doorway is tall enough. His coat smells of wet wool and tobacco.
"Oliver Wright," he says.
Oliver keeps working on the cradle. "That's what they call me."
"You've been taking material from the machine yard."
"The machine yard has material."
"You've been seen."
"That's unlucky."
The man's gaze goes across the ribs, the spars, the canvas. Then it finds you.
"And you are?"
He's asked it the way you'd ask about a chair that's been left in a corridor.
His mouth tightens. "I'm asking for your name."
"You heard me."
Oliver puts down the pliers. The washhouse goes very quiet. Even the gulls have stopped arguing on the roof.

options.label: "A tenant of this building. Which is more than you are."

beats.text: "Are you."
"First floor, front. My aunt pays on the second Tuesday."
You watch him decide whether that's true, and whether it matters, and it's the first time all week he's had to decide anything.
Oliver puts down the pliers. The room goes quiet enough to hear the canvas move.
The Toll Man opens the ledger. "The yard has reported missing brass, linen, copper and tools."
"Then the yard should count more carefully," Oliver says.
"You think jokes will help."
"No. I think they're free."
The man taps the ledger with one finger. "There's a fee for unauthorised use of this district's materials."
A fee.
"I collect on behalf of people who prefer not to come into alleys."
"How convenient for them."
"It's convenient for everyone," he says. "That's the design."
He names a figure. It's four times what's in the pocket under your cushion.
"And if it isn't paid?"
"Then the materials come back to the district."
He says materials while looking at the wing, and every man in the room understands him.
He looks at the chair. Then at the bandage under the blanket.
"You've a sharp tongue for someone who can't stand."
Oliver has gone perfectly still.

options.label: "I've had a great deal of practice sitting down."

beats.text: It comes out flat and bored, which is the only way to say it, and it takes something off him.
Then Oliver moves. Not at the man — between him and the workbench.
"Don't talk to her like that."
The Toll Man smiles. "There it is."
"There what is?"
"The reason I found you so quickly."
You let it sit in the room. It's not the worst thing said to you this month and he can tell.
Oliver can't. Oliver moves — not at the man, but between him and the bench.
"Don't talk to her like that."
"There it is," the Toll Man says, and writes something down, and you understand that Oliver has just cost himself more than the brass did.

options.label: "And you've a soft one for a man who does errands."

beats.text: The cane comes up an inch off the floor.
Oliver is between you before it comes down, and he isn't tall enough for it, and he does it anyway.
"Don't talk to her at all," he says.
"There it is," the Toll Man says, delighted. "That's what I came for. Not the brass."
He reaches for the canvas. Oliver catches his wrist.
The cane strikes the floor. Not hard. Once.
Outside, a constable turns the corner.
Oliver lets go.
The constable comes through the door with a hand on his club. The Toll Man steps aside, leaving Oliver standing on his own in the middle of the floor.
"This boy has stolen from the machine yard," he says.
The constable looks at you. "Did you see him?"
Behind Oliver the frame stands with every rib and joint showing. If the constable searches the room, the work is finished. If he takes Oliver, the work is finished.
It's a lie with a clean edge on it. You've got better at these.
"You weren't present," the Toll Man says.
"I'm present now."

options.label: "I saw him working. Every day. From that window."

beats.text: The constable glances up at your window, and at the alley, and at the distance between them, and you watch him find it plausible.
"You weren't in the yard," the Toll Man says.
"Neither was he. That's the point I'm making."
The Toll Man doesn't answer immediately, and the constable notices that he doesn't.
"Several days," he says.
"Then name one."
The Toll Man closes the ledger over one finger.
"You expect a constable to believe a crippled girl over a written report?"

Your hands tighten on the armrests.

The constable's eyes keep going back to the machine. That's the thing to use. Not the boy. Not the leg. The machine, and the fact that a man came for it before the law did.

"I expect him to read the report," you say.

The constable turns his head.

"If it names a tool, ask which tool. If it names a witness, ask where the witness was standing. If it names a boy—"

You let that one wait.

"—ask why the collector arrived before the law."

The constable looks at the ledger.

stakes.onSuccess: The Toll Man closes his ledger without a word and steps back through the door. For tonight, the frame stays in the washhouse.
stakes.onFail: The Toll Man's hand closes on the nearest strut. "Then the report stands," he says, and the constable takes the frame apart, piece by piece, while Oliver watches from the doorway and says nothing at all.

beats.text: The constable asks to see the report. The man turns two pages, slowly.
"The yard's owner doesn't require a formal complaint for recovered property."
Recovered.
"From the boy."
"Then search him."
Oliver looks at you. You don't look back, because if you look back he'll see that you're guessing.
The constable searches his coat. A pencil stub. A button. Bread. A square of blue cloth.
No brass. No tools.
You breathe out through your nose so that nobody hears it.

options.label: "Then it's not a complaint. It's a shopping list."

beats.text: The constable makes a sound that isn't quite a cough.
The Toll Man's face doesn't move at all, which is how you know you've hit something.
"Search the boy," the constable says, "since we're here."
A pencil stub. A button. Bread. A square of blue cloth. No brass. No tools.
"The property's hidden," the Toll Man says. His voice hasn't changed once.
"In my room?"
"It may be."
"Then search it."
He points at the frame instead. "That structure is evidence."
The constable reaches for the leading spar.
"Don't," Oliver says.
The word comes out rough. The hand stops. For one breath all three men look at him as though he's got bigger.
You have about two seconds before the moment turns into something that gets a boy hit.

options.label: "If it breaks, you'll have damaged evidence before proving it's anyone's."

beats.text: The constable withdraws his hand. Slowly, and as if it were his own idea.
Nobody in this alley has ever once been let off by an argument. You file that away.

options.label: "Take it apart, then. Count the pieces against your list."

beats.text: Oliver's head comes round so fast you feel it.

"Every rib is willow off a fence," you say. "Every thread is off a coat lining. There's four brass fittings and he'll say all four are the yard's, and you'll have to write down which four, and then somebody at the yard will have to swear to it in front of a magistrate."
The constable does the arithmetic and decides against his own afternoon.
His hand comes off the spar.
Afterward Oliver says, "You gambled my wing." You say, "I gambled his paperwork." You are both right.
The Toll Man steps toward you. "You're making a mistake."
"I make several a day. You'll have to be specific."
"You're attaching yourself to a thief."
"I'm attached to a chair."
His eyes narrow. "The boy has no property. That frame can be taken under district ordinance."
There is no ordinance. You'd bet the chair on it.
"You know what I mean."
"I know what you want."
The constable looks between you. "Is there an ordinance?"
The Toll Man doesn't answer.
"I beg your pardon?"
"Ordinances have numbers. My father read them out at supper for nine years. Which number is it?"
The silence goes on one beat too long for a man with a ledger.
"Is there an ordinance?" the constable asks him, and this time it isn't a question.
Oliver's hand has closed on the edge of the cradle. He's ready to pick the frame up and run, and there is nowhere in the world to run with a glider twice your size, and he'd still try.
You speak to the constable.
"If you're here as law, take him on a proven charge. If you're here to carry furniture for a man with a ledger, say so plainly."
The Toll Man turns his cane toward the door. "This isn't finished."
"It never is, with men who keep ledgers."
He goes.
The constable stays, looking at the scraps, the frame, and Oliver's split lip.
"You shouldn't build that," he says.
"Why?" Oliver asks.
"Because it won't work."
"Have you tried?"
The constable almost smiles. He's about to say something ordinary and leave.

options.label: "Does keeping out of the yard apply to him as well?"

beats.text: "Just keep out of the machine yard," he'd started to say, and you asked before he finished it.
The almost-smile goes.
He leaves without answering, and that answer is the one you keep.

options.label: "What's his name? The man with the ledger."

beats.text: The constable looks at the doorway the Toll Man went through.
"He's got several," he says.
"Which one's on the ledger?"
"Miss," he says, almost kindly, "the ledger isn't the part that gets written down."
Then: "Keep out of the machine yard," to Oliver, and he goes.
Oliver waits until the boots have faded off the end of the alley. Then he lifts the canvas.
A strip along the trailing edge has been cut. The knife mark is clean and about nine inches long.
"He did that when he came in," Oliver says.
He's holding the two edges together with his thumbs, as if the cloth might reconsider.
"Yes."
"Then mend it."
He sits down on the floor and threads a needle. His hands shake once and then settle.
"You shouldn't have done that," he says.
"I know."
"He'll come back."
"I know."

options.label: "He did it while looking me in the face."

beats.text: "Yes," Oliver says.
"Why?"
"So we'd know he could."
He gets the needle out and sits down on the floor with the canvas in his lap.
"Don't be angry at the cloth," he says. "Cloth mends. Be angry at the seventh of the month, when he'll come back."
By nightfall the cut is sewn shut with thread pulled out of the lining of his coat.
"You'll freeze," you say.
"I've a blanket."
"The blanket belongs to the washhouse."
"It hasn't complained."
There's a pocket sewn under your cushion. There are three coins in it. They're meant for medicine.
He hasn't asked. He'd never ask.

options.label: Put all three on the bench.

beats.text: Oliver stares at them. "No."
"I didn't ask you to take them."
"You need them."
"I need the frame to stay in one piece."
"That's not the same thing."
"It is tonight."
He pushes them back. You push them over. Neither of you speaks until the last of the light has gone off the window.
At the end of it he takes one.
"A loan," he says.
"A bribe."
"For whom?"
"The future."
You keep your hand on the cushion and say nothing, and that is the sensible thing, and it sits in your chest like a swallowed stone.
In the morning there's a coin on your sill.
Not one of yours. A different one, older, worn nearly smooth.
You'll never find out what he sold. You'll ask twice. Both times he'll say the city is full of generous objects.
Outside, the brown coat is gone from the end of the alley.

textByOption.bench: He closes his fingers round it and puts it in the pocket over his chest, with the notebook, where nothing goes that he means to spend.
textByOption.keep: You put the worn coin in the pocket under your cushion, alongside the three you kept. It's the heaviest of the four.

beats.text: The empty place it leaves feels temporary.
The day after the Toll Man goes, Oliver tries to improve your chair.
You find him underneath it with a screwdriver, one knee on the floor and his cheek against the axle.
He hasn't asked. He's under there like a man who's decided a thing is a machine and therefore his.
"I'm inspecting."
"You're trespassing."
"The wheel's making a sound."
"It's always made that sound."
"The sound's changed."
"You've known it a day."
"That's long enough to notice a change."
You grip the armrests and push back. The chair rolls off him. He sits up and hits his head on the table.
"You did that on purpose."
"I did it with purpose."
There's a pause under the chair.
"You knew."
"I've sat on it for eleven months. I know it better than you know your own frame."
"Then why not say?"
"Because the last man who took it apart kept it for nine days," you say, "and I stayed in a bed."
He comes out from under the chair. "Nine days."
"Nine."
"I'll do it in front of you," he says. "You can hold the screws."
"The left bearing's worn," he says, rubbing his forehead.
"So am I. You're not taking me apart to find out where."
"I wasn't going to."
"You were holding a wrench."
"For the wheel."
"That's what you say about everything."
You take the chair out along the wall behind the bakery. Oliver follows with the repaired frame balanced on his shoulder.
The frame catches every breeze. The canvas lifts and drops and lifts. People turn to watch.
A woman with a basket laughs under her breath. A boy throws a pebble that lands near Oliver's boot.
There are three streets of this to go.
"It needs air."
"It needs fewer witnesses."
He angles the frame so it stands between you and the road. The wind presses the canvas flat against his face.
"That's not better," you say.
"I've become a sail."
"A badly made one."
He looks at you sideways. "They're laughing."
"They're looking. Give them something worth it."
So he lifts it over his head and walks the length of the bakery wall with twelve feet of canvas up in the wind, a boy in a torn coat with a wing on.
The woman with the basket stops laughing. She stands there holding it and watches him all the way to the corner.
That's the first one. There'll be others. You've just seen how it starts.
He pivots. The frame catches a drainpipe and brings down a shower of rust over his back.
You laugh.
"I'm pleased," he says. "My suffering has improved your morning."
The route ends at a shallow set of steps. There are five of them. You stop at the bottom.
Oliver sets the frame down.
"We can go around," he says.
"The road's blocked by the coal cart."
"Then we move the coal cart," he says.
The coal cart does not move.
He strains against the wheel until the muscles stand out in his neck. The horse turns its head and regards him with open contempt.
"The horse dislikes you."
"The horse has no imagination."
"It has excellent judgement."

options.label: "Bring it to me. I'll take the brake."

beats.text: You get a hand on the brake lever while he heaves at the wheel.
It moves four inches. Both of you are astonished.
Then it stops again, because a coal cart weighs more than two children and an idea.
"Four inches," he says, breathing hard.
"Write it down. You write everything else down."
A porter shouts from the warehouse door. "Leave it alone, boy."
Oliver steps away from the cart.
You look at the five steps. The nearest ramp is two streets over. The rain has left a slick black line down each stone.
"I can carry the frame up," Oliver says.
"And me?"
He looks at the steps. "I can carry you."
He's fourteen and he weighs less than the frame does.
"I was going to say I can find another route."
"You weren't."
"I thought about it."
"Thinking isn't asking."
He sits down on the bottom step, defeated by the cart, the frame, and your temper.

options.label: "Do you know what happens if you drop me?"

beats.text: "I wouldn't drop you."
"Do you know what happens."
He doesn't answer.
"They put it back in a bed for six weeks and it heals crooked," you say. "That's what happened the second time. There isn't going to be a third."
He sits down on the bottom step and puts his hands over his face for a second, and then takes them away again.
"Right," he says. "Another route, then."
There's a side gate standing open beside the warehouse wall. Narrow. The wheels would fit.
He hasn't seen it. He's looking at the steps like a problem he can solve by being sorry at it.
Oliver picks up the frame. "You saw that?"
"I have eyes."
"So do I."
"You have eyes at five foot four," you say. "Mine are lower and they've had practice."

options.label: Let him look a moment longer.

beats.text: He looks at the steps. He looks at the cart. He looks up at the warehouse roof, which tells you a great deal about how his mind works.
Then he finds the gate himself, and the relief on his face is so complete that you're glad you waited.
"There," he says.
"Well spotted."
"You'd seen it."
"Some time ago," you admit.
The gate opens on a paved yard behind the warehouse. No steps. No cart. A narrow lane on the far side.
Oliver looks back at the stairs.
"Most people would've tried those," he says.
"Most people can."
He starts to answer, and stops.
The stones in the yard are uneven. The repaired wheel complains at every seam. You can't push fast enough to keep pace with him.
So he walks backward, carrying the frame and watching your wheels.
He's going to walk into something.
"You might fall."
"If I fall, I'll tell you."
"You might not have time."
"I have time to shout."
He turns. The frame goes up over his head like a pale unfinished wing.
He gets nine paces before he backs into a stack of empty crates and brings four of them down.
The frame survives. Nothing else in the yard does.
"You could have said," he says, from the floor.
"I could have."
He turns round after that. You don't have to ask twice, or ever again.
At the mouth of the lane he lowers the frame. "I'm sorry."
"For what?"
"The steps."
He's apologised for the steps, a coal cart, a horse, and the weather, and it isn't nine o'clock.

options.label: "Stop apologising for every object that fails to fit me."

beats.text: "You didn't build them," you add.
"No."
He looks down at the frame for a while.
"I can build a ramp," he says.
"For the city?"
"For the places we need."

options.label: "All right. Apology received. Now do something about it."

beats.text: He blinks.
"You want me to move the steps."
"I want you to stop being sorry at things and start measuring them. It's what you're for."
He gets the notebook out right there in the lane and writes down the height of a step in a city he doesn't own an inch of.
"A ramp," he says. "Not for the city. For the places we need."
The phrase stays with you all afternoon. The places we need.
Your room is full of places other people chose.
The bed's against the wall because it leaves room for the landlady to carry coal. The table is low because it belonged to a child.
The window is high because the room was built for somebody who stood.
At the washhouse he lays two boards over the threshold.
"A ramp," he announces.
The boards bow under the chair. One nail stands up out of the wood like a tooth.
He's very pleased with it.
"It's a first version."
"The first version is a trap."
"You're difficult to please."
"I'm difficult to kill."
He looks. He goes the colour of the plaster.
"That would have gone through the tyre," he says.
"It would have gone through the tyre and put me on the floor of a washhouse for an hour while you ran for help nobody's going to give."
He takes the nail out with his fingers. It takes him three tries and it bleeds.
He adds a crosspiece. You test it with one wheel. The board shifts.
Oliver catches the frame of the chair behind you.
You freeze.
"I have you," he says.
"You have the chair."
"I know."
You reverse onto solid ground. The nail head scrapes the tyre. He takes the boards up again without arguing.
"What do you do when something goes wrong?" he asks.
"I complain."
"After that?"
"I find the part of it that can be changed."
"And if nothing can?"
"I change the plan."
He looks at your hands. "That's why you help me."
He's asked it before, sideways. This is the first time straight on.

options.label: "I help you because you turn up at my window with stolen tea."

beats.text: "That's one reason."
"You're trying to make me answer."
"You're trying not to."
"That could be years."
"Then I've years to think of something that doesn't embarrass me."
He lets it go. He'll ask again, and by then you'll have the answer, and it will cost you everything to say it.
You look at the glider. The wing rests against the wall. The canvas has dried stiff in the morning wind.
"You can reach things I can't," you say. "You can climb walls. You can run when the constables come."
"You can take a piece of the world and carry it back."
Oliver's face changes.
"That isn't all I do," he says.
"It's enough."
"Is it?"
You turn the chair toward the window. "Make the wing work."
He does. The next hours go in small repairs. The nail comes out and a bolt goes in. He sands the splintered board. He changes the angle until your wheels cross without slipping.
You test it six times.
On the seventh you stop halfway across and look down at him.
"Don't say anything."
"I was going to say it works."
"That's saying something."
"It works."
You cross the threshold. The chair rolls cleanly into the washhouse for the first time since you met him.
Oliver raises both hands as if you've landed from a great height.
"No applause," you say.
"It was an important journey."
"It was four feet."
"All journeys are measured by difficulty."
"Who taught you that?"
"A horse."
You look at him. "The horse was very wise," he says.
That evening you sit outside the washhouse while he works. Your crutch lies across the chair arms, ready for the short stand you use when the seat's become unbearable.
You stand once. The muscles above your knee shake. The crutch slips on the stone.
Oliver looks over.
He's halfway off the floor already.
He turns back to the frame.
He doesn't look over again, and it costs him something not to, and you can hear it in how carefully he's sewing.
You lower yourself into the chair. Going down takes longer than standing did.
When you're seated the bandage has come loose. You retie it yourself.

options.label: "Watch, then. If it goes wrong I'd rather you'd seen it."

beats.text: He sits back down on his heels and watches, and doesn't move a muscle, and it is the hardest thing you have ever asked anyone to do for you.
You get eleven seconds. Then you go down into the chair, badly, and the crutch clatters.
"Eleven," he says.
"Was it?"
"I counted. It was nine on Tuesday."
You hadn't known he'd counted Tuesday. You look away toward the chimneys for a moment.
The wing creaks under his hands.
"What if it doesn't stop anything?" he asks.
"What?"
"The chair. The ramp. The work."
A cloud goes behind the chimneys. It's the last question of the day and he's asked it with a needle in his hand so he doesn't have to look up.

options.label: "Then we learn what it does stop."

beats.text: The needle goes through the canvas. The point comes out bright and then disappears again.
"That's a good answer," he says.
"It's the only one."

options.label: "It stopped you being alone in a washhouse."

beats.text: He doesn't answer that. He sews eleven stitches without a word.
Then, without looking up: "Say that again some other time. Not tonight."
"Why not tonight?"
"Because I've the needle," he says, "and I'd rather not have to explain my hands."
You can't reach him if he falls off a roof.
You can't chase him through the machine yard. You can't fight the men who decide where poor children are allowed to stand.
You can make them answer you.
For tonight, that's enough.
He picks the abandoned quarry for the first public attempt, because the quarry has a hill, a long clear slope, and no roof to catch the wing.
It also has a crowd by noon.
Somebody has told the factory boys. They stand along the ridge with their caps tilted back, ready to laugh before anything's happened.
Two women from the laundry watch from behind a fence. The Toll Man is nowhere in sight, which doesn't make the place safer.
You sit at the top of the slope with the chair braced against a sack of gravel. Oliver checks the knots.
He's checked the same three knots four times.
"I could."
"That wasn't permission."
"I know."
His hands stop.
"Have I."
"Four."
He looks down the slope for a moment. "They're good knots," he says.
"I know they are."
He does them a fifth time anyway, and you let him, because he's fourteen and about to leave the ground.
He's wearing the leather belt across his chest, doubled, the way you told him.
Over his eyes there's a strip of grey cloth pushed up onto his forehead, ready to pull down if the wind gets bad.
A rag. He's going up in front of forty people with a rag on his face.
And the locked box is still on the bench in the washhouse, with brass in it, and leather, and two little hinges.
You have worked out roughly what's in that box. You worked it out three days ago, at about two in the morning, and you haven't slept properly since.

options.label: "Why aren't you wearing what's in the box?"

beats.text: He goes still with his hands in the rope.
"It isn't finished."
"It's brass and leather and it goes over a face. Wear it."
"It isn't finished," he says again, "and it isn't mine."
Then he pulls the rag down over his eyes and up again to check it runs clean, and doesn't say one word more.
You sit with that. It's the worst thing anyone's ever done for you and he hasn't even done it yet.
You look at the rag on his forehead and you keep your mouth shut, because if you say it out loud he'll know you know, and then he can't give it to you properly.
"What?" he says.
"The cloth's fraying."
"It'll hold."
"It had better," you say, and turn your face into the wind so he can't see it.
Below, a boy on the ridge shouts, "Fly, orphan!"
Oliver bows to the crowd.
The glider has to be dragged to the top of the slope. It takes four boys and Oliver to move it.
None of the four boys will admit they helped. They put their hands on the frame when nobody's looking, then step back and let the hill take the credit.
You hold the launch rope.
Oliver kneels beside the chair. "When I say pull, pull straight."
"I know how rope works."
"You know how to insult rope."
"It's an underrated skill."
His hand rests on the wheel of your chair. He doesn't turn it. He's only steadying himself.
"If the wing tilts left," he says, "let go."
"Let go."
"If it tilts upward?"
"Don't let go."
"You've made the safest instruction very confusing."
He looks down the slope. The grass is bending in a clean line all the way to the quarry floor.
"The wind's good," he says.

options.label: Put your hand over his, on the wheel.

beats.text: He doesn't move it.
Neither of you says anything for four or five seconds, which at fourteen is an extremely long time.
"If it tilts," he says eventually, "let go of the rope. Whichever way. Just let go."
"And if it climbs?"
"Then hold on," he says, "and don't shut your eyes, because I won't be able to see anything and somebody has to."
You can feel the wind on your face. It smells of chalk and wet iron.
Oliver climbs into the cradle. The frame settles round him. The wing goes up on both sides, tall enough to hide the crowd.
For a second he's completely still.
Then the factory boys start up.
"Mad boy. Mad boy. Mad boy."
Forty voices, and he's sitting in a packing case with a rag on his head.
It comes out of you at a volume you didn't know you had.
The ridge falters. Chanting only works on people who mind.
Inside the frame, Oliver starts laughing. You can't see his face. You can see the canvas shaking.

options.label: "Oliver Wright." Just his name, at the crowd.

beats.text: You say it once, clearly, in the direction of the ridge.
Somebody near the fence repeats it, questioning, to the person beside them.
Forty people who came to watch a mad boy now know what he's called, and that's a different afternoon.
From inside the frame: "Monica."
"Yes."
"Thank you."
Oliver raises one hand.
You pull the rope.
The glider moves. It drags at first. The skids bite into the grass.
Then the wind takes the canvas and the whole frame surges.
Oliver shouts something you can't hear.
The left wing lifts. The right follows.
The skids leave the ground.
The crowd goes silent.
It climbs no higher than a man's waist. But it moves through the air, forward, off the earth, for six entire seconds.
The canvas snaps taut. The frame shudders. Oliver's head turns up toward the clouds.
Then the right spar folds.
The wing drops.
The glider hits the slope and comes apart into a rain of wood and brass and canvas.
Oliver is thrown out of the cradle. He rolls once, catches on the lip of a drainage trench, and goes out of sight below the grass.
You push the chair forward. The gravel sack tears loose behind you.
The slope is too steep. Your hands slip off the rims. You get the crutch off your lap and jam it into the ground and the chair veers hard toward the trench and stops.
He's twenty feet below you. One arm is under the spar. The broken wing shifts every time he tries to breathe.
You have no reach. You have no strength that would move a spar.
The crowd is coming down the hill, and the frame can slide before they get here.
The nearest boy is eight feet away. He's the one who shouted about orphans. He's just standing there.

options.label: "If you can laugh, you can pull!"

beats.text: You've got the launch rope hooked round the chair's axle and you're holding the end of it out at him.
"Take the rope!"
The boy stares.
"IF YOU CAN LAUGH, YOU CAN PULL!"
Three hands seize the line.
You have never said that sentence to anybody in your life.
