It comes out cracked and it carries further than the shouting would have.
The boy's face changes. He's about eleven. He looks at the trench, and at your wheels sunk in the grass, and he understands the whole thing in one second flat.
"Bill!" he screams up the hill. "BILL! Rope!"
Three hands seize the line.
You use the voice your father used on porters.
It's astonishing what a voice will do. The boy has the rope in his hands before he's decided to obey.
"Two more," you say. "Behind him. Feet braced."
Three hands seize the line.

Together you lean back. The rope goes tight over the axle and the chair's frame groans and the whole weight of the broken glider comes onto three factory boys and one girl who cannot stand up.

The spar drags an inch through the grass. Then two.

Oliver's arm is still under it.

encounter.onWin: You get him out before the crowd arrives. The frame is ruined. Oliver is not.

beats.text: He crawls clear. Blood is coming from his temple into one eyebrow.
He tries to stand and goes down onto one knee.
You get the chair alongside him, breathless from shouting.
"Don't move," you say.
"I'm not."
"You're attempting to."
"That's different."
The four boys drag the broken spar off. One of them has opened his palm on a wire. He stares at the blood as though it's betrayed him.
Oliver looks at the crowd. They've found their voices again. Some laugh. Some whisper. One of the laundry women crosses herself.
"How long?" he asks.
"What?"
"How long was it up?"
Six. You counted, because somebody had to, because he couldn't see.
His eyes shut.
"Six isn't nothing," you say.
"It's less than seven."
"You haven't earned seven yet."
He opens one eye. "That sounds like a challenge."
"It's a warning."

options.label: "Long enough that nobody up there is laughing about the six seconds."

beats.text: "How many, though."
"Six."
"Six," he repeats, and lies back in the grass and looks at the sky with blood running into his eyebrow.
"Monica," he says. "It held. The whole way. Right up to the spar."
"I know. I was holding the rope."
"It held," he says again, to nobody, and you understand that he is happy, that this is what happy looks like on him, flat on his back on a hill with his arm bleeding.
The Toll Man comes to the ridge once the crowd's begun to leave. He's chosen a clean place to stand, away from the wreck.
"You've made a spectacle," he says.
Oliver presses a hand to his temple. "People enjoy those."
"The quarry owner will charge for the damage."
The quarry has been abandoned for nine years. Everybody standing here knows it.
"He owns the risk."
You turn the chair so he has to address you from the front.
"The frame was on the grass," you say.
"And now it's in pieces."
"That's the usual result of building something."
He doesn't name an object.
"Grass," you offer. "A trench that was already there. Forty pairs of boots that weren't ours."
"You've an answer for everything."
"I've a great deal of time to sit and think of them."
"You encourage him," the Toll Man says.
"You frighten him."
His gaze drops to your bandage and comes back up to your face.
"You cannot protect him from what he is."
Oliver has stopped moving behind you. He's listening.
Oliver reaches for the broken spar. You catch his sleeve.
"Don't," you say.
He lets go. The Toll Man watches the whole gesture, the reach and the catch and the letting go, and files it.
"This will end badly," he says.
"Then you'll have to wait and see."
The Toll Man considers it, which is worse than if he'd sneered.
"A boy who was going to be dead in a ditch at twenty," he says, "whom somebody has now taught to want things."
Behind you, Oliver doesn't make a sound.
"Get off the hill," you say.
He goes. He's got what he came for. It'll be four years before you understand that this was the afternoon he decided how it ends.
The journey back takes an hour. Oliver carries the smallest pieces. The largest are tied to the back of your chair, where they knock against the spokes.
At the quarry gate the boy with the cut palm comes over.
"It went up," he says.
Oliver looks at him.
"Before it broke," the boy adds.
"I know."
"I saw."
Oliver gives him the one brass hinge that survived the fall.
That hinge cost him a bruise and possibly a rib.
The boy stares at it. "What's this?"
"A piece of the next one."
"You need it."
"I need better witnesses."
The boy closes his hand round the hinge.
The boy blinks at you. "Tom."
"Tom what?"
"Tom Ferris."
"Then it's yours, Tom Ferris," you say, "and when they say in the public house that a boy fell off a hill, you'll say what you saw before it broke."
"Yes, miss."
He'll do it, too. Nine months from now, on a night that matters, in front of a woman with a folder.
On the road his steps start to drag.
You offer him the chair. He refuses it, which you knew he would.
You can't carry him. You can't make him admit the limits of his own body.

options.label: Slow the chair down until he's walking beside you.

beats.text: It takes a mile and a half and he never once notices you're doing it.
That's the whole of what you have. It turns out to be enough for a mile and a half.

options.label: Make him talk the whole way, so he doesn't stop.

beats.text: You ask him about the spar. Why it folded. Which grain. What he'd change.
He talks for a mile and a half without a break, and by the end of it he's walking properly again, because a boy explaining a fault has no attention left over for his own ribs.
"You did that deliberately," he says at the alley.
"Did what?"
"Asked me eleven questions."
"You answered them," you say.
In the washhouse he lays the broken frame out across the floor.
The ribs are split. The cradle's missing a brace. The canvas is torn end to end.
He stands over it until the lantern burns low.
"You can stop," you say.
"No."
"That wasn't a command."
"It sounded like one."
He kneels and picks up a folded piece of the wing. Blood from his temple drops onto the cloth.
"You nearly died," you say.
"Nearly is a distance."
"A small one."
He starts untying knots. His hands have gone clumsy.
The needle is on the bench. So is the cloth. So is the water.

options.label: Put the needle in his hand.

beats.text: "You can't sew with your eyes shut."
"I can try."
"Try after you've cleaned the blood."
He looks at you. There's no joke ready.
You hold out the cloth. He takes it.

options.label: Hold out the cloth and nothing else.

beats.text: He looks at it for a long moment, the way he looked at the coins.
"The wing—"
"The wing will be there in the morning. It hasn't anywhere to be."
"Neither have I."
"You have," you say. "You've here. Sit down."
He sits down on the floor by the wheel of your chair and lets you have the side of his face, and neither of you says anything at all for a while.
The first thing that gets repaired tonight is not the wing.
It's the boy.
By morning the quarry has a story.
By noon it has six.
The glider flew. The glider never left the grass. Oliver fell because he was drunk. Oliver fell because he's cursed. There's a demon living in the frame.
And: the girl in the chair pulled the rope and put him in the ground.
That's the one that travels fastest. Of course it is. It's the only version with a villain who can't run away.
A newspaper boy is shouting it outside the bakery. "Cripple girl crashes orphan boy! Read all about the new danger in the skies!"
Oliver throws a washer at him. It misses by a yard and a half.
He's got a bandage across his temple and one arm in a sling made out of the butcher's apron, and he is now looking round the yard for a second washer.
"I was aiming for obscure."
"You were aiming for a newspaper boy and you missed him by a yard."
"I'm one-handed."
"You were one-handed yesterday and you got a spar off a hill."

options.label: Take the second washer out of his hand.

beats.text: He lets you have it, which tells you how much his arm hurts.
"He's twelve," you say.
"He's loud."
"He's twelve and loud and paid a farthing a shout, and none of the words are his."
Oliver looks at the corner where the shouting's coming from. "Whose are they, then."
"Somebody who can spell."
He goes back to the broken cradle and works at it one-handed.
"People are saying I crashed you," you say.
"People say a great many things."
"They say I ought to be arrested."
"For what?" he says, without looking up.
He considers the wreck laid out across the washhouse floor.
"That charge may stand," he says.
"Whose?"
"Ours. Jointly. It'd be a long trial."
"Is that a law?"
"It is if enough people say it in the same street."
He tightens a knot with his teeth. "Then I'd plead guilty," he says, "and ask for the sentence in writing, so I could frame it."
The machine yard sends a messenger before three.
It isn't the Toll Man. It's a thin clerk with spectacles and a sealed letter, and he stands in the doorway as though the floor might be wet.
"Oliver Wright," he says.
Oliver is sitting three feet behind you with his head down.
He doesn't want to be spoken to today. You can hear it in how carefully he isn't breathing.
The clerk looks directly at Oliver.
"He's out of the conversation," you say.
The clerk decides, visibly, that arguing with furniture is beneath him, and addresses the letter instead.

options.label: "Read it to me. He's got a head injury and I've got a memory."

beats.text: "The letter is addressed to Mr. Wright."
"Mr. Wright is fourteen and can't hold a pen this week. I'm his correspondence."
Behind you, Oliver makes a small sound that might be a laugh or might be his arm.
The clerk breaks the seal.
"The yard requires payment for materials recovered from the quarry."
"Recovered from the quarry."
"The machine broke on land belonging to Mr. Bell."
Oliver whispers, "Don't start."
The clerk blinks twice.
"Because it broke in the air," you say, "and landed on the grass, and Mr. Bell has owned neither for nine years."
"I have started," you add, to Oliver, who has his hand over his eyes.
The clerk turns the letter over. There's nothing on the back.
"The sum is stated as a total."
"Then it's not a bill. It's a number somebody liked."
You've learned that from six weeks of the Toll Man. It's astonishing how much of the world runs on a number somebody liked.
The clerk reads on. "Failure to settle will result in the seizure of property."
You look at the wreck on the floor. Split ribs. A cradle missing a brace. Canvas torn end to end.
"What property?"
The clerk's eyes go to Oliver's coat.
"Anything of value."
Oliver laughs, once.
It's the wrong sound. You've heard him laugh at bailiffs and hills and his own broken arm, and this isn't any of those.
The clerk leaves the letter on the bench and goes.
Oliver takes off the sling and reaches for the cradle.
"You're not helping," you say.
"I'm testing the brace."
"With the arm."
"It's a brace test."
He lifts. Pain goes across his face like a shadow across a wall. He puts the wood down.
"The brace is sound," he says.
"Your arm isn't."

options.label: "'My arm is attached' is not a medical opinion."

beats.text: "I hadn't said it yet."
"You were going to."
"I was." He sits down on the sack. "It's attached."
"That's a low standard."
"It's the standard I was raised to."
That lands in the room and stays there, and he goes on scraping wood as though he hasn't noticed what he said.

options.label: "Give me the small pieces. I'll hold. You look."

beats.text: He hesitates for exactly as long as it takes his pride to lose.
Then he puts a length of split spar across your knees, and a wedge in your left hand, and kneels to look along the grain from underneath, where the light is.
You hold wood for an hour and a half. Your arms ache. It's the best hour and a half of the week.
A strip of the old canvas still carries the fish-shaped patch. The rest of the wing is down to ribs and broken thread.
"The right spar was too light," he says.
"The right spar was attached to a flying machine that fell down a hill."
"Both can be true."
He reaches for the black notebook. The cover's muddy from the quarry and several pages have torn loose.
You pick them up off the floor before the damp can have them.
Then he stops. He's been arranging the broken pieces into a pile, and taking them off the pile, and putting them back in the same order, for a quarter of an hour.
"What do I do now?" he says.
He's asking you. Not the room, not the wing. You.

options.label: "Start with the smallest part. It'll give you somewhere to put your hands."

beats.text: He looks at the pile for a long moment.
Then he picks up a single brass washer and turns it over.
"This is the smallest part."
"Then that's where you start."
He cleans it. It takes four minutes and it saves the entire afternoon, because at the end of it his hands have remembered they're for something.

options.label: "Stop. Before the city takes anything else off you."

beats.text: It's the only honest thing you've got and it costs you to say it.
He doesn't answer for a while.
"If I stop," he says, "they were right."
"They'd be wrong and you'd be alive."
"I'd be here." He gestures at the washhouse, the wreck, the letter on the bench. "Here isn't alive. Here is waiting."
You'll think about that sentence for the rest of your life, and you'll never once find the answer to it.

options.label: "Make them laugh again. Then make them sorry."

beats.text: Something comes back into his face that had gone out of it at the quarry gate.
"That's a plan with two halves," he says.
"Most good ones are."
"Which half first?"
"The laughing. It's cheaper."
The rest of the afternoon goes without work. He sits on the bench with the notebook open and the pencil balanced between two fingers and draws nothing at all.
At the end of the lane, the factory boys turn up.
The one with the cut palm isn't among them.
"There he is," one calls. "The sky king."
Another flaps his arms.
Oliver keeps looking at the empty page.
You turn your chair toward the doorway.
"Don't," he says.
"I haven't done anything."
"You're about to."
They come closer. One of them picks the fish patch up off the bench.
"Is this your flag?"
"Put it down," Oliver says.
The boy throws it at his chest.
There are five of them and one door, and behind you is a boy with one working arm who has just been asked whether he'd like to stop.

options.label: "If you're stealing, take something worth stealing."

beats.text: They look at you.
"That cloth's worth less than the boots you walked here in."
They laugh. It isn't kind laughter, but it's pointed at your mouth instead of at him, and that's the whole trick.

options.label: Start listing everything in the room, out loud, with prices.

beats.text: "One tin of oil, threepence. One bench, nailed down. Four broken ribs of willow, no resale."
"What's she doing?" one of them says.
"One wheel, squeaking. One girl, cannot run. One boy, one arm." You look up. "That's the lot. Which are you taking?"
Nobody wants to answer a question with an itemised list in it. They laugh, because laughing's the only exit left, and their attention has come off him entirely.
The tallest one steps toward you. "You think you're clever."
He's close enough now that you can smell the dye works on his jacket.
"You can't even get out of that chair."
"And yet you came inside to hear me."
His mouth opens. Nothing comes out of it.
It stops him the way it stops all of them.
"Why."
"Because I'll be sitting in this doorway every day for the rest of my life," you say, "and I never forget one."
"You can't even get out of that chair."
"I don't need to get out of it to remember you."
Oliver has stood up behind you. His bad arm hangs at his side.
He looks smaller without the frame round him. But the tall boy sees him upright and takes one step back anyway.
"Come on," one of the others says.
They leave the fish patch on the floor.
Oliver shuts the door.
"You didn't have to say that," he says.
That phrase has become his favourite.
"They could have hurt you."
"They could have tried."
"You can't fight."
"I didn't fight."
He picks the patch up and smooths it out across his knee.
"You made them leave."
"They were bored."
"You made them bored."
"A gift," you say.

options.label: "I did, though. You were about to be hit and you'd have let it happen."

beats.text: He stops smoothing the patch.
"It's cheaper than an argument," he says.
"Is that what you've been doing? Your whole life? Sums?"
"It's kept me alive."
"Here isn't alive," you say. "You told me that this afternoon."
He folds the fish patch into a square and puts it in his pocket, and for a while the only sound in the washhouse is the water in the wall.
That night he takes the right spar out of the wreck. The wood's split clean along the grain.
"It was too light."
"You said."
"It needed weight."
"You said it needed to be light."
"It needed to be light in a different direction."
He scrapes the split clean, slowly, as though the wood might say something if he gives it long enough.
The lantern's low. You've been holding a question for eleven hours.
He doesn't look up. "About what?"
"The sky."
"The sky's above us."
"You know what I mean."
He sets the knife down. "No," he says. "I know what they said."
"That's not the same."
"It is when people are laughing."

options.label: Don't ask. He's holding a knife and a bad week.

beats.text: You keep it behind your teeth, and he answers it anyway, because he's been carrying it too.
"If they're right," he says, to the wood, "then I've cost a girl who can't walk two miles of pushing and a bandage, and I'd rather be dead than right about that."
"Oliver."
"So they'd better be wrong," he says. "That's all. It's simpler than it sounds."
"The first frame was never meant to fly far," he says.

textByOption.smallest-part: He's got the cleaned washer in front of him on the bench, set apart from everything else, like the first word of a sentence.
textByOption.stop: He hasn't said yes and he hasn't said no. He's picked up the knife instead, which is the same as an answer.
textByOption.laugh-back: "The laughing half," he says. "I've thought of something. It involves the whole of Tuesday and a great many witnesses."

beats.text: "How far was it meant to fly?"
"Far enough to prove the next one should exist."
In the morning the repaired bearing on your chair starts to squeal. He hears it from the bench.
He looks at the wheel. Then at you.
He is enjoying this far too much for a boy with a head wound.
"It needs oil."
"You said it."
"You gave me the opening."
He stops with his hand halfway to the shelf.
"You've never once said that first."
"I'm told it's good for the soul."
"It's good for the bearing," he says. "Souls are a separate tin."
He takes down a small tin with the label scraped off. You hold the chair steady while he puts one drop on the bearing.
The squeal goes.
"There," he says.
"The chair's famous now."
"It has a reputation."
He goes back to the frame. The new spar is darker wood, heavier, bent by steam over the wash copper. He sets it down beside the broken one.
Two spars on a bench. One that failed and one that hasn't yet.
"It's the first," he says.
Outside, somebody shouts the newspaper story again — the girl, the rope, the danger in the skies.
He doesn't throw a washer this time.

options.label: "Keep the broken one. On the wall."

beats.text: "Why?"
"So that when they tell you it never went up, you can point at the thing that proves it came down."
He hangs the split spar on two nails above the bench.
It's still there four years later. It's the only thing in the washhouse nobody ever tries to sell.
He puts the pencil to the paper.
The next drawing takes up the whole page.
Oliver wakes you before sunrise by tapping the window with a feather.
You get it open three inches. "If that's a bird, it's become very rude."
"Dress warmly."
"I'm in a nightdress."
"Then dress over it."

He's packed bread, two apples, a tin cup, and the blue cloth out of his coat lining. The glider's nowhere in sight. The bruise on his face has gone yellow, which is the colour bruises turn when they've decided to leave.
It is not yet five in the morning.
"Somewhere the sky's bigger."
"The sky's the same size everywhere."
"That's why we have to test it."
He looks down the alley, where there's nothing to look at yet.
"Because there's no work I can do with this arm," he says, "and if I sit in that room another day I'll do something stupid with the knife or the letter."
"So this is the sensible option."
"This is the sensible option," he agrees, holding a feather.
The landlady will object to the chair leaving the building. You tell him to wait.
You fetch your coat, retie the bandage, and use the crutch to stand long enough to reach the latch. It takes eleven minutes. Nobody sees it, which is the point.
Downstairs, Oliver has bribed the landlady with an apple.
It was your apple. It came out of your basket. He had two and both of them were yours.
"It achieved its purpose."
"Its purpose was breakfast."
"Its purpose was a locked door," he says, "and it is now an open one."

options.label: Note it down. Out loud. In front of him.

beats.text: "One apple," you say. "Owed."
"You're keeping accounts on me."
"Somebody in this arrangement should."
"Add it to the ledger," he says. "I'll settle the whole thing at once, when I'm rich and insufferable."
He takes you west, through streets you've never seen.
The chair handles rough pavement badly. He slows every time the wheels hit a seam, and he never once touches the back of it unless you ask.
Morning smoke lies low over the city. Laundry hangs between the buildings. A butcher gets his shutters up. Somewhere a church bell counts out a time nobody else agrees with.
You've been going north for a quarter of an hour to travel west.
"The short way has stairs."
"You remembered."
"I remember most obstacles."
"Only obstacles?"
"Also useful objects." He points out a dumped wheelbarrow, a broken sign, and a length of rope tied to a post, in the order he'd take them.

options.label: "How many routes have you got in your head?"

beats.text: "Out of the alley? Nine."
"Nine."
"Four are no good after rain. Two have a step at the bakery end that's shorter than it looks. One's only usable on Sundays."
You look at the back of his head for a while.
He's fourteen and he's memorised nine routes out of one alley, and he did it without ever mentioning it, and none of them are for him.
At the edge of the city the road goes pale and hard. Grass comes up between the paving stones. The air smells of salt, though the sea is miles from here.
You stop at a rise where the land falls away toward a wide plain.
Oliver takes the blue cloth out of his coat and spreads it under your chair.
It isn't a blanket.
It's a map.
Charcoal and chalk. Roads looping round hills. Rivers marked in thread stitched straight into the fabric. Some places have names. Most don't.
It's the most valuable object either of you owns and he's been sleeping in it.
"I copied it."
"From where?"
"A railway clerk's office."
"Oliver."
"The clerk left the door open."
"Doors are not invitations."
"They're the nearest thing I get," he says.

options.label: Put your finger on the stitched river.

beats.text: The thread's blue and it's been sewn in tiny, careful, terrible stitches.
"Charcoal comes off," he says. "Rivers don't move. So the rivers had to be thread."
"Who taught you to sew?"
"Nobody."
"It shows," you say, and he laughs, and you keep your finger on the river because your hand has started shaking and you'd rather he didn't see it.
The city's a dark knot in the corner. West of it, the plain runs out into empty cloth.
"You've never been here," you say.
"No."
"Then how do you know the land falls?"
"The birds do."
He points at the horizon. Gulls are working the air above the plain, bright against the morning.
"They use the rising air," he says. "See how they turn without losing height?"
You watch. They're circling over something neither of you can see.
He's watching them the way other boys watch a fight.
"They're showing me where to look."
"That's not the same as proof."
"No," he says. "Proof's what you get afterwards, from a hill, with an audience. Looking's free."

options.label: "How many turns before one of them drops?"

beats.text: He looks round at you.
"Nine, on the left one," you say. "I've been counting since we stopped. It hasn't lost an inch."
He doesn't say anything.
"What?"
"Nothing," he says. "Only that I've explained it to four people and you're the first who started counting."
He takes the apples out of the basket and cuts one with a pocketknife. The blade's dull. Every slice comes out crooked.
You eat out of his palm, because the grass is too soft for the wheels and there's nowhere to put a plate.
He holds the pieces without comment. His fingers smell of metal and bread.
"What'll you do, when you fly?" you ask.
"Look."
"At what?"
"Everything."
"That's too much."
"Then I'll choose."
The horizon's a clean line today. Above it the clouds have built into a long white shelf.
"Do you think there's anything above them?" he asks.
He asks it seriously, which is the only way he asks anything.
"Above the rain."
"More sky."
"That isn't an answer."
"You dislike my practical answers."
"They keep me from being comfortable."
"Good," you say, and take the last slice.

options.label: "Cold. Real cold. The kind that doesn't care."

beats.text: "How do you know?"
"Mountains," you say. "They're only tall. There's snow on them in June. Go high enough and the air stops being on your side."
He's quiet for a moment.
"Then I'll need something over my eyes," he says, "and something over my hands."
"Yes."
"Noted," he says, and you find out later he wrote it down that night, in the book, under a heading, and that he'd already made one of the two.
The sun warms the back of your neck.
For once, nobody's asking either of you to move.
A shepherd finds you near midday, with a crooked staff and a dog that's lost an ear.
"Road's a mile back," he says.
"We know," Oliver says.
"Lost?"
"No."
The shepherd studies the cloth under your chair. "Making one?"
"Trying."
The dog sniffs at the brass hinge Oliver's brought along for luck. Oliver lets it.
"That hill ahead floods in winter," the shepherd says. "River cuts through the lower field. There's a stone bridge under the reeds."
He points with the staff. Oliver puts a mark on the map.
A man has just given away something for nothing, out of doors, in daylight. You've not seen it happen in a year.
The shepherd looks genuinely surprised. "No."
"You should. Everybody else charges for everything else."
"Then pay me with the apple."
Oliver hands over the apple. The dog eats it in one bite.
"That was mine," you say.
"The day's full of sacrifices."
The shepherd leans on the staff and tells you, for eleven minutes, everything the land does when nobody's watching it.
Where the wind turns at the elbow of the hill. Which field holds the last of the frost. Where the air comes up off the quarry face warm enough to lift a hawk without a wingbeat.
Oliver writes all of it down. He doesn't interrupt once.
At the end the shepherd says, "Nobody's asked me that," and sounds unsteady about it, and takes the apple as though it settles the debt the other way.
The dog eats it in one bite.
"That was mine," you say.
"The day's full of sacrifices."
The shepherd goes. Oliver lies on his back in the grass beside your chair.
"You'll stain your coat."
"It's survived worse."
He shuts his eyes.
"Are you asleep?"
"No."
"You look asleep."
"I'm practising."
The wind comes across the plain and bends the grass in one long shining wave. The clouds build themselves and take themselves apart above the far hills.
"What do you see?" he asks.
You could tell him about rising air and the shape of the shelf and the nine turns.
"That's what everyone sees."
"Then a second cloud shaped like a badly cooked fish."
"Better."
"A third cloud shaped like a boy who ought to be repairing his machine."
He opens one eye. "That cloud's rude."
"It has conviction."

options.label: "A day I'm going to want back."

beats.text: He opens his eyes.
"Don't do that," he says.
"Do what?"
"Put it in the past while we're in it."
"I'm not."
"You are. You do it with everything good. You start remembering it early so it can't be taken off you."
You don't have an answer for that, because he's right, and because he's fourteen, and because he learned it somewhere worse than you did.
"A cloud shaped like a boot," you say instead.
"That's what everyone sees," he says, and shuts his eyes again, satisfied.
You name clouds until neither of you can remember the names.
On the way home a wheel catches in a rut. The chair stops hard enough to throw your hands off the rims.
Oliver turns.
He's stopped exactly where he is, with his hands out and empty, waiting.
He stays put. "Do you want the chair moved?"
"Yes."
He lifts the front wheels over the rut and steps back. You push. The chair rolls free.
"Thank you."
"You're welcome."
Nine words. Six months ago that would have taken twenty minutes and cost you both something.
"Front wheels," he repeats, and does exactly that, and puts his hands behind his back afterwards like a man proving he isn't holding a card.
You push. The chair rolls free.
"Thank you."
"You're welcome," he says. "That was very nearly pleasant."
"Don't ruin it."
The road slopes gently back toward the city. He walks beside you instead of ahead. The map's tied round his waist and one corner flaps against his hip.
"Today was good," he says.
It was. You'd rather chew glass than say so plainly.
"That part was good."
"The grass was damp."
"Also good."
"Your map's inaccurate."
"It's unfinished."
He doesn't answer straight away.
"Say that again," he says.
"No."
"You've never agreed with me about anything."
"I've agreed with you about the sky," you say, "which is larger than most subjects."
He looks at the line you drew on the cloth beside the plain. It's crooked, but it marks the place where the land opened.
"You added that," he says.
"I was there."
At the edge of the city the factory smoke has got the sunset. He stops under a row of elms and takes the brass plate out of his pocket.
He holds it up against what light's left.
The hinges open. A narrow band of leather runs through them. It's the beginning of something that would go round a head.
It is not the shape of a thing that fits his face. It has never once been that shape.
"Still."
"You're taking a long time."
"Good work does."
"So does bad work."
"I'm trying to avoid that," he says, and puts it away before you can ask anything else.

options.label: "You measured my head with string in May."

beats.text: His hand closes round the plate.
"I measure a lot of things."
"You measured my head."
"Monica."
"You went up a hill with a rag on your face."

"It isn't finished," he says, "and if you make me say what it is before it's finished, you'll have taken the only thing I've got to give anybody," and he puts it in his pocket and walks on, and you let him, and you don't ask again for four years.
At your building he carries the map upstairs while you take the rear passage. He goes slowly. Every time the chair catches, he waits.
In your room he pins the blue cloth up beside the window.
The city takes up one corner of it.
The blank plain is everything else.
You sit under it until the light's gone.

options.label: Say nothing about the empty half.

beats.text: He doesn't mention it either.
Two people in a room with a map, neither of them saying that half the world hasn't got a name yet.

options.label: "Who fills the rest of it in?"

beats.text: "I do," he says. "Slowly. Badly."
"You can't sew."
"I can't sew," he agrees.
"Then you want somebody who can."
"Where would I find a person like that?"
"I've no idea," you say.
She's eleven months away. She's got a bad chest, a stolen surveyor's rule, and eight hundred place names in her head, and neither of you has heard of her yet.
Remember this day.
Not because anything happens in it.
Because nothing does.
Ada Pike steals the map off your wall on a Thursday afternoon.
You see the fingers first, through the open window. Narrow, brown with coal dust, and unhurried.
She lifts the blue cloth off its pin and folds it with care, which is somehow worse.
You are eight feet away and the chair is facing the wrong direction.
The fingers vanish.
"I said put it back."
Nothing. Then a face comes up over the sill.

options.label: "You've got the top corner. There's a second pin at the bottom."

beats.text: The hand stops dead.
"There isn't," says a voice below the sill.
"No," you agree. "But you looked."
A pause. "That was well done," the voice says, with real approval, and a face comes up over the sill.
She's about Oliver's age, maybe a little older, with a cap pulled low over one eye and a red pencil behind her ear.
She's holding the map against her chest.
"You drew the river wrong," she says.
"I didn't draw the river."
"Then whoever did is a liar."
"You're trespassing."
"You're keeping bad geography."
Oliver comes through the washhouse door with a bundle of wire and stops when he sees her.
"Give that back," he says.
She looks at him. "You've built a wing without marking the wind direction."
His eyes go to the map.
"Give it back."
She folds it once more, perfectly, and sets it on the sill, and keeps one hand flat on top of it.
"The hill west of the quarry isn't a hill," she says. "It's an old spoil bank. The ground shifts after rain. That's why your right skid dug in."
Oliver's whole face changes. "You were there."
"I've eyes."
"You were there."
"I collect information."
Her coat has three sleeves sewn into it. One of them is too short to reach her wrist.
She looks down at it as though noticing it for the first time.
"This one was abandoned."
"By whom?"
"A gentleman careless enough to leave it unattended."
"That's my line," Oliver says.
"Then you've been using it badly."
"The third's a pocket," she says, and turns it out, and there's a stub of chalk in it, a bootlace, and a brass surveyor's rule with somebody else's initials filed off the end.
"You made a pocket out of a sleeve."
"I made a pocket out of a sleeve that didn't fit an arm." She rolls it back up. "Everything's for something. Most things aren't for what they were called."
Oliver has gone very quiet behind her, in the way he goes quiet when a sentence has cost him something.
She slides the map toward you. "The bridge under the reeds is real. The shepherd was right. Your mark isn't."
"It's my mark," you say.
"That's the trouble."
Oliver puts the wire down. "What do you want?"
She points at the glider frame. "A look."
He puts himself in the washhouse doorway. All of him. Bad arm and everything.
She tilts her head. "If I meant to tell the Toll Man, I'd have done it."
"You know him?"
"Everyone knows him."
"You could be working for him."
"I haven't the patience for ledgers."
He hasn't moved out of the doorway. He's waiting for you.
He looks round at you.
"She knows something about the quarry," you say.
"She stole the map."
"She gave it back."
"After correcting it."
"You've corrected worse things," you say.
She gives you a quick look. It's the first time she's been interested in you rather than the cloth.

options.label: "She can look. She tells us where she sleeps first."

beats.text: Her hand stops halfway to the doorframe.
"Why."
"Because if you sell us, I want to know which door to be furious at."
There's a silence. Oliver has stopped breathing again.
"Behind the printing office," she says. "Under the loading step. It's warm on Tuesdays."
She said it too easily, and you'll work out much later that she'd never told a soul before, and that she did it because you'd asked as if the answer had a price.
Oliver steps aside.
She circles the glider without touching the canvas. She looks at the knots, the skids, the angle of the cradle.
"Your left spar's too proud," she says.
"It's meant to hold the wing."
"It's meant to hold the wind. Those are different jobs."
He crouches by the joint. She points. He presses the wood.
The spar shifts.
She's got a joke for every broken thing in the room.
The cracked bearing's a philosopher, because it refuses to move. The missing brace is a widow, because it's lost its partner.
When Oliver tells her that isn't how tools are named, she says, "That's why tools have no poetry."
She finds the weak point in the right spar before he does — a split in the grain under the binding — and taps it once with a finger.
"You want another length here."
"I know."
"You didn't."
"I was going to."
"That's a future tense," she says. "The spar's breaking in the present."

options.label: Enjoy this enormously and say so.

beats.text: "Say that again," you tell her.
"Which part."
"The tenses."
"The spar is breaking in the present," she repeats, obligingly, and Oliver says "Thank you, both," in a voice like a closing door.

options.label: "He's had one arm for a fortnight."

beats.text: She looks at the sling folded on the bench. Then at his shoulder, properly, for the first time.
"The spoil bank," she says. "That wasn't your build. That was the ground."
"It was the spar," Oliver says.
"It was the ground and then the spar," she says. "In that order. It matters which order."
He doesn't answer, but he sits down, and he hasn't sat down all afternoon.
He takes a knife out of his pocket. She catches his wrist.
"Not that one."
"Why?"
"It's dull."
She produces a smaller blade with a bone handle. Bright, narrow, well kept.
"Where'd you get that?" he asks.
"A mapmaker's widow."
"You stole it."
"She gave it me. After I stole something else."
She puts the blade in Oliver's hand, handle first, the way you hand a blade to somebody you've decided about.
She smiles for the first time.
"A map."
"And she gave you a knife for it."
"She gave me a knife because I brought it back better than I took it," Ada says. "Her husband had the coast in the wrong place. He'd been dead nine years and nobody had told the coast."
The smile doesn't arrive.
"No."
"I'm sorry."
"She was eighty-one and she died indoors," Ada says. "That's a good death. I've seen the other kind."
Then she turns back to the spar, and you understand that the subject is shut, and that she's fifteen.
She stays until dark.
For the first hour Oliver keeps asking her to move away from the bench. By the second, he's asking her for the thread.
She holds the spars while he binds them. She knows how to tie a parcel so it'll survive a river. She knows how to fold cloth round something fragile. She knows which knots tighten when they're wet.
"Who taught you?" you ask.
"A man who sold maps."
"Where is he?"
"He sold himself a better life."
"Did it fit?"
"Poorly."
Halfway through the binding she stops and coughs into the short sleeve. It goes on longer than a cough ought to.
She straightens up and carries on with the thread as though the last twenty seconds were somebody else's.
"Since the print works," she says. "It's the paper dust. Everyone behind that building sounds like me."
"That isn't an answer about how long."
"Two winters." She ties off. "It's better in summer. It's summer."
You'll spend the next eleven months quietly worrying about her chest.
Her chest is not what takes her.

options.label: Push the tin cup across the bench without comment.

beats.text: She looks at it. Then at you.
"I didn't ask," she says.
"No."
She drinks the lot and sets it down and says nothing else about it, and after that she starts handing you the small parts to hold without being told to.
You'll spend the next eleven months quietly worrying about her chest.
Her chest is not what takes her.
She marks the blue cloth with the red pencil. A new line runs from the city toward the coast.
"You can't draw a road because you want one," Oliver says.
"You can't fly because you want to."
He looks at her.
"That wasn't an insult," she says. "That was companionship."
"It's accurate."
"Those are compatible."
"Not in my experience," she says, and adds a small circle out past the blank plain.
She goes still for a second, with the pencil on the cloth.
"That was fast," she says.
"You fixed a spar and insulted him inside an hour. There's no faster route in."
"I've been in cities eleven months," she says, to the map, "and nobody's said welcome," and then she adds a small circle out past the blank plain and doesn't look up again for a while.
"What's there?" you ask.
"If I knew, it wouldn't be blank."
She eats the heel of the bread Oliver brought. She bites it with the concentration of somebody working out a difficult problem.
There's a whole middle of the loaf on the bench and she went straight for the crust.
"The middle's where people hide the good part."
"It's also softer."
"Soft things make poor evidence."
She holds the heel out to you.
"I've teeth," you say.
"That isn't a map," she says, which is not a reply to anything, and Oliver laughs from the floor.

options.label: Take the middle yourself and eat it in front of her.

beats.text: She watches you do it with narrow interest.
"You're not going to insist," she says.
"You chose the heel."
"Everyone insists."
"Then everyone's rude," you say, "and there's a second heel, and it's yours, and I shan't mention that either."
Oliver laughs from the floor.
It's the first time you've heard him laugh without using it as a shield.
Ada points at him. "There. That's useful."
"What is?"
"A laugh that arrives before the danger."
"You talk as though danger keeps a schedule."
"It does. I keep a map."
She pulls a folded paper out of her sleeve. It's covered in tiny marks.
Crosses and stars. Mostly crosses.
"Places I've slept."
"Why are some crossed out?"
"They were bad places."
"And the stars?"
"Places where somebody gave me food."
You count them, because you can't stop yourself. Forty-one crosses. Six stars.
She looks up.
"I haven't slept here."
"You've eaten here. That's the qualification, isn't it? The stars."
Her hand doesn't move for a moment.
Then she takes the red pencil from behind her ear and marks the corner of the paper, small, and folds it away.
"Seven," she says.
You'll find that paper in a coat pocket two years from now and you will not be able to open it for three days.
When the glider's covered she asks for the route to the roof.
"There isn't one," Oliver says.
"There's always one."
"There's a ladder."
"Then that's the route."
She's up it before either of you can object. Oliver goes after her with the lantern.
You stay below and listen to two sets of footsteps cross the boards over your head.
The washhouse roof is a hundred and ten years old and has opinions about weight.
"I've fallen through worse," Ada calls down.
"That isn't reassuring."
"It wasn't meant to be."

options.label: "Left of the chimney the beam's rotten. Stay right."

beats.text: The footsteps stop, move, and start again further over.
"How do you know that?" Ada calls.
"I've sat under this ceiling for nine months. I know which parts of it drip."
A pause.
"She's the surveyor," Ada says to Oliver, up above, quite clearly, not meaning you to hear it.
Her face appears at the high window a minute later, with the roofline open above her.
She looks out over the city, then west, where the sky's gone copper.
"You can see the river from here," she says.
Oliver comes up beside her.
"And the old observatory," she says. "There's a road behind it that isn't on any city map."
"How do you know?"
"Because I put it there."
She leaves after sunset. She takes no food, no brass, and no part of the glider.
At the door Oliver says, "Come back tomorrow."
She stops. "Was that an invitation?"
"It was a request."
"Requests are invitations wearing a hat."
"Come back."
She looks at you. "Does she agree?"
Two hours ago she had your map in her hands and one leg over your windowsill.
"I haven't hired you," you add.
"That wasn't the question."
You look at the repaired spar, and the map, and the empty patch of floor where she was standing all evening.
"Bring a better pencil."
She smiles. "I've three."

options.label: "Come early. He gets stupid after four o'clock."

beats.text: "I do not," Oliver says.
"You steam-bent a spar at half past five and put it back in the copper because you'd forgotten which way round it went."
"That was the lantern."
"Early, then," Ada says, to you, not to him. "And I'll bring the rule. It's brass and it's honest and it'll ruin your afternoon."
She disappears into the dark. Oliver shuts the door.
"Her name's Ada," he says.
"I know."
"She sleeps behind the printing office."
"You know a great deal about her."
"I asked."
"And she answered?"
"Some of it."
He's standing in the middle of the washhouse with a bone-handled knife he didn't own this morning.

options.label: Pin the map back on the wall.

beats.text: The new line toward the coast looks uncertain.
It points somewhere, though.
He doesn't say anything for a moment.
"Say that again," he says.
"No."
"You've said it twice this month. The good things."
"I'm ill," you say, and pin the map back on the wall, and the new line toward the coast looks uncertain, but it points somewhere.
Ada comes back with three pencils and a sack of potatoes.
"The pencils are for work," she says. "The potatoes are for bargaining."
Oliver takes the sack. "Who did you bargain with?"
"A woman who wanted the sack gone."
"Why?"
"It was full of potatoes."
The sack weighs more than she does.
"Some bargains are complex," she says.
"That one had two moving parts."
"Then it was elegant," Ada says.
"From Cutler Street."
That's a mile and a quarter.
"Sit down," you say.
"I'm not tired."
"Sit down anyway. There's a bench and it's doing nothing."
She sits on it, one minute, upright, like a person waiting for a train. It's the longest she stays still all day.
The washhouse changes shape once she's in it.
Oliver keeps his tools on the left bench. Ada moves them to the right, because she says left-handed people think better near a wall.
Oliver isn't left-handed. He moves them back. She moves them again.
You appoint yourself keeper of the pliers.
"A wise decision," Ada says.
"A necessary one."
"The difference is usually discovered later."
By noon the three of you have eaten one potato raw and argued about whether steam counts as weather.
Oliver says no. Ada says a cloud is only steam with ambition.
The new frame grows faster with two pairs of hands. She cuts canvas while he shapes the spars. You keep the measurements on a slate.
"The left side's one finger longer," you tell him.
"Which finger?" he says.
"You've several."
"You've two hands."
"That isn't a unit," Ada says, from the floor, without looking up.
"It's the unit we've got."
She has it out of the third sleeve before you've finished saying it.
The left side is three-sixteenths longer. Oliver stares at the number as though it's insulted his mother.
"Fingers were better," he says.
"Fingers were kinder," Ada says. "That's a different quality."
She leans over the slate. "You want a mark for the width of Monica's wheel."
"Why?"
"The wheel leaves tracks."
"The glider won't."
"Not yet."
She adds two curved lines to the corner of the slate. They look like the wheels of your chair.
"That isn't a measurement," Oliver says.
"It's a reminder."
"Of what?"
"That the machine has to get through the door."
He looks at the frame. "It will."

options.label: "You said that about the last one."

beats.text: "The last one got through the door."
"It also got through the ground."
You take the chalk off Ada before the argument turns into an engineering principle.
"I know the door," Oliver says.
"Measure it."
He measures it. It's an inch and a half narrower than he'd have sworn to in court.
Nobody says anything. Ada writes the real number on the slate in red, twice, and circles it.
"Thank you," Oliver says stiffly, which from him is a parade with brass.
Ada's map becomes a fourth member of the household.
It hangs beside the glider. It spreads across your lap when you sit under the window. She adds roads in red, rivers in blue, and places a person can sleep without being moved along by a boot.
"What's this mark?" you ask. There's a star beside the old observatory.
"Warm roof."
"Whose?"
"A widow's."
"Will she let us stay?"
"She lets anybody stay who can mend a kettle."
Oliver raises a hand. "I can mend a kettle."
"You can make a kettle leak in a new direction."
"That's still direction."
She points at the blank ground past the western hills. "There's a tower there."
"How do you know?"
"I saw its shadow."
It's a blank piece of cloth and she's talking about it like a street she grew up on.
"Then the tower isn't a tower," she says, "and we'll sleep beside its shadow."
You mark the place with a small circle.
Oliver watches you do it. "You're adding to it."
"Somebody has to make the map accurate."
Ada looks up from the cloth.
"You said we'd sleep beside it."
"Did I."
"You did."
She goes back to the pencil. "It's a habit of speech," she says, in a voice that isn't hers, and you look at Oliver, and Oliver looks at the frame, and neither of you corrects her.
You mark the place with a small circle.
At dusk she finds a loose wheel on the chair and tries to repair it with a spoon.
"Not that spoon," you say.
She looks at the flattened metal beside your bowl. "This one's got history."
"It's got a lie attached."
Oliver stops in the middle of a knot.
Ada turns the spoon over. "What lie?"
A year ago you stood up in front of Mrs. Vale and said four words.
"Was it?"
"No."
"Then it's a small lie."
"Small lies get large when people carry them."
"Most things do," Ada says.

options.label: "I said I took it. It was him."

beats.text: The washhouse goes very quiet.
"She didn't," Oliver says.
"I did."

"She said it to a woman who'd have had me before a magistrate," he says, to Ada, to the wall, to nobody, "and the woman believed her because of the chair, and Monica has never once mentioned it since, until now."
Ada looks at the spoon for a long moment.
"Then it isn't a lie," she says. "It's a bill somebody paid."
She holds the spoon out to Oliver. "Can you do the wheel without this?"
"Yes."
"Then the spoon's decorative."
She sets it on the bench, upright, against the wall, where a thing gets put when it's been promoted.
"I once told a magistrate I was twelve," she says.
"How old were you?" Oliver asks.
"Eleven."
"That's the opposite of a useful lie."
"He wanted to send me to a home. The home wanted children who could scrub floors."
"Twelve sounded less breakable."
Nobody speaks for a while.
Then she picks up the potato sack.
"There are six left," she says. "Nobody's allowed to make a speech about them."
"He sent me anyway."
"And?"
"And I was out through a coal hatch in nine days, and I'd learned to read a survey plan off the wall in the superintendent's office, which is the only useful thing that building ever did."
She says it flatly, like a road distance.
Then she picks up the potato sack. "There are six left. Nobody's allowed to make a speech about them."
The first time all three of you leave the washhouse together, the city notices.
Oliver carries the folded wing. Ada carries the map. You carry the slate and steer along the patched road behind the foundry.

People look at the three of you and pick a story. Three thieves. Three orphans. A boy with a broken machine, a girl with a broken leg, and another girl wearing a coat made out of other people's mistakes.
At the bridge, Ada stops.
"We've come too far," she says.
"We're still in the city," Oliver says.
"That's what I mean."
There's a sign nailed to the wall. NO LOITERING. NO UNLICENSED CARTS. NO STREET CHILDREN.
Three lines, and between them they've got the whole of you.
"They haven't invented a word for us yet," Ada says.
"They'll get round to it."
"They will," she agrees. "And then they'll nail it up."
"The third," Ada says, without a pause.
"And him?"
"Third and second. He loiters with equipment."
"And me?"
She looks at your chair for slightly too long.
"They haven't invented a word for you yet," she says, "which is the only thing that's ever protected you, and I shouldn't rely on it."
Oliver unfolds the wing. The wind gets into the cloth and lifts it like a sail.
The sign comes loose off one nail.
Ada watches it swing.
"That counts as a map correction," she says.
A shopkeeper shouts from the bridge that you're blocking the road.
Oliver starts folding the wing. Ada's hand closes on the map.
And she takes one step sideways, without appearing to decide anything, so that she's standing between the shopkeeper and Oliver.
She'll do that eleven more times over the next two years, and you'll never once see her think about it first.
He's coming down off the bridge and he's got a broom handle in his hand and no broom on the end of it.

options.label: "We'll move. Give us one minute and a little courtesy."

beats.text: It takes the wind out of him more thoroughly than the wing did.
"One minute," he says.
"Thank you."
He stands there for the whole minute, holding the handle, looking increasingly like a man at a funeral he wasn't invited to.
At fifty seconds he says, "Is that a wing?", and Oliver says "Yes," and he says "Right," and goes back up onto the bridge.
"I've a shop on it."
"So has the baker. So has the man who sells birds. Neither of them owns a road."
"You're blocking it."
"We're four feet wide and there's eleven feet of it," you say. "You've come down off a bridge to be angry at a third of a road."
He goes back up the bridge and slams a door that isn't his either.

options.label: "Charge us for the delay. We're collecting stories."

beats.text: "What?"
"A penny a minute," you say. "We'll write down what you say, and your name, and in ten years somebody will read it."
Ada already has the pencil out. That's the detail that finishes him. Not the words — the pencil.
"Move along," he says, and moves along himself.
"Write it down anyway," Ada says. "Unnamed man. Bridge. Frightened of paper."
Ada watches him go. "You make people go away."

textByOption.courtesy: The shop door shuts on the bridge above you, quietly, which is the strangest part of the afternoon.
textByOption.prove-it: The shop door slams on the bridge above you.
textByOption.stories: The shop door shuts on the bridge above you, and the blind comes down behind it.

beats.text: "Sometimes they make the mistake themselves."
Oliver finishes folding the wing and the three of you carry on along the river.
At a quiet stretch under the bridge Ada takes her cap off. Her hair's been cut short with a knife, badly, by somebody working without a mirror.
She pulls the red pencil from behind her ear.
"What's your mark?" she asks.
"My mark?"
"Every mapmaker has one."
She draws a small square on the slate. Inside it, one line pointing to the corner.
"That means a place worth coming back to," she says.
Oliver looks at the washhouse keys on his belt.
"Then draw one for the washhouse," he says.
She draws the square.
There's room on the slate for another.
"That isn't a mapmaker's mark," she says.
"It is now."
She looks at it. Then she copies it, exactly, into the corner of the blue cloth, where the legend goes.
She doesn't move.
"It's a loading step," she says.
"It's a place you come back to."
"It's a place I go when there isn't another one."
So you take the pencil out of her hand and draw a square on the slate yourself, badly, with a wheel next to it, and say: "Then this one. This is the one you come back to."
She looks at the slate for a long time and doesn't say anything at all, and later that evening you find she's copied both marks into the corner of the blue cloth, where the legend goes.
The rain starts before you get home. Ada wraps the map under her coat. Oliver carries the wing over his head. You pull the chair through water that comes up over the lowest spokes.
At the washhouse door he lowers the wing.
Ada looks at the three of you, dripping, covered in river mud.
"We look respectable," she says.
"You look like a failed parade," Oliver says.
"A parade requires permission."
Inside, you hang the map near the lantern. The blue cloth's begun to fray along the edges. Ada pins it carefully, corner by corner.
Three square marks sit together in it now. One for the washhouse. One for your chair. One for a road that isn't on any official map.
Oliver lights the stove. Ada cuts the potatoes.
They're arguing about the angle of the new wing. You're holding the slate.

options.label: Hold the slate and let them argue.

beats.text: The rain drums on the roof.
Nobody asks who belongs here.
They simply make room.

options.label: Settle it. You've had the numbers on your knees all day.

beats.text: "Eleven degrees," you say. "Both of you were closer than you deserve."
"Eleven," Oliver repeats.
"Eleven," Ada agrees, "and she's had it written down since Tuesday, and let us argue for two hours."
"I was enjoying it," you say.
The rain drums on the roof.
Nobody asks who belongs here.
They simply make room.
There are three of you for twenty-two more months.
You don't know that. Nobody in the room knows that.
The stove is warm and the potatoes are terrible and Ada is laughing at something Oliver has said about the wind.
The authorities begin with questions.
A woman in a dark coat comes to the washhouse with two constables behind her. Narrow face, paper folder held against her chest, brass buttons polished bright enough to show the doorway in miniature.
"Oliver Wright," she says.
Ada is already under the workbench. She got there before the second knock and you didn't see her do it.
"Doing what?"
"Making your visit inconvenient."
One of the constables looks at his boots.
She doesn't blink. "Mrs. Hale. District inspection."
"Written down," you say, and you have nothing to write with, and you say it anyway.
It works on her exactly as well as it worked on the shopkeeper, which is to say for two seconds, which is two seconds Oliver uses to put himself in front of the frame.
Oliver stands beside the glider with one hand on the central spar.
The woman opens the folder. "This structure has been built on municipal property."
"The washhouse is abandoned," Oliver says.
"Abandoned property remains property."
"Then it's very well cared for."
A constable takes a step toward him.
You turn the chair sideways and block the narrowest part of the room.
The woman looks at you. "And you're Monica."
It isn't a question.
She knew your name before she came down the alley.
"We keep records of everyone."
"Then you know my name."
"We know your aunt's name. We know the landlady's name. We know that Oliver has been into the machine yard seven times."
His fingers tighten on the spar.
Under the bench, the pencil in Ada's sleeve knocks against the floor.
"Complaints are received in confidence."
"A brown coat," you say. "Collects rents that aren't his. Stands at the end of alleys."
Her face does nothing at all, which is the same as a signature.
"Seven visits to the machine yard," she says instead. "That's in the folder."
Nobody counts a boy's visits to a yard for free. Somebody was paid to count, or somebody enjoyed it.
"There have been complaints of theft, obstruction, trespass, and dangerous public demonstration."
"The demonstration lasted six seconds."
"The danger lasted longer."
"Did it injure anyone?"
"It could have."
"So could the bridge."
One constable glances at the door.
Her eyes stay on you. "You're obstructing an official inspection."
"I'm sitting in a doorway."
"Move."
There is exactly one place in this building where a chair fits and stops three people, and you are in it.
The door is still blocked.
"That's the most I can offer."
Oliver says your name, low.
You don't look at him. "Don't interrupt your own defence."
It sits in the room.
Because they'd have to lay hands on the chair, in a doorway, in daylight, with a baker forty feet away who has known you since you could walk.
"That would be assault on a girl in a chair," you say, "and it would be written down by somebody, and it wouldn't be you."
The nearer constable takes his hand off his belt.
Oliver says your name, low.
You don't look at him. "Don't interrupt your own defence."
She opens the folder wider. There are drawings of the glider in it, copied from somewhere outside this room. The lines are bad. The shape is unmistakable.
"This machine has no permit," she says.
Somebody stood on a hill with a pencil and sold the shape of it.
"The sky isn't a machine."
"You haven't inspected it."
Under the bench, Ada makes a small muffled sound. It might be a laugh.
A constable bends toward the floor. "There's somebody else here."
"There are several people here," you say. "You haven't counted the mice."
She turns the page slightly away from you, which tells you she agrees.
"The right spar's in the wrong place," you say. "The cradle's missing. Whoever drew it saw the machine from below, at distance, once, and didn't understand it."
"It is sufficient for the record."
"Then your record is of a thing that doesn't exist," you say, "and I'd hate to be the one who signed it."
Under the bench, Ada makes a small muffled sound. A constable bends toward the floor.
The woman folds the drawings shut. "Oliver Wright. You're to come with us for questioning."
"Am I under arrest?"
"You're being asked to cooperate."
"That wasn't the question."
She looks at him properly for the first time, with something like respect, though it isn't the kind he needs.
"Refusal will be recorded."
"Then record it."
The constable reaches for his shoulder.
Ada kicks the underside of the bench. A tin cup rolls out across the floor and hits the constable's boot.
Everybody looks down.
She comes out from under the bench holding the map.
"She sent for me," Ada says.
"Who did?" Oliver says.
"The lady with the buttons."
"I did not," the woman says.
Ada points at the folder. "You've got my drawing."
The woman looks at the map in her arms. "You made this?"
"Some of it."
"You're trespassing as well."
"I've been told."
"How old are you?"
"Old enough to know when a road's false."
The constable grabs for her. She steps behind the frame. Oliver moves to cover her.
Three children, one door, two constables, and a woman with a folder.

There's one opening left in the room and it isn't a physical one.

"If you take them," you say, "you take the machine as evidence. If you take the machine, you must list every piece. If one piece goes missing, the record will show whose hands were in this room."

The woman turns toward you.

"You think paperwork protects you?"

"No. I think it makes people lazy."

She looks at the glider. She doesn't have to understand it to see what it is to the boy standing in front of it.

stakes.onSuccess: The woman closes the folder. "You have until tomorrow morning to remove the structure." It is not mercy. It is paperwork, and paperwork buys time.
stakes.onFail: The woman does not close the folder. "Take the boy," she says, and the constable's hand closes on Oliver's shoulder before Monica can find another word that might have worked.

beats.text: The folder is still in her hands.
That's the only fact in this room that matters, and it means there's one thing left to try.
"You're not a solicitor," she says.
"Neither are you."
"I represent the district."
"Then represent its rules correctly."
The folder opens again. "The district forbids unsupervised mechanical experiment by minors."
"Oliver isn't experimenting."
"What is he doing?"
You look at the wing. It is fourteen feet of willow and flour sacking and it is the only thing that boy has ever loved out loud.
Oliver's face turns toward you.
"Agricultural?" the woman says.
"The wind turns it."
"It could frighten crows," Ada adds.
"That's not a permitted use."
"Then write a new permit," you say. "You're already holding a pen."

options.label: "He's building a flying machine, and you know it."

beats.text: Ada shuts her eyes.

"And there's no ordinance in that folder about flying machines," you say, "because nobody has ever needed one. You've come here with theft, obstruction, and trespass, and you'd have used them on a boy stealing coal. The machine isn't in your law at all."
The woman doesn't answer for a long moment.
"That will be corrected," she says.
"Yes," you agree. "But not today."
Oliver is looking at you as though you've just handed him something out of a fire.
She repeats the word she means to keep — flat, set down carefully somewhere she can find it again.
She doesn't believe a syllable of it. Her eyes stay on the shape of the wing a moment too long for that.
But belief was never what she came to collect. Evidence was. And three children in a doorway with no ordinance to cite isn't evidence. It's inconvenience.
Her mouth goes to a straight line. She looks at the two constables.
Neither of them wants to make a choice they'd have to explain later, involving a broken frame, a girl who was hiding under a bench, and a crippled witness with a clear voice.
She closes the folder.
"You have until tomorrow morning to remove the structure."
"And if we don't?"
"Then it will be removed for you."
She turns to go.
Oliver hasn't taken his hand off the spar in eleven minutes.

options.label: Let Oliver have the last word.

beats.text: "You came for an arrest," he says.
"I came for compliance."
"You found neither."
"I found tomorrow morning," she says. "That isn't the same as losing."
She stops in the doorway.
"Monica. Present throughout. Objected throughout. If anything happens to either of them, I want to be already written down."
For a moment something moves in her face that might be pity and might be something worse.
"Child," she says, "nobody reads the folder until afterwards."
"Then afterwards will have my name in it," you say.
She writes it down. You watch her do it. It's the only thing you get out of the whole afternoon and it will matter, twice, before the end.
They go. Their boots stay outside the door for a long time.
Ada puts the map on the bench. "Agricultural frame?"
"You're welcome to suggest a better lie."
"A device for measuring clouds."
Oliver looks at you. "That isn't better."
"It has a job," Ada says.
"So does the frame."
The washhouse has got smaller. The glider fills it. The door won't open fully with the wing on its stand.
"We move tonight," Oliver says.
"Where?"
"The old observatory."
Ada shakes her head. "The road behind it's watched."
"The quarry?"
"Too open."
"The roof?"
"Too high for Monica."
They have said your name four times in ninety seconds and not once to you.
They stop.
"Don't discuss routes as though I'm luggage."
Oliver drops his eyes.
Ada doesn't. "Noted," she says, and hands you the map, and from that night on the map is carried on your lap when the three of you move.

options.label: "Then ask me what I can do."

beats.text: There's a pause.
"What can you do?" Ada asks. Straight out. No softening.

"Four inches of step with a board. Six with two people and warning. Not a ladder. Not a hatch. Cobbles if they're dry, not if they're wet. I can do two miles and then I'm finished, and I won't tell you when I'm finished, so somebody has to count."
"I'll count," Ada says.
It's the first time in your life anybody's asked the question instead of guessing the answer.
Ada folds the map. "The printing office has a cellar. Two exits. One chimney wide enough for the frame if we take the skids off."
"Will they let us in?" Oliver asks.
She smiles without any humour in it. "They owe me."
The three of you start packing.
He takes the canvas off. She labels every bundle in red pencil. You keep the brass hinges in your lap and count them twice.
Outside, a horse stops in the road.
Nobody speaks.
Through the crack in the door you can see the brown coat. The Toll Man is standing with the woman in the polished buttons.
He points at the washhouse.
Oliver reaches for the frame.
The horse hasn't moved on yet.
"We have to go."
"Not through the front."
Ada lifts the map. "Cellar route."
The horse moves on. The Toll Man doesn't.
"Why," Oliver whispers.
"Because he's telling her something and I want to know how much he knows."
You watch the brown coat's arm through the crack. He points at the washhouse. Then at the roof. Then west, up the alley, at nothing at all — at the empty end where the printing office lane starts.
Ada goes white.
"He doesn't know," she says. "He's guessing."
"He's guessing correctly," you say. "Cellar route. Now."
The horse moves on. The Toll Man doesn't.
You turn your chair toward the rear passage. The boards you laid across the threshold in the spring are still there.
Oliver carries the wing. Ada takes the tools. You carry the hinges.
At the first turn the chair catches on a loose brick.
"Oliver," you say.
He waits.
He is holding fourteen feet of wing above his head in a dark passage and he is waiting.
He takes the left side.
He doesn't ask whether you can manage the rest.
That's the whole of it. That's the entire difference between him and every other person who has ever helped you.
He kicks the brick out of the passage and steps back to where he was, with the wing still over his head, and says nothing.
You get the chair over the gap yourself.
"Thank you," you say.
"For the brick," he says.
"For the brick."
The rear lane comes out behind the bakery. The city's dark except for the factory windows, and people move in the gaps between the lights.
Ada leads. She doesn't walk quickly. She walks at exactly the speed the wheels can go, and she never once looks back to check.
At the printing office she knocks three times, waits, then twice.
Nobody answers.
Oliver looks behind him.
"Again," you say.
She knocks.
A hatch opens at ground level. An old man's eye appears in it.
"What do you want?"
"The cellar," Ada says.
"No."
The hatch is four inches from closing and you are the only one at eye level with it.
You lean forward. "Sir. If you shut that hatch, the authorities find us in your lane. They'll search your building. They may find whatever you're printing without a permit."
The eye narrows.
"We'll be quiet," you add. "We'll leave no mess. If we break either promise you may tell us so in language suitable for a newspaper."
The hatch opens wider.

options.label: "She says you owe her. What for?"

beats.text: The eye moves to Ada and stays there.
"She carried type for us," the old man says, "for eleven nights, when the boy we had was in gaol. Two miles each way. She never once asked what it said."
"I couldn't read it," Ada says. "It was backwards."
"It was backwards," he agrees, "and you carried it anyway."
The hatch opens wider.
"Nobody's ever paid that," he says. "Bring the wing."
"Bring the wing through," the old man says.
Ada grins.
Behind you, a whistle goes in the street.
The frame is still in the washhouse.
The night hasn't finished deciding who it belongs to.
The printing office cellar smells of ink, coal, and wet stone.
The old man gives you one lantern and no questions.
Ada knows the room already. She leads Oliver through stacks of paper and presses under tarpaulin without touching a single thing.
The glider's down to bundles. The long spar rests across Oliver's shoulders. Ada's got the map and a coil of rope. You've got the brass box in your lap and the narrow aisles to steer.
"How far to the chimney?" you ask.
"Twenty-three paces," Ada says.
She said it without pausing to think.
"I count everything."
"Except potatoes," Oliver says.
"Potatoes are temporary."
That's the last joke any of the three of you makes tonight. You don't know it. Nobody in the cellar knows it.

options.label: "Then walk it at my speed and tell me the number that matters."

beats.text: "Twenty-three paces is the number that matters," Ada says, "because eleven of them have paper stacked to your elbow and two have a step, and I'll take the paper down before you get to it."
She's already moving. She takes down eleven stacks of paper with her arms full of rope and map.
She'll do it for four more minutes.
That's the whole of the time left.
Above you, boots cross the printing floor.
The old man's voice comes up. "No, officer. I've not seen them."
A woman's voice answers. "We will inspect the premises."
Ada turns the lantern down.
"There's another exit," Oliver whispers.
"There's always another exit," Ada says.
"Where?"
She points at the wall.
The wall has a door painted the same black as the bricks. She finds the latch under a shelf of type blocks.
It opens onto a service tunnel no wider than your chair.
Oliver goes first with the spar. Ada follows. You come last.
The wheels scrape both walls. Mortar comes down on your coat. Your left leg throbs under the bandage at an angle the passage won't let you change.
"How far?" you ask.
"Forty paces."
"You counted this one as well?"
"I count until I'm safe."
Behind you, the black door opens.
A constable shouts, "There!"
Oliver pushes forward. The spar jams against the ceiling.
"Lower it," you say.
"I'm trying."
Ada turns round in the passage. There's no room for her to get past you.
"Monica. Can you reverse?"
"Quickly isn't required."
The constable's boots come into the tunnel.
You reverse one hand at a time. The rear wheel catches on the wall.

options.label: "No. Go forward. Leave me in the gap — I'm as wide as the tunnel."

beats.text: "Absolutely not," says Ada.
"I am a door," you say. "For once in my life I am a door."
"You're a girl in a chair in front of a man with a club."
"Ada—"
"Reverse," she says, in a voice you've not heard her use, "because I've a plan and it needs eight feet of tunnel, and you are standing in it."
You reverse one hand at a time. The rear wheel catches on the wall.
You will spend a great deal of the rest of your life wondering what happens if you'd refused.
Oliver lowers the spar until it rests across Ada's shoulders.
"Give it me," she says.
"You can't carry it and move."
"Then I'll carry it and not move."
"Ada."
"Go."
She presses herself flat against the wall. The spar fills the tunnel between her and the constable.
Oliver grabs the back of your chair and pulls.
The chair moves.
Your wheels grind over the stone. The pain in your leg goes hot and sharp. You bite the inside of your cheek and keep your hands on the rims.

options.label: "We don't split up. Not for a spar."

beats.text: "It isn't for the spar," Ada says. "It's forty paces and a bend. I'll be behind you the whole way."
"Say it plainly."
"I'll be behind you the whole way," she says, and looks straight at you when she says it, which is how you know she means it, and it is nevertheless not true.
Oliver grabs the back of your chair and pulls.
The chair moves.
The constable reaches the bend. Ada brings the spar up.
"Back," she says.
The man stops. "Move aside."
"There is no aside."
"By order of the district."
"Then the district will have to widen the tunnel."
She glances back at you once.
"Go."
Oliver pulls harder.

The tunnel opens into a low chamber under the river embankment. Oliver drags you through first. Ada stays in the passage with the spar.

The constable lunges. The spar catches his chest and puts him against the wall. He strikes at the wood. She twists it aside, but the blow breaks the binding near the middle.

A second constable comes in behind him.

Oliver sets his end down and runs back.

"No," you say.

He doesn't hear you.

Ada kicks the loose type blocks off the shelf above the tunnel mouth. They come down into the passage and the constables retreat as metal letters scatter across the floor.

The woman in the dark coat appears at the far end. "Ada Pike. You are under arrest."

Ada looks at Oliver. "Don't make that face."

"What face?"

"The one that suggests heroism."

She throws him the red pencil.

Then the ceiling beam gives way.

encounter.onWin: You are faster than you have ever been. You get the chair round, you get the lantern up, you get your voice into the chamber before the dust does. It buys the moment it takes Oliver to reach the spar. That is all it buys. The beam comes down anyway. It was always going to come down. There is no version of this that you win.
encounter.onLose: The beam comes down before anyone can stop it. Ada does not survive the collapse. There is no version of this fight Monica wins outright. The most she buys is the moment it takes Oliver to reach the spar, and the seconds after, when it is already too late.

beats.text: The dust tastes of chalk and ink.
You can't see the tunnel. You can hear Oliver coughing somewhere to your right.
"Ada!"
No answer.
The woman in the dark coat has Oliver by the collar. He's clawing at her hand.
"Let him go," you say.
"Your friend has obstructed officers and endangered the public."
"She's a child."
"She is a repeat trespasser."
"She's under the beam."
"Then she should have moved."
You turn the chair toward her. The chamber swings round the lantern light.
"You wanted a machine," you say. "You wanted a thief. You wanted a charge to put in that folder. Take me."
Oliver says, "No."
"You have no permit," the woman says.
"I have a chair. I have a ruined leg. I have a name already in your records. I'll sit in your station and speak until every clerk in the building knows exactly what happened in this tunnel."
Her face stays unreadable.

options.label: "You brought men into a tunnel you'd called unsafe an hour ago."

beats.text: She doesn't answer.
"You said the tunnel was unsafe. You said it to the old man upstairs. I heard you through the floor."
"Officers accept risk."
"So did she," you say, "and she's fifteen, and she's under your ceiling, and you are going to be asked about it by somebody who can spell."
Something goes across the woman's face. It isn't remorse. It's arithmetic.
Behind the beam, Ada makes a small sound.
Oliver tears free.

He reaches the fallen spar. The wood has her pinned across the shoulder and chest. One hand is showing, fingers curled round the red pencil.

"Don't pull it," she says.

"I can lift it."

"You can break me."

The constables get hold of him. He kicks, twists, bites one man's wrist. The woman orders them to hold him.

You shout for the lantern. The light swings across the chamber. Her face is grey under the dust.

"Monica," she says.

"I'm here."

"The river tunnel goes east. The second turn's flooded. Don't take it."

"You can tell me later."

"No. I can't."

She says it plainly. She doesn't soften it for you.

Oliver goes still.

You put both hands on the rims and drive at the beam. The front wheel hits the wood. It doesn't move.

"Get help," you say.

The woman looks at the blocked passage.

"You have men," you tell her. "Use them."

encounter.onWin: The constables lift the spar together. Ada's body shifts. The beam rises just enough for Oliver to crawl beneath it.
encounter.onLose: The constables hold longer than they should. Oliver strains against their grip while the beam holds, and holds, and will not move. When it finally gives, more of the ceiling comes with it — dust, splinters, a second crack somewhere overhead. It costs him a few more seconds he does not have. But the gap opens, and he reaches her.

beats.text: He drags her clear.
Her eyes are open. The red pencil is broken in her hand.
He puts his coat under her head.
"Look at me," he says.
She does. "Your face is dreadful."
"You've said that already."
"I'm repeating myself. It's a serious condition."
You get as close as the chair will go. It won't fit under the fallen beam. You stop at the edge of the chamber, four feet short, which is where you stay.
Four feet. You have never in your life hated four feet the way you hate these four feet.
The woman kneels and puts two fingers at Ada's throat. She looks at the blood under the coat.
"The nearest is across the river."
"Then send someone."
"The tunnel is unsafe."
"Then carry her."

options.label: "Oliver. Move her hand where I can reach it."

beats.text: He looks up at you. Then he understands, and moves along the floor on his knees, and brings her arm across until her fingers are inside the reach of yours.
Her hand is cold and there's brick dust in it.
"You've got my pencil," she says.
"You threw it at him."
"Then he's got my pencil," she says, "and you've got my hand, and that's the estate settled."
"She needs a doctor," you say, to the woman, to anyone. "The nearest is across the river." "Then carry her."
Ada's fingers find Oliver's sleeve.
