"Don't let them take the frame," she whispers.
"Forget the frame."
"You're terrible at following maps."
He bends over her.
"I marked the bridge," she says. "Behind the observatory. It's higher than the quarry."
"Ada."
"You promised."
"I didn't promise."
"You should have."
There is nothing here that any answer changes. You know that already. You answer anyway, because she is looking at you.
Her eyes come across to you.
"Write it down," she says.
"I haven't a pencil."
"Then remember it. You're better than paper."
"I'll remember it."
"Good," she says. "That's the road done, then."
"That isn't a thing people can do," she says.
"Then do it badly."
Something happens at the side of her mouth that has to stand in for a laugh.
"Monica," she says. "The second turn is flooded."
"I know. You said."
"I'm saying it twice because you'll want to go east," she says, "and I shan't be there to stop you."
You have had an answer for every person who has ever stood over you. Every constable, every clerk, every woman with a folder.
There isn't one for this.
So you hold on, and you say nothing, and she doesn't seem to mind, and that turns out to have been allowed the whole time.
Her fingers loosen.
The lantern flame bends in the draught.
Ada Pike dies before the doctor arrives.
There's no final speech. No sudden strength coming back into her.
Her breathing gets shallow while Oliver holds her hand and goes on asking her questions she can't answer.
You watch the broken red pencil come out of her fingers and roll away under the spar.
You had been worrying about her chest.
For eleven months, quietly, every time she coughed into that short sleeve, you had been worrying about her chest.
The woman in the dark coat stands over the three of you. The constables wait behind her.
"You cannot remain here," she says.
You look at the beam, and the crushed map, and the blood going dark on Oliver's coat.
"Move," she says.
Oliver doesn't.
You put your hand on his wrist. His skin is cold.
He looks at you as though the words are in another language.
"Oliver."
Nothing.
"Oliver. Her cap."
That reaches him. He picks up the cap.

options.label: "Not yet." — to the woman, not to him.

beats.text: "I said—"
"I heard you. Not yet."
"There is no purpose in—"

"Then there's no hurry either," you say, "and you'll give a boy four minutes on a floor with his friend, and you'll do it standing up and silent, because there is a doctor on his way here who is going to ask what happened, and I want you to have something decent to tell him."
She stands there. She's silent. It's four minutes.
It's the only thing anybody wins in this chamber tonight.
The doctor arrives too late. He kneels, checks her, and closes his bag.
The authorities take the broken frame.
They leave the map where it lies.
There are three things on the floor of this chamber that belong to your household and only two hands going out of it that are free.

options.label: The cap for him. The box for you.

beats.text: Oliver carries Ada's cap.
You carry the brass box.
The tunnel out is narrow. Your chair scrapes the stone the whole way to the river.
"Leave it," the woman says. "It is crushed."
"It's stitched," you say. "The rivers are thread. Thread doesn't crush."
You get it with the crutch, dragging it in over the brick dust, and you fold it on your knees, badly, in the dark, with both hands shaking.
Oliver carries Ada's cap. You carry the brass box and the blue cloth.
The tunnel out is narrow. Your chair scrapes the stone the whole way to the river.
Above the embankment the sky is getting light at one edge.
Neither of you looks at it.
Ada's cap lies on the floor of the washhouse for three days.
Oliver brings it back from the river wrapped in paper. He doesn't put it on the bench. He sets it beside the stove, with the brim pointing at the wall.
The frame's gone. The canvases are gone. The tools are gone.
The authorities left behind a torn thread, two bent nails, and the smell of dust.
You go back to your room, because the washhouse hasn't got a clear place for a chair in it now.
Oliver sits below your window every morning.
He doesn't look up.
For three days you let him.
On the fourth day you open the window.
He is sitting on wet brick in the shade with a dead girl's cap on his knee.
"It's a wall."
"It's damp."
"So am I."
He turns the cap over in his hands.
"Don't ruin it," you say.
"It's already ruined."
"That isn't what I meant."
"I know."

options.label: Say nothing. Sit at the open window as long as he sits at the wall.

beats.text: It takes forty minutes.
You're good at forty minutes. You have spent years of your life being the person in the room who cannot leave it.
Eventually he says, without looking up, "You're still there."
"I am."
"Why?"
"Because you're still there."
He puts the cap on his knee and doesn't answer, and doesn't go.
Mrs. Vale brings soup. She leaves it on the table without speaking.
The spoon's new.
You take it to the window. Oliver won't have the bowl until you set it down beside him.
"It isn't poisoned," you say.
"That's what poison would want you to think."
That's the first thing he's said in four days with any shape to it.
He closes his eyes.
You regret the sentence the moment it's out of your mouth.
Not because it's untrue. Because he hasn't anywhere to put it.
The soup goes cold between you.

options.label: "Then eat it and prove me right."

beats.text: He eats four spoonfuls, mechanically, like a man clearing a path.
Then he stops, and sets the bowl on the brick, and says, "She'd have said this soup had no ambition."
"She would."
"I'm going to keep doing that," he says. "Saying what she'd have said. Out loud. In front of people."
"Good."
"It isn't good. It's a symptom."
The soup goes cold between you.
"She hated thin soup," you say.
"She said potatoes were temporary."
"Everything she said was a joke."
"Not everything."
He looks at the cap. "She knew the route."
"She knew many routes."
"She knew the bridge."
"Then we know it too."
"No."
The word's quiet. He doesn't argue it. He just puts it down between you like a stone.
On the sixth day he carries the cap to the washhouse and hangs it from a nail.
The coat with the missing lining hangs beside it. He doesn't go in any farther than that.
The room's changed without the frame in it. The walls seem farther apart. There's dust marking out the shape where the workbench stood.
You park at the threshold.
There is grit on the floor, thread in the corners, and a boy in the doorway who has not moved in a quarter of an hour.
"Why?"
"Because dirt doesn't honour the dead."
He looks at the floor and doesn't pick anything up.

options.label: "Fetch the string. I want the room measured."

beats.text: "There's nothing in it to measure."
"There's the room. Somebody should know how wide it is."
"Why?"
"Because she'd have known," you say, "and now nobody does, and that's a thing that's gone out of the world, and I won't have it."
He stands very still for a moment.
Then he fetches the string and measures the washhouse, and it takes him twenty minutes, and it is eleven feet by nineteen, and for the length of it he is a person with a task.
The broken halves of the red pencil aren't in this room.
One's with the authorities. The other was in Ada's hand.
"I should have stayed," he says.
"She told you to leave."
"She was wrong."
"She was under a beam."
"She knew what she was doing."
"That doesn't make her wrong."
He turns on you.
"You didn't see her."
This is the first time in five years of knowing him that Oliver Wright has used a voice on you.
"You didn't see her when the doctor came."
"No."
"You didn't hear what she said."
"I heard you."
His mouth tightens. "Then stop telling me what she wanted."

options.label: "I was four feet away and my chair wouldn't fit."

beats.text: It comes out flat. It doesn't sound like an argument. It sounds like a measurement, which is what it is.
"Four feet," you say. "I've counted it every night since. I know how long it took you to move her hand where I could reach it. I know I asked you to do that instead of doing it myself."
He looks at the floor of the washhouse.
"That isn't your fault," he says.

"No," you say. "And it isn't yours. And we're both going to say the true thing to each other and go on believing the other one anyway, for about a year, and there is nothing either of us can do about that."
"Then stop telling me what she wanted," he says, but the voice has gone out of it.

options.label: Let him have it. Let him shout at somebody who won't leave.

beats.text: "You didn't see her when the doctor came. You didn't hear what she said. You sat at the edge of the room and you talked to a woman in a coat and you—"
He stops.
You don't say anything at all.
"I don't mean that," he says.
"I know."
"Why didn't you answer?"
"Because you needed somewhere to put it," you say, "and I'm the only thing in this yard that can take it and still be here tomorrow."
He sits down on the empty floor with his back to the doorframe.
You don't answer that.
Your leg's begun to ache with the damp, and the chair's left wheel has picked up grit, and there's a limit to how long you can hold a threshold.
You steer away from the washhouse.
Behind you, Oliver says, "Where are you going?"
"Somewhere else."
"Why?"
"Because this place is full of people who aren't in it."
He follows you.
The road to the river is longer than you remember. The rain has filled the ruts.

options.label: Take the side lane. Flatter pavement, ten minutes more.

beats.text: Ten minutes more, and no ruts, and your leg forgives you by the halfway mark.
Oliver walks it without once asking why you'd gone the long way.
He learned that from watching somebody. You know exactly who.

options.label: Straight down the rutted road. You want the fight.

beats.text: The wheels drop into water twice. The second time, Oliver has to lift the front of the chair, and your leg goes white-hot, and you make no sound at all.
"There's a flat lane," he says.
"I know where the flat lane is."
"Then why—"
"Because I wanted something to be difficult on purpose," you say, "instead of by accident."
He doesn't argue. He puts his hands on the back of the chair and pushes you the rest of the rutted way.
At the water, Oliver stops beside the embankment. The river runs brown and fast beneath the bridge.
"She'd have marked it," he says.
You look at the stonework. There are no map lines on it. No red pencil. No square for a place worth coming back to.

textByOption.cap: You look at the stonework. There are no map lines on it. No red pencil. No square for a place worth coming back to.
textByOption.map: You have the blue cloth folded on your knees, brick dust still in the creases. Neither of you has been able to open it since the tunnel. It sits there being a thing she made, which is somehow harder to look at than a bare wall would have been.

beats.text: "She did mark it," you say.
"The bridge behind the observatory. Not this one."
"The bridge remains."
"That isn't the same."
"No."
He grips the railing. Ada's cap is in his other hand.
"I don't know how to make this useful," he says.
The river carries a dead branch under the bridge.

options.label: "You don't have to make it useful yet."

beats.text: "Everything's useful," he says. "That's the whole of how I was raised. Everything's for something or it's thrown out."
"That's how the orphanage was run," you say. "It isn't a law of the world."
He watches the branch go.

options.label: "It isn't useful. It won't be. That's what it is."

beats.text: He looks at you.
"You want me to tell you it was for something," you say. "It wasn't. She was fifteen and she was clever and a ceiling fell on her, and there's no ledger anywhere that this goes into."
"Then what am I meant to do with it?"
"Carry it," you say. "That's all. That's the whole instruction. I've carried a leg for nine years and I'll tell you honestly, nothing about it was ever useful, and I'm still here."
He watches the branch go.
That night, Oliver brings the brass box to your room.
He sets it on the floor. The lid's scratched from the tunnel. The bent nail that served as its lock is gone.
Inside are the brass plate, the leather band, and two small curved pieces you've not seen before.
"What is it?" you ask.
"Nothing."
"You didn't carry nothing through a collapsing tunnel."
The two curved pieces catch the lamp. They are the size of a person's eyes.
He shuts the lid on your question.
"It isn't finished," he says, "and it isn't mine."
It's the second time he's said that sentence to you, and you still don't ask whose it is, because on both occasions there's been something in his face that shuts the subject like a door.

options.label: Don't ask. He'll tell you when it's finished.

beats.text: You look at the two curved pieces and you say nothing, and he watches you not asking.
"You're not going to ask," he says.
"No."
"Why?"
"Because it isn't finished," you say, "and I've got some idea of what it's like to be looked at before you're finished."
He shuts the lid very gently.
"She wanted to see the bridge," he says.
"Then take her there."
"She's dead."
"Her cap isn't."
He flinches.
You regret that as well. You don't take it back. This room can't survive only on the words that cause no pain.
Oliver closes the box.
"I'm finished," he says.
"With the frame?"
"With all of it."
He has said this on each of the last four days. Today he's said it while holding the box.
"You've been saying that for four days," you say. "This time you mean it, I suppose."
"This time I do."
"You don't."
He looks at you. "How would you know?"
"Because you brought me the box."
He hasn't got an answer to that. He puts his hand flat on the scratched lid and leaves it there.
It stops him.
"You're meant to argue," he says.
"I'm not going to spend a year making a dead girl's argument at you. If you're finished, you're finished. You're twelve years old and you can be a boy who used to build things."
"Then why are you still here?"
"Because I never came for the machine," you say.
He sits down on the floor with the box in his lap and doesn't say anything for a long time.
He sits on the floor with his back against your chair. His head rests on the wooden wheel.
"She was the first person who understood the route," he says.
"She was the first person who corrected your map."
"She made it better."
"So did you."
"I made a machine that killed her."
"The beam killed her."
"The machine brought us there."
"The authorities brought the beam."
"I asked her to come back."
"She came because she wanted to."
"I should have stopped her."
You look down at the crown of his head. His hair's still got tunnel dust in it, six days on.
He is going through the causes one at a time, hunting for the one with his name on it.

options.label: "You're choosing a single door for a house that's burned down."

beats.text: He doesn't move.
"That sounds like something Ada would say," he murmurs.
"She'd say it better."
"Yes."

options.label: "If you want a cause with a name on it, use mine. I found you."

beats.text: He goes very still against the wheel.
"You were nine and watching birds through a fence," you say. "You'd have grown up, and been apprenticed, and been fine. I'm the one who came back the second day."
"Don't," he says.

"Then you see how it works," you say. "You can run that back as far as you like. You'll get to my grandmother eventually. It doesn't stop, and it doesn't help, and it's a house that's burned down and you're stood in it choosing a door."
"That sounds like something Ada would say."
"She'd say it better."
"Yes."
The silence that follows isn't empty. It's got the river in it. The broken pencil. The cap by the stove.
You keep your hand on the armrest of the chair, half an inch from his shoulder, for a very long time.
You don't move it any closer. Neither of you is any good at that yet.
In the morning, Oliver takes the glider's measurements out of his memory.
He writes them on the washhouse wall in charcoal. The numbers come out uneven. Twice he rubs them away.
The third time, he leaves them.
"I said I was finished," he tells you.
"You did."
"I can still be finished and write things on walls."
"That's true."
He draws the first spar. Then the second. He leaves a space where the cradle ought to go.
"No more flights," he says.
"I didn't ask."
"No more bridge."
"I didn't ask."
"No more authorities."
"That one may be difficult."
His pencil stops.
"Monica."
"What?"
"Why do you keep answering?"
This is not the question he means. It is nine months early, and it is the same question, and you can hear the shape of the real one underneath it.
You look at the charcoal lines on the wall.
He puts the pencil down.
The cap by the stove throws a small shadow across the floor.
He'll ask you the real question in nine months, in a worse room, and you won't have an answer ready then either.

options.label: "Because one day you'll ask me a harder one and I want the practice."

beats.text: "What's the harder one?"
"You'll get to it."
"I hate when you do that."
"I know. Ada hated it too. You're both wrong."
He puts the pencil down, and something goes across his face that is not quite a smile but is at least in the same trade.
The cap by the stove throws a small shadow across the floor.
Before he goes, Oliver lifts Ada's cap off its nail.
He folds it once and puts it in the brass box. The broken half of the red pencil goes in beside it.
"She'd say that's poor storage," you tell him.
"She'd say it's a foolish place to keep a mapmaker."
"She was usually right."
"She was unbearable."
"Also true."
He closes the lid.
Outside a factory whistle goes. The city starts its work. Carts move. Doors open. A man shouts about coal.
Oliver stands under the window with no cap, no map, and no glider.
"I'll come tomorrow," he says.
You rest your hand on the latch.
He nods.
Then he leaves it on the chair beside your bed instead, which is not what you asked for and is a better answer than the one you asked for.
He nods.
Then he sets the brass box on the chair beside your bed anyway, and doesn't explain it, and goes.
He's leaving you something to be responsible for overnight. He's twelve, and he's worked out that this is how you keep a person here till morning.
You don't open it again that day.
You put one hand on the scratched lid before the lamp goes out, the way you might on a shoulder.
Oliver asks the question while tightening the chair's left bearing.
He's come every day for three weeks. He brings the brass box. He brings no frame, no map, and no plans.
He sits on the floor and mends whatever's nearest his hands.
"Why do you help me?" he asks.
The chair's tipped onto its side. You're on the bed with the bad leg stretched out and the crutch inside reach.
He has picked a moment when you cannot leave the room. He is getting better at this.
"You do."
"I criticise you."
"You do that as well."
"Because nobody's ever done it," he says, "and I've been waiting three years for the invoice."
That lands somewhere under your ribs and stays there.
"There isn't one."
"Everything's got one."
"That's how you were raised," you say. "It isn't how the world's built."
"Then tell me why."
He turns the bearing with his thumb.
"Why do you keep showing up?"
"I live here."
"Why do you open the window?"
"It gets stuffy."
"Why did you lie to Mrs. Vale?"
"The spoon was innocent."
He looks at you.
You look at the ceiling.
"That's a question with too many parts," you say.
"It's got one answer."
He sets the chair upright and tests the wheel. It turns without a sound.
"There," he says.
"You've become very fond of that word."
"It's useful."
He parks the chair by the window. You lower yourself into it on the crutch.
It's difficult after too much sitting. The knee won't bend properly and the floor is farther away than it ought to be.
Oliver watches the chair, not your leg.
He has watched the chair instead of the leg every single time, for three years, and has never once been caught at it.
"I wasn't."
"You were thinking."
"I was thinking the bearing works."
"Coward."
He smiles faintly.

options.label: "You always look at the wheel. I've noticed. For years."

beats.text: His thumb stops on the rim.
"Was I meant to look at the leg?"
"No."
"Then I'll go on with the wheel."
"It isn't a complaint, Oliver."
"I know what it is," he says, and goes back to the rim, and his ears have gone red.
The brass box is on the table. Ada's cap is inside it.
You know because he's never mended the torn crown, and the cloth shows through where the lid closes.
"Does it need a reason?" you ask.
"Everything needs a reason."
"That's a very expensive belief."
"It's cost me plenty."
He touches the box.
You get the string out of the drawer — the one he measured your head with, in May, two years ago. It's knotted round itself.
Fine. He wants the reason. Start somewhere you can say out loud.

options.label: "I help because you don't look away."

beats.text: Oliver watches your fingers on the string.
"From what?"
"From me."
He frowns.

options.label: "Because you've never once called me brave."

beats.text: "Is that bad?"
"It's the word people use when they want a thing to be finished," you say. "You're so brave. Meaning: I've had my feeling about you now, and I'd like to go."
Oliver considers this.
"You aren't brave," he says. "You're difficult."
"Thank you."
"I wasn't being kind."
"I know. That's the part I'm thanking you for."
"People look at the chair," you say. "They look at the bandage. They look at the door behind me and work out how long it'll take to get me through it."
"You look at the wheel. You look at the road. You look at the thing wanting doing."
"I look at you."
"Not first."
He takes the correction without argument.
"You've also never asked whether I want to be brave," you say. "You ask whether I want the latch opened. You ask which route's level. You ask before you move the chair."
Oliver sits on the edge of the bed.
"Is that all?"
"No."
"What else?"
Below the window nothing moves. The sky over the chimneys is the colour of tin.
He looks out toward the alley.
It's a good sentence. It's also a smaller one than the truth, and you both let it stand for a moment as though it weren't.
"What?"
"When you were nine. You'd been in that yard four years and you knew how many mice lived under the coal store and which of the birds came back in March."
"That's just paying attention."
"Yes," you say. "Nobody had ever done it in my direction before. I wanted to know what it was like from the inside."
He looks out toward the alley and doesn't say anything for a while.
Oliver takes the string out of your hand.
"You could have let me go after Ada," he says.
He says it flatly, the way he says measurements. He has been carrying it for three weeks.

options.label: "You weren't the only one who lost her."

beats.text: He stops turning the string.
"No," he says. "I know."
"You don't, quite. You've been grieving as though you had the lease on it."
"She was mine."
"She corrected my map as well," you say. "She was eleven months in my life and she made a joke about my chair and it was the first joke about my chair I'd ever laughed at."
He puts his hand over his eyes for the space of four seconds, and then takes it away, and that's all there is.

options.label: "I was angry enough to keep you alive."

beats.text: "At me?"

"At the beam. At the woman with the folder. At the tunnel for being three inches too narrow. At the ceiling. At the district surveyor, whoever he is, and at whoever built a service passage no wider than a chair."
"That's a great many things."
"I'd four feet and nothing to do with them," you say. "You have to put that somewhere, so I put it into getting you home, and I'm not sorry, and I'd do it again worse."
He winds the string round his finger until the end goes white.

options.label: "If you leave, the window becomes a wall."

beats.text: He goes still.
It's the most honest thing you've said in this room, and it costs you more than the other two would have, and you say it anyway.
"That isn't fair," he says quietly.
"No."
"You can't put that on me."
"I'm not putting it on you. I'm telling you what's true and then not asking you for anything," you say. "That's the difference. It took me nine years to learn it and I'd like some credit."
He winds the string round his finger and doesn't look up.
He folds the string into a small circle.
"You said you can't fly," he says.
"I said I can't walk freely."
"That isn't the same."
"It's near enough for people who want me to stay put."
He turns the circle of string between his fingers.
"I can make you something."
"You already have."
"The headpiece isn't finished."
You take the brass box and set it on your knees. "You made this after we met."
"I made parts of it."
"For what?"
"For seeing."
"I can see."
"You can see what's in front of you."
The words are careless. He knows it the instant they're out.
You close the box.
He is twelve. He has just said the sort of thing that gets said to you in shop doorways.

options.label: "And you can see what's above you?"

beats.text: "Not yet."
"Then perhaps neither of us should boast."
His face tightens.
"I didn't mean it that way."
"You meant it some way."

options.label: Let it pass. He'll find it himself by tonight.

beats.text: You put the box on the table and talk about the bearing.
He answers about the bearing. He answers about the bearing for four minutes and then stops in the middle of a sentence about grease.
"I said something," he says.
"You did."
"You let me."
"I let everybody," you say. "You're the only one who's ever come back to it."
"I didn't mean it that way."
"You meant it some way."
He doesn't answer at once. Whatever you said, it stays with him a moment before he lets it go.

textByOption.carriage:
He doesn't answer at once. Whatever you said, it stays with him a moment before he lets it go.

He still remembers how you told him about the carriage — plain as weather, in a scrap yard, with a broom in your hand. He has never once tried to make it a smaller story than it was.
textByOption.deflect:
He doesn't answer at once. Whatever you said, it stays with him a moment before he lets it go.

He never did get an answer about the leg, not really. He stopped asking years ago, and you've never decided whether that was a kindness or a retreat.
textByOption.too-big:
He doesn't answer at once. Whatever you said, it stays with him a moment before he lets it go.

You told him once that the question was too big for a scrap yard. He's remembered the shape of it ever since without ever asking again, and today the room is finally the right size.

beats.text: Oliver takes the box off your knees. He doesn't open it.
"When I fly," he says, "I can tell you what's there."
"Birds."
"You don't know that."
"Clouds."
"You don't know that either."
"More sky."
"You've said that."
"It remains likely."
He looks down at the brass lid. "Ada wanted the bridge."
"She wanted to map the road past it."
"I want to finish because she saw the route."
"And because you want the sky."
"Yes."
"Good."
He looks up.
There is a way for a boy to spend the rest of his life carrying a dead girl instead of a wing.

options.label: "Don't turn her into an excuse. Don't turn me into one either."

beats.text: "What should I turn you into?"
"A person who's here."
The answer troubles him. You can see it go somewhere he can't reach.

options.label: "If you fly it for her, you'll be finished the moment you land."

beats.text: "Then I'll be finished."

"No," you say. "You'll be twelve, and standing in a field, with the one thing you wanted spent on a debt. And then you'll come and find another debt, and after that another, and you'll be forty and you'll have flown eleven times and enjoyed none of them."
He stares at the box.
"You're allowed to want it," you say. "That's what I'm telling you. You're allowed to want it for no reason but the wanting."
"Nobody's ever said that to me."
"Nobody's ever said it to me either. I've had to work it out from scratch, twice, and I'd rather it were said out loud in a room."
He goes back to the chair's bearing.
Not because it wants repairing. He's already fixed it. His fingers go round the rim, hunting for another job.
"I thought helping you would be the nearest I came," you say.
"Nearest to what?"
"The edge."
"Which edge?"
"The one everyone says is there."
He waits.
"The edge of the road," you say. "The edge of the room. The edge of what a body's allowed to do."
"I thought if I could stand beside somebody going past it, the air might reach me."
Oliver says nothing.
You rest the crutch against the chair.
There it is, then. The room is the right size and he has asked twice and there is nobody else here.
"I didn't ask for noble."
"You asked for a reason."
"I asked why you help me."
"There it is."
He nods slowly.
The room holds the answer without improving it.

options.label: Say the whole of it, plainly, once.

beats.text: "I can't fly, Oliver."
"I know."

"No — you know I can't walk. Listen to the other one." You keep your hands still on the armrests. "I can't fly. Not with a frame, not with a better chair, not if you spent your whole life on it. Not ever. There's no version of me in the sky."
He's stopped breathing properly.

"I worked that out when I was eleven," you say. "In a bed, in November, with a doctor talking about me in the corridor as though I were furniture. And I decided that if I couldn't go, then somebody had better go, and they had better come back and tell me, and they had better be somebody worth sending."
"And you picked me."
"You were nine and counting birds through a fence," you say. "You never stood a chance."
He nods slowly. He is crying, in the extremely economical way he does everything.
The room holds the answer without improving it.

options.label: "And it's the most use I'll ever be. Take it."

beats.text: "Don't say it like that."
"Why not?"

"Because you say everything like that," he says, with more heat than you've heard from him since the tunnel. "Like you're a tool somebody's going to put down. You're the only person who's ever come back to that yard twice. That isn't use. That's—"
He can't find the word. He's twelve. Nobody's taught him the word.
"I'd sit in a doorway for you," he says finally. "That's all I've got."
"That's the word," you say. "That's exactly the word."
The room holds the answer without improving it.
When Oliver goes, he takes the brass box and the old washer out of the bearing he mended.
"What'll you do with that?" you ask.
"Keep it."
"It's worn out."
"It carried you."
"It carried a wheel."
"That's where you were sitting."
He puts the washer in his pocket.
Outside, the cloud's opened over the alley. A narrow bar of blue shows between the chimneys.
Oliver stops underneath it.
"Tomorrow," he says, "I start again."
"Start with the spar."
"I will."
"Then the cradle."
"I know."
There is one more item on the list and you have spent two years not naming it.

options.label: "Then the parts for the thing on my head."

beats.text: He turns.
"You said you wouldn't ask."
"I've changed my mind."
He smiles. It isn't the old shield. It's smaller, and it stays.

options.label: "Then a stone with her name spelled right."

beats.text: He stops in the middle of the alley.
"They wrote Pike with a Y," you say. "In the district book. I sent Mrs. Vale down to look."
"Then we'll have it cut properly."
"And after that," you say, "the parts for the thing on my head."
He turns round. "You said you wouldn't ask."
"I've changed my mind."
He smiles. It isn't the old shield. It's smaller, and it stays.
Oliver brings the new frame to the washhouse in pieces, under a tarp, three loads a day for four days.
The first rib is blackened oak. The second's ash. The third's been cut from the straight leg of a school desk.
They don't match. He's chosen them for what they can bear, not for how they look together.
It is the ugliest object anybody has ever built on purpose.
"It's unfinished."
"It was ugly before."
"Now it's got purpose."
"The parish school's."
"Oliver."
"They've forty desks and thirty-one children," he says. "I did the counting first."
"That's the most Ada thing you've ever said."
"I'm aware." He sets the leg on the trestles. "It's straight-grained beech and it's held a hundred boys' elbows for twenty years. It'll hold a spar."
Ada's cap hangs from the nail above the bench.
Oliver's stitched the broken red pencil into the band. The brim points west.
The new central spar's thicker than the last. It takes two hands to lift.
The cradle's deeper, with a second belt across the hips and a brace for the shoulders.
"You've made it safer," you say.
"I've made it harder to break."
"That isn't the same."
"It's the part I can do."
He sets the spar on the trestles. The washhouse fills with the sound of a saw.
You keep the measurements while he cuts.
The slate's covered over with old numbers. Ada's marks are still in the corners, red pencil pressed so hard into the surface that the wood's scarred underneath.

"You're using her map," you say.

"The map's gone."

"Her marks aren't."

textByOption.cap:
"You're using her map," you say.

"The map's gone."

"Her marks aren't."
textByOption.map:
"You're using her map," you say.

The blue cloth is pinned open on the wall behind him, brick dust still in the folds where you carried it out of the tunnel on your knees. Neither of you has said a word about it in three weeks. He has been working from it the whole time.

"I'm using her map," he agrees, which is not the answer you expected, and he doesn't look round when he says it.

beats.text: He follows the line of an old measurement with his thumb. "She was right about the wind."
"She was right about most things."
"Not all."
"Give me an example."
"She said the potatoes were temporary."
"They were."
"They lasted two days."
"That's temporary."
He starts to smile, then catches himself. The smile leaves a pale gap in his face.
He has been doing that for three weeks. Catching them. Putting them back.
"I know."
"You can remember her without making every room a grave."
"I know."
"You don't have to agree with me."
"I know that as well."
The saw starts again.

options.label: "That's four you've swallowed today. I've been counting."

beats.text: He puts the saw down.
"You've been counting my—"
"Somebody has to. She's not here to do it."
He stands with his back to you for a while.
"It feels like being caught," he says.
"I know. It isn't, though. She'd have wanted a running total and she'd have shown it you every Sunday."
"She'd have written it on the wall."
"She'd have written it on your coat."
He laughs. It comes out badly, and it's the first one he's let through since the cellar, and it doesn't get put back.
The saw starts again.
The new wing's got a hinge at its centre.
He's built it out of the brass plate from the box, cut into two sections and reinforced with teeth.
You know that plate. You have had it on your knees. It has your head's measurement filed into one edge.
"A part of it."
"You've sacrificed it."
"It was the right brass."
"It was mine."
"It's still yours."
His hands stop.
"I was going to argue for ten minutes," he says. "I'd prepared it."
"Deliver it anyway. I'll pretend."
"It was the right brass," he says. "There isn't other brass like it in the district and I'd have had to steal a doorplate, and you'd have made a speech about the doorplate."
"That was a very short argument."
"You took the wind out of it."
"Then it's the right brass twice over."
He fits the hinge into the spar. The teeth click together.
"You're robbing my future device."
"Borrowing."
"The Toll Man uses that word."
Oliver looks at the cap.
"Sorry," you say.
"Don't be."
He turns the hinge with a key. The frame folds inward and halves its width.
"That's useful," you admit.
"The old frame couldn't pass the river tunnel."
"Neither could Ada."
His hand stops on the key.
You said it before you heard yourself say it.
You put your palm flat on the workbench.
"You shouldn't have to be," he says.
"Neither should you."
He turns the key again.

options.label: Don't take it back. It's true.

beats.text: "She couldn't pass the tunnel," you say. "It was three inches. Somebody in an office decided three inches, and a girl who knew eight hundred place names couldn't get out of a room."
Oliver keeps his hand on the key.
"That's why the hinge," he says.
"I know that's why the hinge."
"Then don't apologise for it," he says. "It's the only part of the whole machine that's got a reason I can say out loud."
He turns the key again.
The frame takes two weeks.
The city goes on round it. Smoke darkens the sky. Rain swells the river.
The Toll Man doesn't appear, and his absence is its own kind of watching.
Oliver works until his fingertips split. You make him wrap them. He makes you hold the thread.
Neither of you says the other's name when asking for help. You've both stopped needing to.
One morning he brings the cap to the window.
"The bridge is past the observatory," he says.
"Ada's road."
"The rise behind it's high enough."
"For what?"
"The launch."
You look down at the machine. The new wing rests on its folding hinge. The canvas is pale brown, stitched through with darker panels.
It resembles no bird you've ever seen.
"When?"
"Soon."
"That isn't a date."
"The wind doesn't keep a calendar."
"The authorities do."
"Then we go before they read it."
He puts the cap back on its nail.
Oliver asks you to test the cradle.
The seat's built for his body, not yours. He takes off the back brace and drops the footrest until your bad leg can rest without pressure.
"You're not flying," you say.
"I know."
"Then why make it fit me?"
He has spent an hour on adjustments for a person who will never leave the ground.
"Because the machine has to fit whoever's in it."
"It's you who's in it."
"It'll carry me."
"That isn't an answer."
"It's the answer I've got."

options.label: "Because if it fits me, it isn't only yours."

beats.text: He doesn't deny it.
"You can't fly," he says.
"No."
"You can sit in it."
"That's a very small thing to have spent an hour on."
"It's an hour," he says. "I've got a great many of them and nothing better to put them in."
You get into the cradle. The leather belts cross your chest.
The frame closes round you, all ribs and canvas. From inside, the washhouse roof disappears.
The open doorway becomes a slice of sky.
Oliver checks the buckle.
"Don't tighten it."
"It needs to hold."
"I need to breathe."
"Both can happen."
He adjusts the strap.
For a second the glider doesn't look like his machine. It looks like a room with no walls.
Your hands close on the side rail.
There are nine belts and buckles between you and the floor and every one of them is out of reach of your own hands.
He frees you at once.
"You asked," he says.
"You remembered."
"I remember most obstacles."
The phrase has become his.

options.label: Stay in it. Thirty seconds. Make yourself.

beats.text: You count to thirty with your hands shut on the rail.
It's the worst half-minute you've had since the tunnel. Nine belts, and none of the buckles within reach, and a boy's hands the only way out.
At twenty-two you understand something about the chair you have refused to understand for nine years, and you decide not to look at it directly.
"Out," you say at thirty.
He frees you at once. He doesn't ask what the counting was.
"You asked," he says.
"You remembered."
"I remember most obstacles."
You roll back from the cradle. The front wheel catches the new ramp.
It holds.
"That part works," you say.
"You sound surprised."
"I'm building a list."
The list grows on the wall beside the charcoal measurements.
Ramp holds.
Hinge folds.
Belt does not choke.
Left wheel quiet.
Oliver adds one line under them.
Wind test pending.
You take the charcoal out of his hand.
"What's the difference?"
"The wind's waiting for you to stop being frightened of it."
"The wind doesn't know me."
"It knows you're making it work."
He rubs out pending and writes waiting.

options.label: Add a line of your own.

beats.text: You write it under his, in letters he'll be able to read from the doorway.
Pilot comes back.
He stands and looks at it for a long moment.
"That isn't a test of the machine," he says.
"No. It's the only item on the list I care about, and I'd like it written where you'll see it every morning."
He doesn't rub it out. He puts a small square beside it — Ada's mark, a place worth coming back to.
That night, the authorities come to the end of the road.
You see them from the window. Three lanterns. The woman in the dark coat. The Toll Man with his ledger.
Oliver's below, fastening the last strip of canvas.
He has not looked up. The lanterns are ninety feet away and coming no closer.
He looks up.
You point at the road.
His face goes still. He shuts the washhouse door and turns the lamp down.
You count. Three lanterns. Two constables. The Toll Man half a pace behind the woman, which is new — he used to walk beside her.
They don't come down the road. They stand at the mouth of it in the rain and the woman writes in the folder.
She's not writing about the washhouse. She's facing the wrong way. She's writing down who goes past.
Then you tap the glass, and Oliver looks up, and you point, and his face goes still.
"They're taking names at the corner," you tell him later. "Not ours. Everybody's."
"Why?"
"Because they mean to know who helps us before they come for the frame."
The authorities don't come in. They stand in the rain ten minutes, then go.
"They know," Oliver says.
"They've always known."
"They'll take the frame."
"Not if we move it."
"The bridge is watched."
"Ada left another road."
He looks at the cap.
"Her road," he says.
"Your map hasn't vanished because the paper did."
He touches the brim.
"We leave before dawn."
The rain is still on the window. The wind has been wrong for four days.

options.label: "No. We leave when the wind's right."

beats.text: He turns.
"You're not allowed to trade one sort of foolishness for another," you say.
He nods.

options.label: "Before dawn tomorrow, or before dawn on the right morning?"

beats.text: He opens his mouth to say tomorrow.
Then he doesn't.
"She'd have asked me that," he says.
"She'd have asked it worse."
"She'd have asked it with the wind figures in her hand." He rubs his face. "The right morning."
"Say it properly."
"We leave when the wind's right," he says, "and not because a woman in a coat stood at the end of a road and made me hurry."
"Good."
The new glider stands under the washhouse roof.
It's darker than the first. The ribs are thick. The seams show.
Nothing about it suggests a miracle. It suggests work done after the miracle failed.
Oliver checks the shoulder brace. You check the ramp. The cap hangs above the both of you.
"D'you think she'd approve?" he asks.
"She'd find three errors before breakfast."
"Only three?"
"It's a new frame."
He laughs. This time he lets it happen all the way to the end.
You take the brass box off the shelf.
The headpiece inside has lost its main plate to the hinge, but the leather band's there. Two curved pieces sit beside it, filed smooth.
They are lenses. You have known they were lenses since the night he brought the box to your room.
"Why?"
"You said it was for seeing."
"It isn't finished."
"Neither's the sky."
He looks at the box, then at the wing.

options.label: "Leave it. I'll not have you carrying my things up a hill."

beats.text: "It's four ounces."
"It's four ounces of me on a machine that has to hold you," you say. "Take the cap and the pencil and go."
He puts the box in the sack anyway, on top of the rope, where he thinks you can't see it.
You can see it. You let him think otherwise, which is a thing you have got better at.
He looks at the box, then at the wing.
Before dawn, the three square marks off Ada's map get copied onto the new spar.
One for the washhouse.
One for the chair.
One for the road worth coming back to.
The authorities arrive before the wind does.
They block the road with two carts and a line of men in blue.
The woman in the dark coat stands between them, dry under an umbrella. The Toll Man waits by the first cart with his ledger under his arm.
Oliver's got the glider half-folded in the washhouse doorway.
"We could use the river road," he says.
Ada's route runs behind the observatory. The bridge is past the line of carts.
Count them with him. There are four ways out of this yard and you have used all of them at some point in three years.
"The river road's watched," you say.
"The roof?"
"Too high for the frame to reach from inside."
He looks at the narrow lane behind the bakery.
A constable steps into it.

options.label: "Then we go out of the front, slowly, in front of everybody."

beats.text: "They'll take it."
"Not in daylight with the shutters open."
"You can't know that."
"No," you say. "But every other route's got a man standing in it, and I've been reading that woman's face for two years, and she does not like an audience."
He looks at the lane behind the bakery anyway.
A constable steps into it.
They have closed every route, Ada would say.
You hear her voice with such precision that you turn toward the cap.
Oliver puts his hand on your shoulder. "Monica."
"Don't."
"What?"
He said your name the way he has been saying hers for two months.

options.label: "Don't say my name as if it'll bring me back."

beats.text: His hand comes off your shoulder.
"That isn't—"
"It is. You've been doing it for a fortnight. Ada, Ada, in the doorway, at the bench, to a nail on a wall."
"I know."
"I'm still here, Oliver. Use it on somebody who can answer."
"Monica," he says.
"What."
"The lane's closed."
"Then we use the road," you say. "Thank you."

options.label: "I'm here. Say it as though I'm here."

beats.text: He looks at you. He hasn't got a word ready.
"Say it again," you say.
"Monica."
"Better."
"The lane's closed."
"I know. I wanted the name first."
The woman in the dark coat calls through the doorway.
"Oliver Wright. Surrender the structure and come forward."
Oliver folds the wing another inch.
"You have no permit," she says.
"You said it was agricultural."
"You lied."
"You believed me for almost a minute."
The Toll Man opens his ledger. "The frame is subject to seizure."
"You've already seized the first one," you say.
"This is a separate violation."
"Then it's a separate frame."
The woman turns her attention on you. "You aren't helping."
"That's never stopped me."
"If you obstruct, you'll be detained as well."
Oliver's hand finds the back of your chair.
"Don't threaten her," he says.
"I am explaining consequences."
"You explain them like you enjoy them."
The woman lifts one finger. A constable steps forward.
The doorway is four feet wide. Your chair is three feet two.

options.label: Put the chair in the doorway.

beats.text: You move into the gap and set the brake.
"There," you say. "Now you've a practical obstruction."
Two years of being an obstacle, and for once in your life you have chosen the doorway yourself.

options.label: Turn side-on and take up the whole four feet.

beats.text: You bring the chair round until it sits across the doorway with a wheel against each post.
"That's obstruction," says the woman.
"That's a girl in a doorway," you say. "You'll want to be careful how the next part looks. There are eleven windows on this road."
Two years of being an obstacle, and for once in your life you have chosen the doorway yourself, and chosen the angle.
The constable stops less than a yard off.
He's young, like the one from the washhouse, but he isn't the same man. His club hangs at his belt. His eyes keep dropping to your leg.
"Move aside," he says.
"I can't."
"You can."
"I can move backward. The glider's behind me."
He looks past you. "Then move the glider."
"It hasn't got wheels."
Oliver says, "It's got skids."
"I wasn't asking you."
The woman steps forward. "Monica. This is your final warning."
It is the third one she has called final.
"You've given me three," you say.
"This is the final one."
"You should number them."
The Toll Man says, "She is buying time."
"Yes," you say. "That's what conversations are for."

options.label: "What's your name? You've never once given it."

beats.text: It stops her for a full second.
"That is not relevant."
"You've my name in a folder. You've his. You had Ada Pike's, spelled wrong. I've been talking to a coat for two years."
"Inspector Harrow," she says, and you can hear her regret it before the word's finished.
"Thank you," you say. "Now there are two people in this doorway."
The Toll Man says, "She is buying time."
"Yes," you say. "That's what conversations are for."
The constable reaches for the arm of your chair.
His hand is six inches away. Above the road, forty windows.

options.label: Grip the rims and shout at the street.

beats.text: "Witnesses!"
Shutters go up along the road. Faces come to the glass.
The shopkeeper from the bridge steps out of his door. The newspaper boy stops with a bundle under his arm.
The constable takes his hand back.

options.label: Say it quietly, to him, only to him.

beats.text: "You'll have to lift me out," you say. "Both arms. In front of the whole road. And then you'll go home and eat your supper and be the man who lifted a girl out of a chair."
His hand stops.
"Take your time," you say. "I've nowhere to be."
Behind him, shutters are going up along the road. The faces come to the glass on their own. The shopkeeper from the bridge steps out of his door.
The constable takes his hand back, and does not look at his superior when he does it.
The woman comes close enough for you to see the rain gathered on the brim of her hat.
"You think a crowd changes the law."
"A crowd changes what can be denied."
"Oliver is a danger to himself."
"Then take him to a doctor, not a cell."
"He has already caused injury."
You look at Ada's cap. It's hanging off the spar behind him.
"You did that," you say.
The woman's face tightens. "Careful."
"You sent men into a tunnel after children."
"We responded to a disturbance."
"You arrived before anybody called for help."
The Toll Man steps forward. "Enough."
He has carried that ledger past you eleven times in two years and never once opened it where you could see.
He says nothing.
"Read where it says you found her alive."
The crowd's grown. The woman watches the faces at the windows.

options.label: "You told me once that everything's borrowed. Was she?"

beats.text: The Toll Man doesn't answer.
"You said the district lends and the district collects. You said it to me in the rain outside a scrap yard and I've thought about it every week since."
"Girl—"
"She was fifteen. What was the term of the loan?"
He looks down at the ledger under his arm, and for the first time in two years he looks like a man holding an object rather than a position.
The crowd's grown. The woman watches the faces at the windows.

You put both hands on the rims.

"Give us the road. The frame leaves the district tonight. Nobody's hurt. Nobody has to explain why your net caught a dead girl and still can't hold a boy."

stakes.onSuccess: The woman studies the crowd a long moment, then lowers her hand. "Clear the road," she says, and the Toll Man does not argue with her.
stakes.onFail: The woman's face does not move. "Take the frame," she says, and the district's men close in on the launch site before the glider ever leaves the ground tonight.

beats.text: But the road hasn't cleared and the road hasn't closed, because there are forty windows open above it and neither of you is the only person in this street any more.
That's the only fact left in the road that matters.
The woman looks at the Toll Man.
He shakes his head.
She looks at Oliver. His hands are on the folded wing.
He's standing between the frame and the road with no weapon, no permit, and no reason on earth for anybody to believe he can do it.
"You are asking me to authorise an escape," she says.
"I'm asking you to stop pretending this is orderly."
"The district has rules."
"Rules didn't save Ada."
The crowd shifts. Somebody whispers her name.
The woman hears it.
The newspaper boy says, "Everybody knows about the tunnel."
The Toll Man turns on him. "Go home."
"I'm working."
"Then work elsewhere."
The newspaper boy is about ten. He is standing in the rain with a bundle under his arm and no idea what he has just done.
Nobody says anything for four seconds.
Four seconds is a very long time in a road with forty windows open.
The woman shuts her eyes for one of them.

options.label: "He's working. Ask him what the six papers said."

beats.text: The boy straightens up. "Cripple girl crashes orphan boy," he says. "That was two years back. That one sold."
"And this one?" you ask.
He looks at the carts, the umbrella, the line of blue, the chair in the doorway.
"This one'd sell better," he says.
The Toll Man says, "Go home," again, and it comes out weaker than the first time.
The woman shuts her eyes for a second.
When she opens them she points at the lane past the bakery.
"The road is clear as far as the observatory," she says. "Beyond that you are trespassing on private ground."
"That isn't permission."
"It isn't protection either."
Oliver starts to unfold the wing.
The constable looks at his superior.
She says, "Let them pass."
The glider goes up the lane. Oliver pushes from behind. You steer.
The skids scrape the walls and leave pale marks in the soot.
The authorities follow at a distance. The woman walks with them. The Toll Man stays by the carts.
At the end of the lane the observatory comes up over the roofs. The dome's cracked. Ivy's over the lower stones.
Behind it, the ground climbs to a bare ridge.
The road isn't marked on any sign.
Ada's road.
Oliver stops at the foot of the rise.
"We made it," he says.
"Not yet."
The wind's turned. It comes hard out of the east, pushing cloud over the ridge.
Oliver tests the wing. The canvas hauls against the frame.
This is the wind you told him to wait for and it is not the wind you told him to wait for.
"It's enough."
"Those are different."
"I know."

options.label: "Then say the number. Out loud. To me."

beats.text: He wets a finger and holds it up, which is not measurement, which is what people do when they haven't got measurement.
"I can't," he says.
"No."
"She could have. She'd have counted the reeds bending."
You look down at the pale line of the bridge in the reeds.
"Then count them badly," you say, "and tell me the truth about the answer, and I'll not stop you either way."
He counts them badly.
"It's too strong," he says. "It's also the only morning we're going to get."
"Those are different."
"I know."
The woman reaches the observatory gate. "You have no right to launch from here."
"Neither did the birds."
"The birds are not subject to district law."
"They're lucky."
At the ridge the ground drops away toward the western plain.
The bridge lies below, a pale line through the reeds. Far past it the hills go under cloud.
You brace the chair behind a stone wall. Oliver sets the glider on its skids.
The authorities spread out along the path. The woman raises her voice.
"Oliver. If you get into that machine, I'll have you detained."
"After?"
"Now."
Two constables start up toward him.
You roll forward. The front wheel strikes a root and stops dead.
Pain goes through your leg as you lurch against the strap.
"Monica," Oliver says.
"Keep working."
The woman reaches the top. "Move away from him."
You look at the open drop past the wing. "I'm not near him."
"You are involved."
"Yes."
The constables are ten paces off.
Oliver checks the shoulder brace. His fingers are shaking.
Ten paces. There is one thing in your lap and about four seconds to use it.

options.label: Hold out the brass box. "Finish the promise."

beats.text: He sees the unfinished headpiece in your hand.
For the first time all day, he breathes.
It's the oldest trick you have. Give him a task. It has worked every single time since he was nine years old.

options.label: "Ten paces. Nine. Count them out for me."

beats.text: "What?"
"Count. Out loud. Nine. Eight."
"Eight," he says, and his hands go steady on the brace, because they always do the moment there's a number in the air.
"Seven," you say, and put the brass box into his hands. "Finish the promise."
He sees the unfinished headpiece.
For the first time all day, he breathes.
He fits the leather band round your head.
The brass pieces rest above your temples. They're unfinished, but the hinges hold.
A narrow plate crosses your brow. Small lenses sit either side, cloudy with scratches.
"You can't see through those," Oliver says.
"Then don't make me wear them."
"The glass isn't clear."
"Neither's the weather."
He adjusts the band until it sits without pressing on your skin.
The authorities reach the ridge.
"Oliver," the woman says.
He climbs into the cradle.
You take hold of the launch rope.
The wind drags the canvas toward the cloud. Ada's cap snaps against the spar.
Oliver looks at you.
"If it tilts left…"
"If it tilts right…"
"I let go."
"If it rises?"
You tighten the rope.
"I hold on."

options.label: "I let go." — Say it. Mean the other thing.

beats.text: "If it tilts right…"
"I let go."
"Say it properly."
"I let go," you say, and you have no intention whatever of letting go, and he knows it, and he gets into the cradle anyway, because there is nobody else on this ridge who would lie to him about that.
"If it rises?"
You tighten the rope.
"I hold on."
The launch waits, because the wind changes its mind.
By dusk the ridge is under fog.
The authorities stay below the observatory with their carts. They can't see the glider clearly, and they don't go.
Oliver takes you back to the old keeper's room under the dome.
A broken telescope lies across the floor with its glass taken out. The stone walls hold the whole of the day's cold.
You sit by the window with the unfinished goggles still round your head.
"They pinch," you say.
Oliver kneels beside you and slackens the leather.
"Better?"
"Now they slip."
He puts a strip of cloth under the band.
He has been at this for twenty minutes. He is going to be at it all night if nobody stops him.

options.label: "You're making me look like a badly assembled insect."

beats.text: "You asked for sight."
"I asked for comfort."
"You asked for both."
He works the left hinge. The lens catches the lantern and throws a pale ring on the wall.

options.label: "Leave it. It's good enough and you've a wing to check."

beats.text: "It isn't good enough."
"Oliver."
"It's the one thing tonight I can get right," he says, and goes on with the band.
So you let him. You sit still for another twenty minutes with your head under a boy's hands, in a cold stone room, and neither of you says a word.
The lens catches the lantern and throws a pale ring on the wall.
Somewhere below the ridge, somebody coughs.
"They're waiting," you say.
"So are we."
Oliver's brought one loaf. He cuts it with the bone-handled knife Ada gave him.
The slices come out uneven.
"You're cutting it wrong," you say.
"There's a correct way?"
"Ada would say there is."
He holds the knife over the loaf. "What would she say?"
He is asking you to do her voice. He has never asked before.

options.label: "That you've confused a meal with a map."

beats.text: "She said that about everything."
"She'd have found a new line for you."
He cuts the bread. The crust breaks under the blade.
He puts the knife down.
"Why not?"
"Because I'd be good at it," you say, "and then you'd ask me again, and in five years you'd have a version of her in your head that's mostly me, and she'd be gone twice."
He sits with that for a while.
"She'd have said something about the bread," he says. "I can't get it."
"No. That's the whole of it. That's what it is."
He cuts the bread. The crust breaks under the blade.
"She wanted to see the bridge," he says.
"She saw it."
"From the tunnel."
"That still counts."
"No."
You take the slice out of his hand.
"You don't get to decide what counted for her."
He leans back against the stone.
"You always do that," he says.
"What?"
"Make the answer harder."
"Easy answers have done enough damage."
Night comes over the ridge. The fog thins. Below, the lanterns mark the line of the authorities.
Oliver checks the glider every hour. Belts, hinge, canvas, skids.
You read the measurements off the slate.
"The shoulder strap's secure."
"The left spar's straight."
"The hinge has one loose tooth."
Oliver's head comes up.
His face has gone the colour of the fog.
"Don't joke about hinges."
"You're becoming Ada."
He turns back to the machine.
"That wasn't an insult," you say.
"I know."
"You said one loose—"
"I was joking. Go and look anyway."
He goes and looks. It takes him six minutes. The tooth is sound.
"That was cruel," he says when he comes back.
"That was six minutes of you doing something instead of sitting in the dark thinking about a beam," you say.
He looks at you.
"You're becoming Ada."
"That wasn't an insult."
"I know."
On the wall the old telescope mount points up at the ceiling. Dust has settled in its gears.
A small gap in the dome shows the stars.
Oliver follows where you're looking.
"When I'm up there, I mightn't see anything," he says.
"You'll see cloud."
"What if it covers everything?"
This is the last question he will ask you from the ground.
"What if there's no edge?"
"Then you've found something."
He nods, as though you'd given him an instruction for the machine.

options.label: "Then come back and tell me exactly what nothing looks like."

beats.text: "That's not much of a report."

"It's more than anybody in this district has got," you say. "Nobody's ever been up. Nobody knows what the inside of a cloud does to the light. You'll be the only person I've ever met who knows a thing I can't get at, and I want it in detail, and I want it wrong the first time so we can argue."
He nods, as though you'd given him an instruction for the machine.
Near midnight, Oliver sits down beside your chair.
He hasn't asked you to sleep. He hasn't admitted that he's frightened.
He says, "What should I hear from you before morning?"

options.label: "Come back with an answer worth arguing about."

beats.text: "That's all?"
"That's the entire commission. One answer. Wrong for preference."
"And if I've nothing?"
"Then invent something and I'll catch you at it," you say, "and we'll have the argument regardless, which was always the point of the arrangement."
He almost laughs.

options.label: "If you fall, I'll still be here to insult you."

beats.text: He doesn't answer straight off.
"That's the only promise I can actually keep," you say. "I can't catch you. I can't run down the ridge. I can be at the bottom being unpleasant about your technique."
"That's worth more than it sounds."
"I know exactly what it's worth," you say. "I've been on the receiving end of nobody being there."

options.label: "Take Ada with you. Not the cap. Her whole impossible map."

beats.text: "I've the cap tied to the spar."
"That's cloth. I mean the rest of it. Eight hundred place names and a bridge behind an observatory and a girl who thought a river was drawn wrong and said so to a stranger."
He looks at the lantern.
"She'd have wanted the numbers taken up," he says.
"Then take them up. Every route she ever marked. Fly over the whole lot of them and come down knowing which ones were right."
"That's a great deal to carry."
"You're carrying it either way," you say. "You may as well get it airborne."
Oliver reaches for the brass box. He opens it and takes out the goggles' spare hinge.
"I didn't finish them for you," he says.
"I noticed."
"I thought you'd see what I saw."
"That's a dangerous wish."
"I know."
He turns the hinge in the lantern light. "I thought if you could see the distance, it'd be easier."
"Easier to do what?"
"Stay."
You touch the brass plate above your brow. The scratches in the lenses pull the room apart. The lantern doubles. Oliver's face turns up at the edge of both images.
"I have stayed," you say.
"Not because you had to."
"No."
"Not because you were trapped."
You look at the door, the steps past it, the road going down to the authorities.
"Those things can both be true," you say.
He folds the hinge back into the box.
The answer settles between the two of you.

textByOption.believe:
The answer settles between the two of you.

You told him, that first day in the alley, that you believed him. You've never once taken it back — not through the fall, not through the tunnel, and not tonight, with the ridge waiting and the fog not yet lifted.
textByOption.worry:
The answer settles between the two of you.

You told him, that first day, that he'd get himself killed. He's going to try it in four hours, and the old fear sits exactly where it always has, right under the ribs, and has never once been proved wrong enough to leave.
textByOption.honest:
The answer settles between the two of you.

You told him, that first day, that you weren't sure — and you said it plainly instead of choosing a kinder lie. He built three frames on the strength of a girl who wouldn't pretend. That is what your honesty turned out to be worth.

beats.text: At one in the morning, Oliver asks whether you want to go home.
"Which home?"
"The room."
"The window."
"The chair."
"You're naming furniture as though it were a family."
"It's what I know."
You look through the goggle lenses. The stars smear into faint lines.
There is one sentence you have never said in three years, to him or to anybody.
Oliver's hands go still.
You haven't said it before. Not about the chair, the roads, the authorities, or the machine.
"Of me falling?" he asks.
"Of you coming back."
He waits.
"If you come back unchanged, I'll have to find a way to be glad," you say. "If you don't come back, I'll have to keep a window open for somebody who isn't there."
Oliver looks at the ridge.
"I don't know how to answer that."
"Good."
"Good?"
"It means you heard it."

options.label: "Then let's name it properly. It's a room, a window, a chair, and you."

beats.text: He goes very still.
"That's four things," he says. "Three of them can't leave."
"Yes."
"That's what you're afraid of."
It's the first time in three years anybody has said the sentence for you.

"If you come back unchanged, I'll have to find a way to be glad," you say. "If you don't come back, I'll have to keep a window open for somebody who isn't there. Those are the two outcomes. There isn't a third."
"I don't know how to answer that."
"Good. It means you heard it."
He rests his forehead against the wooden handle of your chair.
He stays there a long time. You don't move your hand from the rim.
The fog lifts before dawn.
The plain comes up under the ridge, silver with frost. The bridge is visible. Past it, the hills go up into a bank of cloud.
Oliver moves the glider to the launch point.
The authorities see him. Lanterns start up the path.
He comes back and kneels beside the chair.
"I need you to hold the rope till the second gust."
"I know."
"Don't pull too early."
"I know."
"Don't let go because they shout."
"I know."
"If something breaks, I'll call."
"I know."
He looks at the goggles. "Can you see?"
"You're doubled."
"That isn't an answer."
"Neither's the sky."
He puts his hand on the arm of your chair.
"Thank you," he says.
He has said that twice in three years and both times it sounded like a door closing.
He takes his hand back.
"Say something you'll have to keep," you tell him.
"I'll be back before the frost goes off the reeds."
"That's better. That's a thing I can hold you to."
He looks up, surprised. He had a whole argument prepared for you.
"You're not going to say it's not finished?"
"Not this morning," you say. "This morning you may thank me and I may accept it, like two people in a story where nothing goes wrong."
He keeps his hand on the arm of the chair a moment longer than he meant to.
The cap's tied to the central spar. The red pencil sits under the belt.
The woman in the dark coat reaches the ridge.
"Oliver Wright," she calls. "Stand away from the machine."
Oliver climbs into the cradle.
The first gust hits the canvas and twists the wing. The frame holds.
You take the rope.
The woman says, "Monica. Don't do this."
You look at her through the scratched lenses. Her face splits into two pale figures, both wearing the same polished buttons.
The second gust is coming out of the east. There is time for exactly one sentence.

options.label: "You should have said that before the tunnel."

beats.text: She stops walking.
It's the only blow you land on her in three years, and you land it once, and you don't need to land it twice.

options.label: "Stand still and watch. You'll want to have seen it."

beats.text: "I am here to prevent it."
"You're here to write it down," you say. "You've been writing it down for two years. This is the page."
She stops walking.
You will find out, much later, that she did stand still, and that she did watch, and that what she wrote in the folder was not what she'd been ordered to write.
The second gust comes from the east.
The glider shifts.
Oliver looks back.
You hold the rope.
The authorities shout. The plain waits below. The cloud hangs over the hills with its lower edges going bright with the first light.
Oliver raises one hand.
The rope pulls against your palms.
You do not let go.
The second gust becomes a third.
The glider moves over the ridge grass. The skids rattle against the stones.
Oliver leans forward in the cradle with the shoulder brace tight across his chest.
The woman in the dark coat shouts for the constables to take the rope.
Your palms are already going. The rope is going to come out of your hands in about four seconds.
The chair jolts. Both wheels slide toward the drop.
You brace your feet on the stone and pull the crutch out from beside your knee.
Nine years of this chair being the thing that held you down, and here it is, finally, holding something else.

options.label: Keep it in your hands. You want to feel the moment it goes.

beats.text: The rope bites. Your palms open and the hemp goes through them and takes the skin with it.
You don't let it out. You wrap it twice round your right fist and put your back into the chair and take the whole weight of a flying machine through two hands and a bad leg.
It's the single most useful thing your body has ever been asked to do, and it is going to cost you both palms, and you would do it again tomorrow.
"Monica," Oliver calls.
"Fly."
The left skid strikes a ridge stone. The frame lurches sideways.
One constable reaches the rope and gets a hand on it.
He is nineteen at the most. His knuckles are white on the line.
He looks at you.
"That isn't a suggestion."
He releases the line.
The second constable catches it instead.
It stops his hands. It always stops their hands.
"Bell," he says, before he can help it.
"Bell. Two years ago a man called Bell told a boy the sky was private property. Was that you?"
"That's my uncle."
"Then let go of the rope, Bell, and be the better one."
He releases the line.
The second constable catches it instead.
The glider pulls hard enough to drag your chair forward.
Oliver reaches for the wing hinge.

The rope burns through your hands. The front wheel leaves the ground. Beyond the stone wall, the ridge falls away.

The woman grabs the second constable's shoulder. "Cut the line."

He draws a knife.

You speak before the blade reaches the rope.

"If you cut it, the glider turns."

The constable hesitates.

"The wind's crosswise," you say. "The frame will roll toward the crowd."

The woman looks down the slope. The authorities have gathered too close. A dozen people stand between the ridge and the plain.

"You are bluffing."

"I'm reading the wind."

Oliver shouts from the cradle, "She's right."

You keep your eyes on the woman. "Let the rope go together. Clear the slope. Or cut it, and explain why the first human flight became a falling machine aimed at your own men."

stakes.onSuccess: The woman raises her hand. "Release the rope," she orders. The constables obey, and the line falls clean across the grass.
stakes.onFail: The constable's knife finds the rope before the woman decides. It parts in a single stroke, and the chair's front wheel leaves the ground half a breath early. The glider lurches off the wall at a bad angle, canvas snapping taut too soon, Oliver thrown forward in the cradle before he is ready. It is still a flight. It was never going to be a clean one.

beats.text: Either way, the rope's off the axle and the glider's at the edge.
That's the only fact left on this ridge that matters.
The burn across your palms is bright and clean.
Oliver looks back at you. "Are you hurt?"
He is nine feet from the drop and he has turned round to ask about your hands.
"That isn't an answer."
"It's the one I've got."
It's the first time you have ever answered that question straight, in three years, in either direction.
He goes very still in the cradle.
"Go anyway, Oliver."
"I'll come back and see to them," he says, which is the most ridiculous sentence anybody has ever said on the edge of a ridge, and you will keep it for the rest of your life.
The wind changes.
The canvas fills from the leading edge to the tail. The ribs bend in sequence — not like a bird flapping.
Like a door opening into a room bigger than itself.
Oliver puts his head down.
The skids race.
You push the chair backward. The front wheel lands. The rear wheel strikes the wall. The jolt goes through your body hard enough to loosen the goggles.
The glider reaches the edge.
For one breath, Oliver is still on the ground.
Then the skids stop touching it.

The machine drops.

Oliver pulls the wing hinge. The central spar folds by one tooth. The glider noses down toward the plain.

The crowd screams below.

You cannot reach him. You cannot call him back by strength. You can only see, through the scratched lenses, a dark line where the right wing has begun to collapse.

"Oliver!" you shout. "Left brace!"

He turns his head.

"The shoulder brace. Pull the red strap."

He hauls the strap. The brace releases. His body shifts left. The damaged wing rises just enough for the wind to get under it.

The glider drops another twenty feet.

The canvas tears along the seam.

Oliver reaches for the hand lever by his knee — the one that opens the second hinge. His fingers miss it.

"Use your elbow!"

He strikes the lever. The wing opens.

The frame turns. The plain rushes sideways. The bridge flashes beneath him.

encounter.onWin: The wing catches. The frame turns, and turns true. Oliver rides it out over the bridge and does not fall.

beats.text: The glider rises ten feet, then twenty.
Oliver disappears behind the central spar. The cap tied to it snaps in the wind.
You grip the stone wall.
Below, the authorities run along the ridge. The woman's forgotten her umbrella. It lies open and empty near the launch point.
The glider doesn't climb like a bird.
It climbs like a thought somebody has refused to give up. Each gust hands it another piece of height.
Oliver turns the frame toward the western hills.
He passes over the bridge.
The plain gets smaller.
A shelf of cloud waits ahead of him, grey and bruised underneath. His glider is a dark mark against it.
Through the scratched glass there are two of him. Without it there is one, very small, very far.

options.label: Take them off. Then put them back on.

beats.text: Without them the distance loses its doubled edges and the machine becomes smaller.
You put them back on.
The lenses show two Olivers — one made of brass light and one of shadow.
Both rise.

options.label: Keep them on. See it the way he built it to be seen.

beats.text: The scratches take the light and split it. There are two Olivers up there — one made of brass light and one of shadow — and a doubled cap on a doubled spar.
It's a poor instrument. It was filed by a boy in a washhouse out of a plate that was meant for something else.
You wouldn't trade it for the observatory's telescope.
Both Olivers rise.
The glider enters the cloud.
The crowd goes silent.
Oliver vanishes.
There is nothing left that you can do with your hands.
One. Two. Three.
The cloud swallows the wing.
Four. Five.
You count out loud, on a ridge, in front of the district authorities, because a girl with a stolen surveyor's rule once told you she counted until she was safe.

options.label: Count. Say her name at every fifth.

beats.text: One. Two. Three.
The cloud swallows the wing.
Four. Five. Ada.
Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Ada.
The constables hear you doing it. One of them takes his hat off, which is nothing, which changes nothing, and you notice it anyway.
The woman comes and stands beside you. Her coat's wet through.
"He'll fall," she says.
You keep counting.
"The cloud's too thick."
She is standing close enough that you could take hold of her sleeve.
"Neither have you."
"That's why I'm not giving an opinion."
She hasn't got an answer. Nobody in the history of the district has got an answer, which is the entire point of the morning.

options.label: "Then watch him do it, and put that in the folder."

beats.text: "I write what occurs."

"Then write that it was a boy from the parish orphanage," you say, "and that he built it in a washhouse out of a school desk, and that a girl called Ada Pike found the route, and spell her name with an I."
The woman looks up at the cloud shelf.
"You have never once asked me for anything else," she says.
"No," you say. "That's the whole list."
At twenty, a shadow appears above the cloud shelf.
It isn't the glider.
The shadow grows wings.
Oliver rises through the top of the cloud.
The first human being to see above the clouds turns the machine in a wide, shaking circle.
Sunlight strikes the canvas. The dark seams go gold.
He's so high that the authorities have become small figures on a ridge.
You can see him.
He can see everything.
Oliver doesn't land until the sun has crossed the sky.
The glider comes down in the western plain, past the bridge, where the shepherd with the one-eared dog once told you the ground floods in winter.
The canvas is torn. One skid's missing. The cradle has held.
By the time he gets back up to the ridge he's walking badly and laughing at the same time.
There's something shut in one hand.
"What?" you ask.
He kneels beside your chair.
"There's another sky."
"I suspected."
"The clouds have an upper side."
"Did they?"
"They do."
He opens his hand. A small white feather lies on his palm.
It isn't from a bird. It's come loose from the glider's patched canvas, and the fibres are lit through with sunlight.
He is holding it out flat, the way he held out the first one, through a fence, when he was nine.
"I saw the edge."
He looks at the goggles. "Can you see through them?"
"Farther than before."

options.label: "That's the second feather you've given me."

beats.text: He stops.
"The first was a gull's," he says. "Off the coal store roof. You said it was a poor specimen."
"It was."
"This one's off my own wing."
"Then it's a better specimen," you say, and close your fist round it, and can't for a moment say anything else at all.
He looks at the goggles. "Can you see through them?"
"Farther than before."
The brass headpiece is finished before nightfall.
Oliver replaces the cloudy lenses with clear glass out of the observatory telescope.
He files the hinges smooth, adds a small wheel above the right temple, and fastens the leather without a single sharp edge on it anywhere.
When you turn the wheel, the lenses shift.
The bridge comes clear.
The western hills draw nearer. A narrow road behind the observatory appears where the old maps left nothing but blank cloth.
Past it, roads you have never travelled begin to separate out across the land.
The gamekeeper's daughter brings word up from the town.
Every gate will open to you now. No road will charge you. No known place will be closed to you.
The places hidden behind distance, and fog, and old maps are yours to reach.
You do not receive wings.
You receive the horizon.
Oliver sits under the window with the white feather between his fingers. Above him, birds cross the evening sky.
"Beyond that eye," he says, "what can you actually see?"
You turn the brass wheel. The farthest road comes into focus.
He doesn't ask what you mean by start.
He's already looking at the road with you.

options.label: "Eight hundred place names. And a bridge behind an observatory."

beats.text: He goes quiet under the window.
"She'd have wanted the numbers checked," he says.
"Then we'll go and check them," you say. "All of them. Every road she ever marked, and the ones she never got to."
"That would take years."
"I've got years," you say. "For the first time in my life I've got years and somewhere to spend them."
The city below stays crowded, and poor, and full of men who believe the world ends at the edge of their ledgers.
The sky has proved otherwise.
